Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What happens if trauma is not resolved?
Answer: If you were exposed to toxic stress for a long period of time, then the consequences will also last long and they can become a hindrance in your life. If the stress/risk/threat that caused the trauma was only one event, then the symptoms will disappear slowly but certainly. It will also depend on your level of resilience, and/or the way you deal with adversity. If you tend to worry a lot, or are normally fearful, you could stay traumatized for years. Many individuals “learn” to live with the disorder —whether PTSD or C-PTSD— and could have very functional lives even when they carry the burden of a system that is never well regulated, and therefore, never works in optimal conditions. That could appear as emotionality (emotional dysregulation), as disengagement and emotional numbness, as physical problems, or a combination of them. We were not aware of the phenomenon of trauma until relatively recent (the 1980s). People had no idea what was happening to them for decades, and all sorts of diagnoses were given to traumatized people, making them feel defective, mentally ill, depressed, anxious, bipolar, and so on. Those people either were medicated without much improvement, or learned to rely on being numbed by either legal or illegal drugs, alcohol, or emotionally draining relationships. Most of the time, people will not even give attention to their symptoms and just assume there was something wrong with them, and therefore, not deserving much. What I mean is that people can live with trauma for a very long time without clear dysfunction, but at some point, the system breaks, and many problems arise. Reading your question again, it may be the case that you are using the term “trauma” to refer to the situation and not to the disorder. In that case, if the traumatizing situation doesn’t end, the person just keeps getting sicker and sicker, and their nervous system gets more and more dysregulated. There is no healing of trauma (PTSD or C-PTSD) until the traumatic stress and the dangerous circumstances disappear.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Do therapists share their true feelings about their clients, even if they are positive?
Answer: One of the characteristics that make therapy successful is trust. Trust unfolds more easily when the client feels the authenticity of the therapist. The idea that everything a therapist does is solely in the client's best interest is idealistic. Therapists are not mind-readers or oracles who can predict exactly how a client will respond to interventions. The client’s reaction can depend on their mental state at a particular moment. One day, they might respond one way, and the next week, they might react differently. What the therapist says might be seen as flattering one day, inappropriate the next, and fantastic another day. You can’t be sure! Therapists need to be brave and willing to receive a negative response from the client. Otherwise, as I have seen with many therapists, they may not learn much about the client because they avoid taking risks. Being honest, objective, and authentic may involve having positive thoughts and feelings towards clients. This means that these feelings can influence how the therapist interacts with the client. Whether the therapist shares these thoughts and feelings with the client is a matter of timing and approach, but it is impossible not to reflect what we observe. Therapists are mirrors through which clients see themselves safely. If trust is already established, the client will not only accept the therapist's honest feedback as valid but also as a way to feel seen and understood without any hidden agenda.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Do many people have a headache/feel tired after therapy sessions (even if it wasn’t intense)?
Answer: Feeling tired, yes. Headache may indicate something else. Some therapies can trigger a stress response, especially while discussing challenging or sensitive topics, which could include physical symptoms like headaches. If your therapist is the type of inviting you to go over your worst experiences and remember details, it may be easy to experience a headache because of the effort of finding information that either is not really available, or is available but charged with negative emotions. The headache may be worse if there is a part of you that prefers not to remember. It may be great if therapists that were trained many years ago shift their approach to the understanding that therapy should not be about talking over and over about the negative aspects of life. We know life is full of challenges, and therapy should be about building up resilience and resources to get more and more skilled when the challenges come. When therapy is just about the negative stuff in the past or present, the client gets weaker and feels less able to overcome the difficulties. On the other hand, if during therapy, you naturally speak about emotional stuff, the emotions may activate your system and you will feel tired because of the extra energy that your system spends while activating that emotionality. Even the exercise of reflecting on what you discuss with the therapist can contribute to feelings of exhaustion since you are using your brain in ways that you may not be used to do. In general, the tension that some people carry during sessions whether it comes from the content or from the idea of therapy alone, could induce some physical discomfort, tiredness, and even headaches. Some people may even feel nausea, but that’s because they tense extremely. Therapy should be pleasant and manageable even when processing heavy material. Just relax and trust that you are there to grow and improve the quality of your life, not to make it more difficult.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is the Window of tolerance, and why is it important to therapy? How does someone identify their window of tolerance? Does it really play an important role in therapy?
Answer: The Window of Tolerance (WoT) is a very useful construct to explain how people’s nervous system develops certain level of immunity to strong emotions in order to function in the world. Imagine you live in a house where everyone frequently gets angry and yells at each other. Your system may adapt to this environment by becoming less reactive to yelling. As a result, you might not perceive yelling as a threat and therefore not activate your survival mechanisms. This adaptation means your window of tolerance is wider than that of someone who immediately feels shaken or endangered by others yelling at them. So, the WoT is a representation of that range where you can experience emotions without getting activated. When someone’s emotions move within the WoT, they can manage many circumstances without an extra toll to their system. Those that have a very narrow WoT, have more difficulties managing challenges, and even remembering certain aspects of their lives bring their system to the feeling of being under threat. So, widening the WoT of clients is extremely important in therapy, since that could facilitate the person’s nervous system to open space for healing. If session after session, just by remembering, the person feels overwhelmed, that client can be getting worse instead of better. Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is it possible to develop complex post-traumatic stress disorder (C-PTSD) later in life? If so, what are some common symptoms?
Answer: This question is important to answer because most people get it wrong. From what I have observed, most C-PTSD develops later in life. The traumatization may start early but the disorder may not develop until many years later. Many children living in stressful and toxic environments may begin to develop symptoms early, and their systems may be affected in various ways. However, the brain is remarkably adaptive, making small adjustments in the nervous system to help the child remain as 'healthy' as possible while continuing to develop. Complex PTSD (C-PTSD) arises when the nervous system loses its internal equilibrium, or to use the technical term, when it reaches allostatic load. This occurs when the cumulative stress and all the small changes get to the point of overwhelming the system's capacity to adapt, leading to a state of chronic dysregulation. Many times, kids develop well and have functional lives rewardless of the circumstances, but more stress later in life pushes their system to reach the point of dysregulation and that’s when we could say that the person suffers from C-PTSD. We may attribute the symptoms to what’s happening in the present, but it’s important to considered the circumstances the person went through early in life. It’s also possible that childhood had been good and not traumatic whatsoever, but that the adult lives in an extremely stressful environment, and that the stress doesn’t go away, or that threat comes and goes for a long time. That’s when people can develop C-PTSD late in life. C-PTSD doesn’t really depend on the time in life, but in the prolonged, repeated, constant, and intense stress that pushes the system to move into survival mode because that’s the only way for the brain to safeguard the integrity of that body. My book explain this issue at detail (Traumatization and Its Aftermath).

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How can I recall all the details from a bullying event 12 years ago with all the details? I used to remember it the first 3-4 years very clearly then I forgot it. Now when I try to recall I get mixed details and it's driving me nuts.
Answer: If you don’t remember the details is because the brain considered them irrelevant and deleted them. Why is not remembering driving you nuts? The brain stores information to help us adapt to the world. While you were being bullied and shortly after, the memories were vivid and accessible because it was very important for you to recognize bullies and avoid them. However, if you no longer remember the details or a lot of the information related to it clearly, it means that once you regained confidence and no longer felt at risk of being bullied, your brain deemed that information unnecessary and proceeded to delete it to make space for new information. You should actually be very happy. Not remembering is good news because it indicates you don't live in the past, there are not many triggers related to that experience, and you have developed trust, resilience, and confidence in your ability to set boundaries and stand up for yourself. Congratulations!

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What, if anything, makes a narcissist feel guilty?
Answer: Many people may think that pwNPD have a limited capacity for genuine guilt, but neurobiology and experience have taught me otherwise. It’t true that people suffering from personality disorders have an issue with the connection between their prefrontal cortex and their “heart” but this disconnection—due in part for the failure of the ventral vagus—is never absolute (unless they are ASPD). All the others PD, and probably NPD in second place after ASPD, have an intermittent connection with their higher order feelings, and with their emotions. In the moments they have a connection, they experience very painful emotions like guilt and shame, which propels them to disconnect again before they become “weak” and get “discovered.” pwNPD work hard to pretend they have no clue about the accusations they receive. When they are vulnerable, they risk “confessing” and accepting either that they were aware of their actions all along or that they are indeed bad people. Some authors call that splitting, but I prefer to use the term fragmentation because splitting is more related to the black and white mentality seen clearly in BPD. Narcissist are capable of seeing grays. I call it fragmentation because they have one or more parts that yearn to come clean and release the heavy baggage of guilt and shame. At the same time, other parts are fiercely protective of their 'kingdom,' whether it is large and powerful or small and relatively insignificant, but still their own labor. These parts resist any threat to their domain with great intensity and often cannot agree with each other. The parts that hide the guilt are exiled and largely unavailable, only emerging occasionally in search of respite, respect, and freedom. I find it sad that society so easily demonizes people. Once we assign a label and start publicizing the worst cases associated with it, we create additional shame for those who struggle to meet expectations. This not only hurts them but also drives them to hide more and lose faith in their ability to be considered good people. They may lose trust and hope in themselves, becoming even more distant from disclosing their suffering. In the end, we all bear the consequences of labeling and treating people with cruelty. So, yes, narcissists feel guilty because they know they hurt people, specially when they get confronted and realize the feelings of others. They are capable of feeling regret but stop themselves from showing it due to the fear of losing what they have been able to achieve by using the manipulative techniques they used more to survive than to harm. They develop those skills without the awareness of the consequences, and once they become aware, they may despise themselves, hide, retreat, and carry the guilt as a form of penance.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why do people like to change the way they look after being through a traumatic life experience?
Answer: Do they? I don’t think that’s a fair generalization. They may behave differently, but saying that “they like to change the way they look” sounds inaccurate. I have worked with hundreds of them, and I have never noticed people being too invested in changing their looks. Many people gain or lose weight, they may care less about their appearance, they may lose the sense of what’s appropriate or not, etc., but those would be consequences of their internal struggle more than an active interest of changing their looks. If you know someone that did, maybe you can share your experience to help us widen our repertoire of characteristics.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can you love someone and leave them? My ex girlfriend said we were too different and left though she said she "loved" me?
Answer: You may love chocolate, but if you have diabetes, you can’t eat it, right? When someone says 'I love you,' their true meaning may be unclear, as love includes a range of feelings: romantic or passionate emotions, physical attraction or possessiveness, familial or affectionate bonds, platonic friendship, practical and enduring commitment, obsession, emotional dependency, excitement, comfort, or unconditional and selfless care. Unconditional love is rarely practiced in human relationships. While we may not necessarily condition our love, it is challenging to navigate the world while accepting and caring for others without any expectations. In romantic relationships, loving unconditionally can be problematic, as it might involve prioritizing the other person’s needs over one’s own, which can lead to imbalance and potential problems. Even when we experience deep and positive feelings for others, we need to maintain self-care, which sometimes means acknowledging that a long-term commitment may not be feasible. There are many reasons why someone might leave a relationship, even if they wish they could stay. What I have learned over the years is that we can hold multiple feelings simultaneously. We are capable of loving someone while also fearing them or finding them unattractive in certain ways. It is even possible to love and hate someone at the same time. This is because we have various parts within us, and these parts can experience different emotions towards the same person. From your question, it sounds like your girlfriend has different parts within her that perceive the relationship in various ways. Some parts may believe that you are not compatible, while others enjoy your company and may even wish to stay. Ultimately, she listened to the parts that wanted to leave and had to suppress or negotiate with the parts that loved you, for the benefit of the whole system. Be grateful she didn’t stay. Eventually, the incompatibility might have become unbearable, leading to resentment. In such cases, people may forget that they once loved you and leave you feeling unlovable. At least you can find comfort in knowing that she will carry positive memories of you in her heart.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How do you cope with attachment, like a teacher attachment or your therapist?
Answer: The attachment we form with 'attachment figures,' such as teachers and therapists, often mirrors the attachment style we developed in childhood. If you have an insecure attachment style, you may form an insecure attachment with your teacher or therapist, which can lead to problematic dynamics characterized by stress, insecurity, or avoidance. That prolongs the emotional suffering you already had from childhood. If you developed an insecure attachment to your caregivers, it means they were inconsistent in meeting your needs. As a result, you had to adapt to a attachment style to manage the stress of their unreliability. This might have led you to develop habits such as frequently checking on their availability or dismissing them to protect yourself from the pain caused by their inconsistency. The goal of forming an attachment with a therapist or teacher is to address and resolve emotional issues, so it is crucial that this attachment is secure. A reliable attachment figure helps you feel confident and safe, knowing they are available if needed. However, this attachment should also promote independence, allowing you to make your own decisions, form relationships with others, and feel secure in the world. When someone 'suffers' or feels the need to 'cope' with their attachment to the therapist or teacher, it may indicate a failure on both sides to recognize insecurities and to provide each other with the freedom and pleasure of being connected. The dependent person might be expecting too much or not expressing their needs, while the therapist might be overstepping by doing too much and inadvertently removing the person's sense of agency, creating insecurity about the therapist's constant presence. So, you don’t have to cope! You have to develop confidence, trust, freedom, curiosity, and independence to enjoy your life. Your therapist or teacher should provide the security for you to feel safe.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Narcissists sabotage your achievements, yet seem to hate the dependent person you've become. Do narcissists like independent partners or dependent ones?
Answer: It depends at what stage on the relationship. If you are dating the typical narcissist, it sounds they are ready to discard you since you are using the word “hate”. If you have become dependent, and they hate it, that may mean they find you more like a burden than the person they need for them to look good and be great. It’s not only about being dependent or not, but about how you can still be of use to them in maintaining their image or their sense of grandiosity. If being dependent serves them, they will not hate it. They hate it if it doesn’t serve them. In general, narcissists like partners that help them look amazing, help them in their pursues one way or another and are capable to deal with the stuff they dislike or has the potential to distract them from shinnying. Imagine you are dependent but you still organize the most lavish parties for their friends. They will keep liking and needing you because you are still providing something they value. Now imagine you become so dependent you claim or feel that you can’t manage the finances of the house, or you gain weight, don’t like seeing people, and need them to make decisions about small things. That type of dependency not only distracts them but also create problems to their grandiosity. In that case, you lose value and they may begin preparing (even if only in their head), leaving you. It may be just a matter of time when you’ll find out they are already living their life without you. The other possibility is that you are under the leaving phase. If you are there, it doesn’t matter what you do, they will use it to blame you, make you feel inferior, and devaluing you as a preparation to either do whatever they want with you on the side, or to leave you for good. Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What goes through your mind if a client DOESN'T cry when it would otherwise be appropriate (talking about past trauma, etc.)?
Answer: I remember a client that was completely shutdown from his emotional experiences that used crying as an argument when I mentioned he seemed to be disconnected from his emotions. He said “I normally cry at the movies.” It’s very common to equate crying with experiencing emotions, but that’s not accurate. Crying may only manifest one or 2 emotions or may be a way to hide many others, but it’s not the only way a person can process sadness or similar feelings. It’s true that crying can facilitate emotional processing and help individuals work through complex feelings. But crying also serves as a form of social communication, signaling distress or the need for support from others, and maybe the clients are looking more for healing than just support. Also, crying doesn’t have the same meaning for everyone. People with high emotional sensitivity may predispose them to cry more easily for many different reasons like anger, and people with huge awareness of their emotions might find it harder to express themselves through tears and prefer words. Finding the message and the meaning of the emotion is more effective than crying. What I find more troubling is when someone cries because they are supposed to. I notice some people forcing their tears to seem, like you said in your question, “appropriate”. That seems to me less appropriate than not crying. When a client discusses something sad and I don’t see tears, I may assume they are processing the experience cognitively rather than emotionally. To activate the emotions connected to a memory, it’s essential to engage with specific details of the event, which allows the amygdala to become active. This activation can then facilitate the retrieval of emotions from the past that have been stored there. But if the person is just connecting to the story at a cognitive level, there have no reason to cry. In summary, as a therapist, I’m not expecting the client to cry. If they do, then instead of thinking about it, I become curious and I ask what’s going on. I may interrupt the narrative and focus in the emotion to see if we can find it’s message. Emotions bring information that are clinically important. When the emotion is “alive,” there is a window of opportunity to process it, find a new meaning, and reconsolidate the memory with the new meaning. That’s how you resolve many of the emotional struggles.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can anyone give me a list of phases of a narcissist relationship? What comes after that?
Answer: This is how I have observed pwNPD behave in terms of relationships. OBSERVING: They take their time to entice the target (or prey) once they found it. They observe their moves, their taste, their routines. They pretend to be uninterested but begin showing off around the prey. They showcase their charisma without direct engagement to allure them. APPROACHING: They initiate love bombing, showering the target with attention, compliments, and affection to create a sense of excitement and euphoria. GLAMORIZING: They present an idealized version of themselves to their target. They may showcase their achievements, connections, or material possessions to enhance their desirability and create an aura of success. The narcissist aims to charm and impress their target, making them feel special and privileged to be in their company. During this phase, they create a strong emotional bond by portraying themselves as the perfect partners and even mirroring the target's interests. NEEDING: During this phase, which may be the longest, they exploit their partner's empathy and compassion by portraying themselves as vulnerable or in constant need of support. They may create dramas or crises to keep their partner emotionally invested and to maintain control over the relationship. The narcissist expects their partner to prioritize their needs above their own, gradually eroding their boundaries and self-esteem. DISCARDING: Normally, people think that narcissists discard their partners suddenly or abruptly. However, what I have observed is that this phase can be prolonged. They want out, but they still need the relationship for various reasons. So, they withdraw affection, abandon their partner emotionally, and make them question their reality. This phase is filled with gaslighting, accusations, devaluation, abuse, and a lack of commitment, loyalty, accountability, or support. The partner is left to their own devices but remains under the illusion created by the narcissist that it’s their fault and that they deserve “punishment.” This phase is really hard for the partner because, normally, they are now aware of the narcissism. LEAVING: This phase is mostly ignored by most of the literatura. The narcissist knows they are “gone”, but want to leave with some type of power and protection. They will attempt to regain control and preserve their self-image as they prepare to exit the relationship. This is when the narcissist will try to create smoke screens out of fear of being exposed for their falsity, imperfections, “true nature”, and the low value they believe they possess. They may offer apologies, confess some wrongdoings, or express remorse in an attempt to appear as the "good person" and absolve themselves of any guilt. The narcissist might use sweet-talking, emotional pleas, or other forms of manipulation to convince their partner to maintain a positive image of them, even as the relationship ends. Regardless of the partner's response, if the narcissist ultimately depart, or when they understand is imminent, they will construct a narrative that portrays them as the victim. They may claim their partner made their life difficult or took away something that belonged to them, such as children, assets, or social status. In the end, the narcissist often resorts to bad-mouthing their partner, harboring resentment, and even hating the person they once shared a life with. This phase is crucial to understand, as it sheds light on the narcissist's true intentions and the long-lasting impact their behavior can have on their partners. Once you realize you are free, and can see them in their struggle, your new phase is of reconstruction of your damaged sense of Self.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: I have BPD, why can't I control my impulses even though I've recognized what they are and know when I'm spiraling?
Answer: That’s the first step! Once you develop more PFC “muscle” by practicing that awareness, you’ll be able to gain more control over your impulses. Impulsivity is highly connected to the slow response or inactivity of the prefrontal cortex and with the need to find some type of reward, which dopamine provides when the person acts impulsively. You may well know that BPD is highly correlated to lack of emotional regulation. The difficulty managing emotional responses and feeling easily overwhelm creates kind of a need to scape or find something that alleviates the unsettled state. That’s why the body reacts fast when it sees the “desired object” and the person feels the impulse to go get it. That could range from having a glass of wine to engaging in high-risk activities like racing a car. There is also a sense of urgency when people are caught in their emotional turmoil or experiencing intense anxiety. The brain is already activated, and the easiest response is to act; the problem is that this often involves little decision-making, resulting in a lack of awareness of the consequences. Now that you have developed the capacity to recognize these impulses, it’s important to incorporate the decision to pause, breathe, and reflect on the potential consequences. It’s actually more effective to reflect on these consequences when you are calm and to work on making them available as resources for when your emotional system becomes heightened. Once you have clarity on how much you want to avoid acting impulsively, you’ll be better equipped to access those insights, thoughts, or schemas when you feel the impulses arise. Practice, practice, practice, and one day you’ll find that you respond differently to your impulses.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: After being discarded by someone with borderline personality disorder, do they ever come back? Is there any hope?
Answer: We “discard” stuff when it’s useless, right? Well, pwBPD don’t discard their partners because they always need them one way or another, even if they are not together anymore. Imagine a pwBPD that dates someone for their money, but then, for whatever reason, the person doesn’t have money anymore or doesn’t make it available. Then, the pwBPD may end the relationship because there is no reason for them to stay. That doesn’t mean that they will completely disappear. pwBPD develop their sense of self in connection with who they have dated. Even when they end a relationship, they carry that person in their psyche as part of what defines them, and it’s not rare that they reach out, maybe not to date again, but “to be friends.” They need friends and they feel safer with people that already know their reactivity. It’s also the case that pwBPD date people for what they can contribute to their lives. If the contribution is done, they leave the “agreement” but not necessarily the relationship. They only completely leave if the person they were dated rejected them in an explicit and hurtful way, mostly by exposing them with others, but even in those cases, if they still need them, they will stay. So, to answer your question, I think it’s always possible that the pwBPD “comes back.”

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Do verbal abusers mean what they say when they attack you verbally?
Answer: I bet you have been angry and have said something you didn’t mean to say. Anger that becomes rage clouds our thinking and pushes us to “eliminate” the adversary one way or another. Anger’s job is to protect us from enemies, opponents, and actually, predators. When we are very angry, the frontal part of our brain doesn’t receive enough energy because the energy goes to our survival and we can’t think clearly. That’s why it’s hard to know the meaning of what we say under that type of activation. What we say means “protect yourself by “putting an end” to the threat you feel under. When you “go back to your senses”, you may regret what you said, or you may try to justify yourself to feel less bad about having lost your temper. That’s “normal”. That’s different from becoming a “verbal abuser.” A verbal abuser is someone who, whether they are angry as a form of protection or not, has learned to use words, voice volume, and even body language to control others and to put their garbage out. They abuse others to gain power, to intimidate, to avoid responsibility, etc. Verbally abusive individuals have the intention to gain control and do not care about the truth of their statements, whether they are true or completely false accusations. The meaning lies not in the words themselves, but in the intention behind them, and their aim is to hurt. Once someone has become an abuser, there is often little self-reflection or consideration of whether their behavior is hurtful. They have already justified their actions in some way and feel entitled to behave as they do. Other emotions, such as guilt or shame, may be lurking beneath the surface, out of their awareness, but at some point, they will have to face the consequences. Their unconscious emotions can lead to internal pain that may even manifest as physical pain. From my years of observation, I believe that no wrongdoing goes unpunished. Our own internal system holds us accountable.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What are some examples of distorted thinking in BPD?
Answer: The distortions are related to their level of insecurity in the relationship, in their obsessions, and in the level of splitting. I’ll give you some examples, but take into account that each person is different. They could get very impatient and imagine people are going to dump them for insignificant things. If they see someone crossing their arms, they may think they are boring them. If they don’t get a response from a text soon, they may imagine the other person is about to dump them. If someone laughs or smiles without knowing the reason, they may imagine that the laughter is about them or that they are being mocked for something they did. If someone is upset or in a bad mood, they will imagine they were caught on something they did wrong. If someone looks at them and smile as in flirting, they may imagine their pants are unzipped, or something is showing that “provoked” the advance. Issues related to sexuality are also very important, even if we rarely talk about them. Individuals with BPD may feel 'provoked' or ill desired by many people in various regular situations. For example, imagine someone is in a hospital wearing a typical gown with the opening in the back. They might think that the nurse provided the gown to see their backside; they may feel that a massage therapist is attempting to abuse them sexually; they might perceive a dentist's actions as 'penetrating' them orally; or they may recall a parent “exposing” themselves after taking a shower or when they were in their underwear.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Therapists, do you ever ask your client a question because you’re “just wondering”?
Answer: It’s not the same to just wonder if the client went to an expensive hotel in their last trip than to just wonder whether they enjoy their vacations. The information about the hotel may be pure curiosity and may provide little insight into the client’s experience. However, learning about their level of satisfaction with the vacation, the meaning the client assigns to the price of the hotel, and their capacity to experience enjoyment, contentment, or even happiness are all crucial pieces of information for the therapist regarding the client's mental state. That’s the difference between “just wondering” as an intervention versus getting information to satisfy the therapist personal curiosity. I’ll give you a practical example. Today, I was talking to a supervisee, and they mentioned that one of their clients seemed very tense during sessions. I asked if they had addressed it, and they responded that they were afraid of shaming the client. When people are in therapy, it’s important to recognize that there are certain topics they may be more sensitive about than others. As a trauma therapist, I know that many clients may feel easily judged, struggle with trust, and may have experienced criticism, shame, or guilt in the past. Therefore, the therapist must be cautious about how they ask questions. Asking a question like, 'I’m just wondering if you…' is a way to minimize the risk of shaming the client. If the therapist genuinely wonders whether the client is aware of certain things, such as tension in their body, they might say, 'I wonder if you feel tense or experience muscular pain around your neck frequently.' This approach invites the client to bring their awareness to the tension in their body without making too obvious what the therapist perceives. It’s also a way to make sure that what the therapist is correct or not. So, as a therapist I wonder a lot of things every sessions. If I notice that it’s just my personal curiosity, I don’t ask the question, but if I notice that I can expand my curiosity to add something that could be used for the betterment of the client, then I’ll ask.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why is developmental trauma disorder diagnosis not being discussed more?
Answer: Well, because the psychiatric community has blocked its inclusion as a formal diagnosis, and if there is no diagnosis, there is no way to use it as a foundation for research or further investigation. Dr. Van der Kolk and his colleagues within the National Child Traumatic Stress Network came up with a diagnosis to give ‘a home’ (their words) to the traumatization a child experiences while developing, and offered full criteria to be used for this specific manifestation of PTSD under the name of DTD. Some members of the group have spent years doing research that demonstrates the DTD validity. The proposed diagnosis overlap with—but extend beyond—those of PTSD; it asks for “children’s exposure to a) interpersonal victimization and b) primary caregiver attachment disruption,” and states that “these types of childhood adversity are more closely related to the complex symptoms involved in DTD than to PTSD”. DTD includes the effects of attachment ruptures, which is completely understandable to be packed together but in my view, that may be the reason it was not accepted. I prefer to separate the aftermath of traumatization during development and after attachment failure into two different syndromes. I imagine that the DTD proposition had to be all-encompassing to increase the chances of making it into the DSM, but more specificity in terms of symptom clusters will always help in better designing interventions. The proposed DTD diagnosis criteria (Ford et al., 2013) list the first criterion as “lifetime contemporaneous exposure to both types of developmental trauma: A1. interpersonal victimization: victim of or witness to physical or sexual assault or abuse, or witness to domestic/adult intimate partner violence; and A2. primary caregiver attachment disruption: prolonged separation from or neglect or verbal/emotional abuse by a primary caregiver. In my book I make a clear distinctions between the 2, and give a lot of attention to both. Having the injury of the separation from the mother (Attachment wound) apart from the injury of growing up in fear helps focusing on the root of the problem. Each issue cause specific symptoms. Development takes long and happens in stages, and therefore, developmental delays can be of a different kind depending on whether traumatization is continuous (affected in every developmental stage) or temporary (only in one or two stages). When the toxic stress is short-term and is followed by periods of calmness, play, and curiosity, the child may not show signs of dysfunction even when some seeds might have been planted that could germinate years later. That’s why it’s a good exercise to recognize areas where the child may have suffered delays and those where the kid thrived before jumping into the catastrophizing idea that they suffer DTD because they grew up with adversity. Each developmental stage has specific milestones and tasks and it has not been possible to create a box for all the different issues that could arise from abuse, or from neglect, or from other type of stressors growing up. That’s what I think. It’s so broad, that it may be a disservice to use a general term. Still, I’m with you in terms of discussing more about the developmental issues that are caused by early traumatization, the struggle of the kid’s system between surviving the environment or developing.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How do you know if you truly love someone or just want them?
Answer: John says he truly loves Lynn but when she doesn’t want to have sex, he gets angry, he mocks her often in front of the others, and corrects or criticizes many things she does. He also tries to please her with big gifts and expensive dinners and often brags about her qualities, especially with his family. What do you think That he truly loves her? or just wants her? In my head “true love” includes full acceptance of the person. When you truly love someone, you respect the person, enjoy their abilities, capacities, and freedom, and feel deeply connected even without words. You let them be and share their dreams, goals, and days. Wanting someone is more similar to the need to possess. When you want someone, you may have a strong physical desire or attraction to the person, maybe based on their appearance or charisma rather than a deeper emotional connection, and want to feel as if the person belongs to you. The feelings for someone you want may resemble infatuation or obsession, where the focus is on the idea of the person being yours than in the deep meaning of whole relationship. When someone wants a person instead of loving them, the feeling may come from neediness, and you may be looking for validation, comfort, or security from the other person without really wanting to do much or go deep into what the other needs. In general, relationships that are based on want instead of true love tend to be transactional, lacking commitment or long-term plans. They often involve superficial interactions, with little sharing of each other’s inner worlds. Such relationships can also be marked by possessiveness, emotional distance, and idealization of the partner. When you truly love someone, you may expect little because you feel satisfied and fulfilled with the feelings you have, with the trust you feel, with the respect and acceptance for the other. True love makes you selfless. You forget about the problems and limitations and enjoy the abundance of your experience. If you also share values, have open and fluid communication, enjoy physical connection and feel supported and motivated, then you probably would like a long term commitment. You may then have the capacity to appreciate each other and grow together. But let’s be real! It’s not easy to truly love someone without a certain level of expectation. Most of us operate on a continuum, where we sometimes have needs and sometimes accept what we receive. We may need certain aspects while accepting others. True love is sooooo special that it’s not easy to find. That’s why, most of the time, we make compromises. The key is to be aware of what you are willing to accept and what you cannot compromise on. Be true to yourself is a good start.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is it usual to feel panic or nausea when you miss a loved one?
Answer: You may be talking about having ANXIOUS ATTACHMENT. Since we are social beings, strong attachments to loved ones are necessary to feel safe in the world, to feel that we belong and that someone has our back. When we separate from someone significant, our stress response can be activated which manifests as physical symptoms, including a racing heart, nausea, or other gastrointestinal discomfort. This is especially true if the relationship is a primary source of comfort or security. Anxious attachment is a type of insecure attachment style characterized by fear of abandonment and a strong desire for closeness and intimacy. This attachment style often develops in childhood based when caregivers didn’t deliver the level of reliability that the baby needed. When the Kid experiences fluctuations in their caregiver's availability, support, and responsiveness, the inconsistency makes them feel uncertainty and insecurity in relationships. That’s what causes excessive worry about their partner leaving them or being unresponsive. When the partner is absent, it’s easy to experience intense emotions, including jealousy, anxiety, or sadness, especially in response to perceived threats to their relationship. The perception of not being loved enough may lead a person to catastrophize, creating mental images of their partner being with someone else or never coming back. This can be enough to provoke a panic attack, often accompanied by symptoms such as nausea. So, even when it happens for those that are insecure about the availability and reliability of their partners, feeling nausea or panic is extreme and should not be felt frequently. If it happens often, the person’s system may go through something that resembles complex traumatization and can end of having very negative consequences. If you are that insecure about your loved one, find out if it’s just your insecure attachment or if the person is reliving the insecurities you experienced as a child. If they are contributing, talk to them and find the way for them to help you developing trust and confidence they are there for you. If it’s only you, get help. You should not have that high level of insecurity.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: I feel the urge to share with my therapist the positive feelings I have for him and all his qualities. I think we could share a sweet moment of connection and strenghten our relationship. Is this a valid reason? Should I?
Answer: Did you ever see The Invention of Lying? It’s a very fun movie about a world where people don’t lie. Could you imagine how amazing it’d be to tell the truth without fearing consequences? There is too much fear in our lives because we are not used to the truth. Sharing positive feelings should be a normal experience for everyone. Saying you see qualities in someone else doesn’t mean you are expecting something in return, right? Or do you want to say those things with a clear expectation of getting something out of it? When I was a child I met a person that told me that if you try to find something positive in someone, you’ll find it. And if you focus on finding something negative, you’ll find it too. From that day, I’ll focus on seeing the positive and find many beautiful things. If I know that the person is able to receive it, I’ll share it. If I feel that it will not be well taken, I’ll keep it to myself and enjoy it anyways. A therapist should be able to take in your positive feelings and observations. I’m pretty sure it’ll be pleasant to know that their client has a good opinion of them. If I were you, I’d go for it. But again, I kind of live in the world where lies have not been invented ;-)

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is P.T.S.D. permanent?
Answer: PTSD is a diagnosis which means that it’s only a name. Diagnosis have a different criteria everytime the DSM gets modified. Those criteria is a set of symptoms that get reviewed because the psychiatric community learns something new about the disorder, or because they get somehow pressured by either the pharmaceutical industry or insurance companies. Diagnosis are basically design to medicate and to have a system for insurance companies to determine whether they will pay for services or not. So, P.T.S.D as a diagnosis is not permanent. If what you are asking is whether the posttraumatic stress symptoms are permanent, that’s a different story. Almost no symptom of a mental disorder is inherently permanent unless there is a biological issue like in the case of Bipolar. Otherwise, we can modify the way our brain operates. We now for certain that the brain has amazing plasticity and that never stops growing, which is what allows symptoms to be eliminated. The brain can be reprogrammed with work and well identified challenges. Whatever has become habitual for the brain that creates dysfunction should be targeted for reprograming. The brain develops habits to save brain energy for other tasks, and can develop new ones and replace old ones if it learns that the more functional is prefered by the mind. How does it know? Because the person may come back to the more functional option over and over again until the brain develops the new habit. Let’s imagine that the brain learned to react with aggression every time the person felt criticized. The person can start developing awareness that reaction with aggression is making their life difficult, and instead, decide to respond with a smile. After many times of practicing this new response, the brain will assume that it’s preferred over aggression and will automatically smile instead of responding with aggressiveness. So, yes, diagnosis can be removed if we work in reducing symptoms.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How many cheaters regret getting caught?
Answer: We have emotions whether we want to address them or not. For example, Lu has been caught several times. The first time, they felt devastated after losing their partner of several years. They had a great relationship, and Lu never thought that a casual sexual encounter with another person would break what they had. Lu became disconnected from their pain and emotions and felt freer to act in ways that were considered forbidden. They had other relationships, and they got caught too, but they felt “nothing.” Lu thought they could escape the horrible feelings they experienced the first time. Like having the cake and eat it too ;-) Getting caught has consequences because, unless you suffer from ASPD, you are going to experience fear, shame, stress, and/or other emotions, including regret—unless you learn that there are no consequences. If there are no consequences, then it’s not cheating because it’s like you got permission to do it, right? These emotions may not be in your awareness, but they are happening in your body. Your system will activate protections, assuming that you are somehow in trouble and possibly in danger. It’s not the cheating itself, but knowing that cheating is something you are not supposed to do. That’s why it’s called cheating. Playing around is the only synonym that is not penalizing, but if you are in a clearly defined monogamous and exclusive relationship, it is expected that you are not having sex or even romantic feelings for anyone else. Being caught may easily make your nervous system react by activating centers associated with fear and emotional processing. This response will trigger a mix of feelings, including disappointment and anxiety. The brain begins to reflect on past choices, highlighting the gap between what you hoped for and what actually happened. In this state, you may feel a rush of emotional intensity, as if a weight is pressing on you. This is your brain’s way of signaling that something didn’t go as planned, prompting you to think carefully about your decisions moving forward. If you are aware, as you process the emotional turmoil, you become more conscious of your actions and their consequences, which can ultimately guide you toward better choices in the future. However, if you ignore the emotional load after being caught, you may miss the opportunity to learn from the experience and improve your options in the future. But not only that! Failing to acknowledge feelings such as shame, guilt, or anxiety can result in an accumulation of unprocessed emotions, which may eventually manifest as increased stress or anxiety, leading to emotional outbursts or mood swings. When emotions are not processed, the body may remain in a heightened state of stress. This can trigger the release of stress hormones like cortisol, which, if sustained over time, can negatively affect both mental and physical health, contributing to conditions like anxiety disorders or depression. Some individuals may begin to disconnect from their emotions entirely, leading to a state of dissociation where they feel detached from themselves or their surroundings which can obviously damage the ability to engage fully with life and forming meaningful relationships. Unprocessed emotions are never a good idea. That’s actually what creates most of our emotional issues. So, hopefully cheaters regret being caught, and cheating.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is cheating a man's nature?
Answer: A man’s as in males? Well, there are anthropological factors that can play a role here. In many species, females have limited days of fertility each cycle, and when they are ovulating, they may actively seek out a male for procreation. As a result, males often engage in elaborate displays or “dances” to be chosen as a mate. This biological characteristic leads to a scenario where males are "available" for mating year-round, while females are only interested during specific times. I once heard the saying that "there is no man strong enough to resist the advances and insistence of a woman." While I don't fully agree with this notion, it prompted me to reflect on this primitive aspect of male behavior. However, as humans, we possess a brain that enables us to understand rules, consequences, and the importance of commitment. While it's true that many behaviors can be traced back to our primitive tendencies, that does not justify them. For example, we might feel instinctual urges for dominance or aggression, but those impulses do not excuse violent behavior or infidelity. So, the answer is NO; cheating is not in men’s nature. Humans have a unique capacity to establish cultural, social, and individual norms, as well as agreements for when those norms are violated. For instance, many cultures place a strong emphasis on fidelity within marriage, creating social expectations around commitment. It is also part of our consciousness to recognize when an action is harmful to others. This awareness allows us to make ethical decisions that prioritize the well-being of those we care about. While our primitive instincts may drive certain behaviors, we can choose to act or not in the interest of maintaining long-lasting relationships. Our primitive tendencies should not be used to rationalize unethical actions, especially when boundaries have been clearly established. Ultimately, it is in our nature to desire peace and harmony in our interactions and in our lives.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is soul loss and how is it connected to complex ptsd?
Answer: Even when the term “soul loss” belongs more into the spiritual world, psychology and neuroscience can explain it. I think the term, which has existed for a very long time, was used to describe a type of dissociation. In several indigenous cultures, soul loss is understood as a state in which an individual's spirit becomes fragmented or "leaves" the body. The term often emphasizes a deep, existential sense of disconnection that occurs suddenly and manifests as a lack of vital essence. In psychology, soul loss can be interpreted as a manifestation of dissociative symptoms, where a person's sense of self becomes fragmented or disconnected. Since dissociation is increasingly linked to trauma, it is easy to see the relationship between the two concepts. When someone suffers the type of dissociation where the person shuts down or collapses emotionally, they may look as if they have lost their soul. The brain is working so slow, and with a few functions operating normally, than the eyes lose their presence. However, I believe it’s easier to see soul loss with PTSD than with C-PTSD. Why? Because soul loss is often associated in spiritual contexts with a sudden change in the individual, similar to the disconnection from reality or from one’s body following shock or a severe traumatic event. Of course, individuals with C-PTSD also experience fragmentation of their sense of self, and deep states of dissociating from their bodies, surroundings, and emotions leading to feelings of disconnection or emotional numbness. I can see how they may appear so absent that others might interpret it as if their soul has left their body. In the context you are using in your question, which comes from times of superstition, I wonder if someone with C-PTSD may be perceived as more "soulless" than someone who has lost their soul due to pain. Do you understand what I’m saying? Since C-PTSD, especially when it begins in childhood, may be difficult to identify as a consequence of their circumstances. It is more common to attribute the symptoms of C-PTSD to the individual's nature rather than to the conditions in which they grew up. Soulless people are thought to be born like that, and we know now that’s not possible, but it’s possible to have kids so disconnected because they carry the pain of the failure to attach to someone that find them valuable.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What happens when you criticise a borderline?
Answer: By the third month of dating Ben, who had BPD, Jenny was having dinner at his apartment. They were enjoying a romantic moment when she asked, “Where did you buy the chicken?” Suddenly, Ben erupted in anger. He grabbed her plate, threw it in the garbage, and shouted, “Don’t eat garbage! Get out! You’d be better off eating somewhere else!” He then pulled her by the arm, opened the door, and forcefully pushed her out of his apartment. The most important point I want to make with my example is that Jenny didn’t criticize Ben at all; however, he felt criticized for some reason and couldn’t handle it. As a therapist, I could see more clearly what was going on. Jenny happened to earn more money than Ben, who grew up poor and was accustomed to buying bargains. He had bought the chicken at a very inexpensive supermarket, on sale, and he interpreted her question as an attempt to highlight their economic differences. Jenny had no idea but he experienced a trauma reaction and because his low tolerance, he overreacted. It was all in his head, of course, but how could Jenny have known? When someone has experienced criticism, rejection, or invalidation—common in the upbringing of those who later develop BPD—they not only become highly sensitive to criticism and rejection but also relive the accumulation of past negative emotions when something similar occurs, even if it’s just an interpretation or connected to one of their insecurities. This makes it almost impossible for them to differentiate between what is happening in the present and what happened in their past, or what’s actually true versus what they experience as true. We know that pwBPD have serious problems regulating their emotional responses, which often leads to intense, unpredictable reactions that later make them feel ashamed. The shame is so overwhelming that it feels easier to pretend nothing happened rather than explain themselves. They may feel incapable of articulating what’s going on when they react this way. The internal turmoil they experience can create a sense of helplessness, where articulating their emotions feels impossible. This fear of not being understood or accepted can lead them to believe that the relationship is irreparably damaged, deepening their sense of isolation and rejection. So, criticism or feeling criticized can end a relationship.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Are there any potential dangers for clients in therapy?
Answer: Many more dangers than we wish! What I have heard from clients after they had a bad therapy experience could sound like this: I. “My therapist said many times that I was like family to her but when my mother was ill, she didn’t even visit. When I asked her why she had not come or showed some interest in me, she responded very defensive and said that she had many more clients to attend and that she didn’t like hospitals. She broke my heart! ” II. "I felt completely unseen when my therapist used my deepest fears against me. He knew how bad my fear of abandonment was and yet, he made me feel as if I was a burden every week. One day he even said ‘it's only a matter of time before your partner leaves you, just like your parents did, because it’s so difficult to deal with you’. I was devastated and when I complained, he finished treatment!” III. “Once, I expressed feelings of uncertainty about a changing jobs and my therapist right away stepped in with great advice, telling me how I needed to follow her guidance on the decision. She said I didn’t have the skills to make a good choice on my own. I followed her advice and everything went great! But at some point, I noticed that while working with that therapist, I always felt incapable of making decisions without her input. Whenever I faced a challenging situation, I became paralyzed with fear until I talked to her, but if I reached out between sessions for guidance, she got mad or ignored me.” I could give you more stories but let’s go over the 3 I used as examples. The danger depicted in the first example is disappointed. The client had high expectations about the relationship with the therapist. We can’t blame the therapist fully, but we have to accept that the therapist made a mistake not understanding the effect that calling the client “family” was going to have in her. The therapist knew that becoming too close and going to the hospital ay be a boundary violation, but in words, the therapist had already violated a clear limit by making the client believe they were closer than they could be. In the second example, the danger is vulnerability. When someone feels that sharing some of their information is equivalent to “getting naked” in front of the other, they become hypersensitive and any comment may feel like criticism, disapproval, or an attack. That’s why it’s not good to open up right away, before knowing the communication style of the therapist. What the therapist said made the client feel exposed, judged, The third example is the clear danger of developing dependency. When the therapist plays the role of the parent and wants to help resolving the life situation of the client, the therapist unconsciously may be removing agency from the client. On top of that, the advice was good in the example, but sometimes the therapist can give a misguided advice that goes wrong and the client is the one paying the consequences. Other risks are re-traumatization by using the wrong treatment, by intervening too soon, too hard, or lacking a thorough understanding of the methods employed. Ethical violations, unnecessary emotional distress, wrong diagnosis, confidentiality breaches, or even invalidation—whether intentional or with the best of intentions—are also risks that client go through during therapy. However, the benefits of therapy generally outweigh these risks. Every activity we engage in carries some level of risk. We can’t avoid life simply because it’s not entirely safe. The beauty of therapy is that even obstacles or challenging moments provide opportunities for growth.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can being a people pleaser make you a toxic person?
Answer: I know a woman who frequently described her husband as "toxic," and eventually announced she was getting divorced, claiming his toxicity was "killing her." Curious about her use of the term "toxic," I asked her what she meant. Here’s her story: “A few years ago, my computer started failing frequently. Frustrated, I bought a new one, but it failed in exactly the same way. I took it to the store, where after several tests, they suggested it might have been exposed to radiation. We discussed possible sources of radiation, but I couldn't find anything in my home that seemed problematic. The computer kept malfunctioning. On a subsequent visit to the store, the technician noticed my ring and suggested it might be the source of the issue. Apparently, many diamonds are radiated to remove impurities and enhance their color. I removed the ring, and immediately, the computer started working properly. That’s when I realized my husband was like that ring—his negativity was radiating out and affecting me. He was “radioactive” and the source of all the malfunction in my life. That’s the best way I can describe it.” Her explanation might not be scientifically precise, but it illustrates how some people can be so emotionally charged with negativity that their presence can affect others' well-being. In many other contexts, I have noticed that when someone says toxic, they also describe individuals whose behavior negatively impacts others' emotional well-being but also for those who exhibit traits or behaviors that are consistently harmful or damaging to those around them. On the other hand, the term "people pleaser"— more common and accepted in the psychology world and self-help discussions— describe individuals who prioritize pleasing others and seek approval, often at their own expense. I don’t think people pleasers could be considered toxic. They avoid conflict, they take on too many responsibilities, they may struggle drawing boundaries, but they don’t aim to harm others or carry a malicious intent.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Do you think it is possible for an adult who is a sociopath, resulting from childhood trauma, to change? I'm currently getting my MSW. Presently, I'm learning about trauma and the impact it has on children. I'd love to hear your input!
Answer: I wonder how you got the diagnosis. It’s not even a diagnosis anymore, and therefore, a psychiatrist could not give it to you. You may get an APD (Antisocial Personality Disorder) but not sociopathy. But lets assume that you got it from the previous criteria, before it was discontinued that was: Have you read the Confessions of a Sociopath, by M.E. Thomas. Did you identified with her? I hope you do not meet the criteria for ASPD. It’s a serious disorder often resulting from severe, constant, repeated, and intense physical, emotional, sexual abuse or most probably, a combination of them. This might involve living in fear due to parental drug use, access to or use of weapons, aggression towards you or loved ones, or other seriously threatening circumstances that affected the way your brain grew., and that adapted by not caring about anyone but your survival. Developing sociopathy implies significant underdevelopment in brain areas involved in decision-making, emotional regulation, and social behavior. One contributing factor is the lack of activity in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), which can lead to almost complete disconnection from the neurons that connect with it. Other areas of the prefrontal cortex would also need to be compromised for sociopathy to develop. It remains a mystery why certain brain regions, such as those involved in emotional regulation, become disconnected while others, like those responsible for cognition, remain intact. For instance, individuals with ASPD may exhibit high levels of intelligence and cognitive ability but struggle with forming social connections. One possibility is that dysfunction of the vagus nerve’s ventral branch could contribute to this issue, leading to an inability to establish social bonds due to a persistent sense of unsafety. But assuming you meet the criteria for sociopathy, and to answer your question, healing from sociopathy is theoretically possible. If sociopathy results from neural disconnection, it's always possible to form new synapses from the existing neurons, even in areas related to compassion, impulse control, empathy, concern for others, and understanding of consequences that were underused. The key to improve the symptoms of sociopathy would be to reprogram your brain. This involves stimulating underactive regions, such as those involved in empathy and impulse control, and modulating areas that may be overactive. Regularly engaging in mindful exercises to develop the prefrontal cortex (PFC) should become part of a daily routine to see progress. Reprogramming the brain requires more than just weekly therapy sessions; it demands full determination, commitment, and discipline. While challenging, it is certainly achievable with consistent effort.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can romantic love affect PTSD? If so, how?
Answer: Even when it may sound strange to you, knowing that someone has PTSD says very little to me. A diagnosis doesn’t give you the whole picture about a person. Some people get assigned the diagnosis after reporting a large number of symptoms and long years of insecurity and threat, while others get assigned it after a car crash with no casualties. Some people may have received the diagnosis many years back or yesterday. There is a big difference between the symptoms that unfold right after the traumatic event versus the symptoms developed through years of unresolved trauma. On the other hand, romantic love could go from just temporary infatuation to life-long commitment/passion/intimacy/selflessness. Not everyone love the same way or has the capacity to go in all the way loving a person. Then there is the other question: Does the person that is romantically in love with the PTSD person knows the diagnosis, the roots, the symptoms, and what it implies to deal with that person? Are they wanting to fix them, or it’s more like a sacrifice thing? There are many people that fall in love for the wrong reasons. Having said that, working with couples has provided me with a unique insight into how trauma affects relationships. Whether one or both partners have experienced traumatic events and their aftermath, the search for safety is always part of what we crave to find in a relationship. Love is always a medicine if it provides safety. But it is also well-known that trauma affects individuals neurobiologically, psychologically, and socially, leading to trust issues, difficulty with boundaries, fear of intimacy, and a need for control. We often overlook how trauma specifically shapes relationship expectations. Research indicates that couples in which at least one partner has experienced trauma are twice as likely to report relationship dissatisfaction. That may come from the fact that people with PTSD are commonly emotional numb, irritable, and have difficulty trusting others which strain romantic relationships and lead to misunderstandings or conflict. But it’s obvious that a supportive and understanding romantic partner can provide a sense of security and comfort that may help the individual with PTSD to deal better with stressors and find a sense of safety and belonging that could be absolutely positive for their healing.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is it okay to want to forget about childhood traumas instead of addressing them in therapy?
Answer: I say jokily that our brain is dumb but it’s really not a joke. If you try hard to forget something, your brain will believe it’s important to remember it. Of course it is OK to have the desire and even the determination to not bringing into your awareness something painful, but it’s not as easy as it sounds. There are several reasons for this: When you actively focus on trying to forget something, your brain is actually paying a lot of attention to it. This attention makes the memory more salient and strengthens its neural connections. The more we think about something, even with the intent to forget, the more we reinforce its presence in our cognitive landscape. The brain uses repetition and rehearsal to encode memories. When you attempt to forget, you are repeatedly engaging with the memory, either directly or indirectly. This repetition makes the encoding and retrieval pathways stronger, making the memory harder to erase. Memories associated with strong emotions are often harder to forget. If you're trying to forget the memories from events in childhood that are loaded with fear, horror, and pain, the emotional intensity will make these memories to be more irremovable and even more negatively charged. This happens because when we try to forget something, we may be remembering more details than necessary, opening the emotionality connected to the memory. Once the emotionality is open, we can feel flooded, and making the negativity of the emotion grow. But there are ways to do this without the risk of making the memories to become even more disturbing. The secret is to avoid details. A good therapist knows how to pace the disclosure of the traumatic occurrences in a way that doesn’t make the brain believe you are at risk again. It needs to be slow and timely. The way I work, we don’t bring any information from the traumatic events until we are ready to process them and to transform their meaning. Once the client is ready, I know their brain has many possibilities to find regulation and safety in a short amount of time.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can a person change from being emotionally unavailable to becoming more available and loving, or are our core personality traits fixed and unchangeable?
Answer: Is it emotionally unavailability or is it love language lost in translation? Being emotionally unavailable is not a personality trait. It’s more like a condition or state. When someone is emotionally unavailable, they may not have the ability to have emotional intimacy, engage in meaningful emotional connections, or express their emotions openly due to the need to protect themselves. People that are emotionally unavailable were not born that way. The avoidance is normally a defense or protection after having suffered something traumatic, because they become afraid of being vulnerable, due to issues with their attachment style influenced by early relationships, or even temporary stressors. Emotional availability can fluctuate based on circumstances. For example, someone can become emotionally unavailable after receiving a negative assessment of their emotionality (a break-up, criticism, etc), after becoming emotionally numb as a way to disconnect from suffering (abusive relationship), or after putting much bigger value to certain aspect of life over psychological issues (career versus romance). Someone can also be emotionally unavailable to certain people and not to others. For example, an older professor can become emotionally unavailable when teaching but emotionally available when dealing with people their age; a priest or even therapists are emotionally unavailable with their clients to maintain a professional distance. I wonder from your question is you are calling “emotionally unavailability” to being emotionally reserved or introverted. Those may be more like traits and perceived as unavailability even when those individuals experience a full range of emotions, just not expressing them externally. Change is always possible, and the journey to becoming more emotionally aware and expressive depends on understanding and addressing the underlying reasons why a person may have become less in touch with their emotions or less able to express themselves fully. By exploring and resolving these barriers (through self-reflection, therapy, or other forms of support), everyone can develop whatever necessary to reconnect with their emotions and communicate them more effectively. Since “being loving” may mean different things to different people, it may be necessary to “train” your person to use your love language. Even when not being demonstrative may be a trait, everyone can learn to act differently.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is it acceptable to date someone who is legally married but separated and living apart from their spouse?
Answer: Marriage is a commitment that becomes official with a legal document but deep down, the legal document doesn’t make the relationship more or less committed. When someone is not committed anymore, and goes onto recovering their freedom, moves away, and starts their new phase apart from the spouse, they may consider themselves practically “divorced” even if the legal process has not been finalized. There are several reasons for the legal divorce to be delayed, many of them pragmatic, but if the person you are considering dating has emotionally moved on from their marriage, and is genuinely working towards finalizing their legal married status, there may not be real reasons to see dating them as unacceptable. But of course, we have to consider the weight of the word “acceptable.” Your community may have a lot to do with your decision. If you are highly religious, and for you marriage is a sacred institution, it may be unacceptable for you and your values to date someone that is still married under that church. For many people, it’s unacceptable to date someone who’s church does not accept divorce. That’s up to your values and the values of your community. In my personal view, we should not live our lives based on seeking acceptance from others for our decisions. We should be the ones assessing whether something is acceptable for us or not. Other people may offer opinions on what is acceptable or not, but they likely do not know the person you are considering dating or the nuances of your relationship. The decision ultimately should seem acceptable to you. Dating someone that was previously in a serious relationship has its issues and risks. If the previous relationship doesn’t seem “final” to you, whether there is a paper that says it’s over or not, you may have to deal with more stuff that you should consider. It may be more important than the legal document. I know many people that get legally divorced and are still emotionally connected to their ex. Nobody warranties you that the person you are dating is emotionally available, ready to fall in love again, or if it’s warded, hurt, numb, desperate, unavailable, jaded, or still holding on to their previous romantic partners.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is the impact of experiencing flashbacks on a person's mental state? What occurs in the brain during a flashback?
Answer: The same as experiencing nightmares. The impact can be small or huge, depending on how scared the person still is after experiencing something scary. Imagine someone was assaulted at gun point during a trip. Their brain stored the face of the attacker in their memory in such a way that wants them to remember it as a way to alert them the attacker is a dangerous person. That’s why the face of the attacker can come up to awareness unannounced and unsolicited. That’s what a flashback is, a brief but intense remembering (and maybe re-experiencing) a past traumatic event. Flashbacks engage the brain's sensory and emotional processing neural circuits, activating the same areas of the brain that were activated during the original traumatic experience. While flashbacks can activate some of the same neural circuits that were involved in the original traumatic experience, it's not the same level of intensity as the full survival cascade response. The most common flashbacks are visual, but they could also be olfactory, auditory, or tactile. So, in my example, the assaulted person may see the face of the attacker everywhere, at anytime, several times a day. As time goes by, the intensity of the “warning” diminishes, and they see the face les and less. That’s the normal life of these types of memories unless the person re-engages with the trauma response and reacts with fear. Let’s see the 2 scenarios about the effects that the flashbacks can have: 1. one where the person has recovered confidence that the chances to even meet the attacker again are very low because they don’t live in the same place, and find safety by carrying a pepper spray with them. 2. the other possibility is when the person has developed the fear of being assaulted again because they are an easy target. Person 1 may understand that flashbacks are intrusive and disturbing but they find ways to feel safer and to regulate their reactions. Their fear diminishes and becomes “normal”, meaning within their tolerance. For these type of people, flashbacks are not as impactful. Person 2 may react to each flashback with the same of more fear than when they encountered the attacker. Their brain may assume that they are being attacked again and again, and will continue running the survival mechanisms trying to protect their life. Hence, the flashbacks will not dissipate, they may even increase, and other flashbacks may add to the ones of the face.
