Other symptoms may increase in number and intensity and the whole system will get altered, until maybe, the person becomes dysfunctional. The new symptoms may not even be related to the attack. These type of cases stop trusting everyone, they may dissociate and/or become numb, they may isolate themselves to avoid people or risks, etc. The traumatization keeps going even when there is no imminent threat and at some point, they may develop a trauma disorder. In this cases, flashbacks are triggers of traumatic memories and of survival mechanisms, as if they were at risk again. Anyone can be like type 1 with awareness, help, and development of resources. Trauma is not and should not be a life sentence.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What are the symptoms of narcissistic abuse?
Answer: Lisa married recently. Her husband has NPD but she has not realized it yet. Let’s say that they are still in their honeymoon phase, and maybe that’s why she is still handling his manipulation with humor. For others, it’s becoming evident that her responses are less joyful, and that she is starting to show behavioral changes and psychological issues. He is already doing all the typical: love bombing combined with gaslighting and objectification, but he also belittles her at every step, diminishing and contradicting her arguments with sarcasm in front of others. Lately, she has been asking him about their finances because he has 100% control over the money even when he claims that everything he owns is hers. He’s also controlling her friends, isolating her from her regular activities and from her family with excuses about his surprise dinners, his hobbies, his trips, etc. It’s clear that he wants her to be totally dependent on him. She has not noticed either how he’s already projecting his insecurities on her. The other day they went to a party and a friend criticized something he said. Once they were alone, he said: “Did you notice how he disliked your dress? and he was making fun of how you were eating.” She was completely flabbergasted but obviously believed him. Why would he say something like that unless he believed it? Because they are still at the beginning of the relationship, he has not had anger outburst or have tried to intimidate her, but could happen soon. The other day she didn’t want to have sex and he first offered her a foot massage in exchange, but when she said no, he said “it really doesn’t matter much. You are not that great in bed anyways.” Imagine how she felt. her response? She had sex with him almost every day after the comment, trying to be better lover. So, what symptoms do you expect Lisa to start developing? First, she will develop insecurities she didn’t have, her self-esteem will start draining, and she will question herself, her taste, her abilities, and at some point, even her sanity. From the insecurity, fear and stress will start draining her internal resources and resilience until she sees reality trough the eyes of the husband, probably internalizing the criticism and coming from her limitations. She will continue blaming herself, like what she did after the sex comment, and may develop negative self-talk, shame, and distrust of others. If the relationship continues and he gains control over her mind, she may probably develop fear, which will activate her autonomic nervous system until it may shift into survival mode. That means that she will have all sorts of physical, medical, and psychological issues due to the dysregulation of her nervous system. She may even dissociate for good or for bad, which means that she may stop feeling joy or other positive emotions. By then, she’ll be convinced of her lack of worth, and may even develop a trauma bond. She may do everything posible to gain his love again, and will numb her awareness even more to the abusive tactics he’s using. She’ll lose her boundaries, and will allow almost anyone to maltreat her, resigning more and more to have her needs met. Depending on the level of narcissism the husband has, and the duration of the relationship, Lisa can develop all sorts of symptoms that are characteristics of complex PTSD. Her support system could play an important role on her health; if she has a good one, she may stay more connected to reality and may notice the abuse. But if she is kind of isolated, she may not find her way out of the emotional dominion. That’s why pwNPD try so hard to keep their spouses separated from others’ “bad influence”, meaning witnessing, noticing the abuse, and advising them out. Remember that it’s very common that the abuse ends not when the abused wants, but when the narcissist finds their new supply and discard the previous one. In this case, Lisa.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is dissociation in BPD?
Answer: At the beginning of a relationship with someone suffering from BPD, it may seem cute how “adaptable” they are. They can be serious and formal, but also playful and childish. They can have a conversation with all sorts of people. They see the best on you, admire your qualities, are able to “read” you like no other, and they even start behaving like you in more than one way. Everything goes well until they start finding flaws in you, your friends, or in anything you do together. The typical but always surprising shift from 'Dr. Jekyll' to 'Mr. Hyde.' I have observed that they get exhausted from always trying to adapt, and they let their “tired” part have a role. They may not be evil or completely extreme to the adaptive one, but they definitely have different personalities. This fluctuation is the most important “dissociative” stamp of BPD. It’s normally called “splitting.” Splitting is evident in BPD as the tendency to view oneself and others as either all good or all bad, with little room for shades of gray or ambivalence. For example, they may idolize you one moment (viewing you as perfect or wonderful) and then demonize you the next (seeing you as entirely bad or evil). They can’t hold both views of you because their brain circuits that assimilate each are not connected. They are dissociated and they have been since they were infants because their main caregivers were not consistent and their brain had to separate the love for them from the fear or anger towards them. Splitting can be seen as a behavioral manifestation of B&W (Black and White) thinking, another characteristic of the disorder. This way of rapidly switching between extreme positive and negative evaluations is mostly a cognitive distortion, but also relates to the way their brain works, separating realities in their head and having problems connecting them, clear sign of dissociated circuits. Other manifestations of dissociation, such as compartmentalization or derealization, are not unique or different for people with BPD. They may experience these manifestations of dissociation like anyone else, and not all individuals with BPD experience them. Another significant aspect that may be more apparent is feeling uncertain about their identity, values, or goals, which often accompanies the pervasive sense of inner emptiness or confusion that many individuals with BPD experience. Some argue that this lack of a stable sense of self can also be attributed to dissociation. Some authors propose that because during the early life, their brains may have been preoccupied with survival, potentially neglecting other developmental needs and suffering dissociative experiences, such as depersonalization and identity alteration. In those cases pwBPD may suffer further complicating with their sense of self, contributing to their psychological challenges.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What are some signs of childhood trauma that may go unnoticed?
Answer: Let’s use Mikey and Pam as references. Mikey grew with addicted parents that had no time, energy, or wiliness to care for him. He basically raised himself: had to go out and look for food, clothes, etc. He kind of put himself to school but had to learn how to make money before he was 10. He was malnourished, neglected in every sense, didn’t have kids around to play with or adults to trust. Pam is the same age but was raised by very religious, abusive, cruel, and sadistic parents. She was overprotected but also severely punished, sometimes to the point of making her sick to her stomach or causing inexplicable fevers. While she was cared for, she also faced constant criticism and demands regarding the goals she needed to achieve. No matter how well she did, her parents were never satisfied or approving of her conduct, weight, looks, grades, friends, choices, or hobbies. The love she received was conditioned on her performance and never lasted more than a couple of hours. Those two kids had traumatic childhoods. They exhibit hundreds of signs of their traumatic upbringing that go unnoticed because their suffering occurred gradually, with one small issue at a time, much like the progression of normal development and the emergence of issues when development cannot proceed as expected. Both kids experienced a lack of safety during childhood that caused their nervous systems to react to their environment in extreme forms. As a result, both suffered from underdevelopment, which can manifest in a multitude of problems. For example, Mikey didn’t grow muscles or height. He’s shorter compared to his family and can’t gain weight regardless. If his appearance reflects a lack of growth, imagine how ‘small’ his organs, functions, or internal maturation may be. This implies all sorts of signs—poor digestion, slow metabolism, immune system issues, or even underdeveloped kidneys. He may have difficulties with fine motor skills, while Pam may struggle with gross motor skills. Both may experience concentration issues, but Pam may feel anxious while Mikey may be depressed; conditions that may be interpreted as hyper-activity for Pam and distractibility for Mikey. They both may have low self-esteem even when Pam does great at school and Mikey is great at negotiating and selling goods. He is unable to read a book while Pam is socially distant. The list of potential impacts can be extensive. However, more than an endless catalog of characteristics caused by interrupted development, I wanted to emphasize that every child may exhibit a unique set of signs or symptoms. These can often go unnoticed because each child's body responds differently to their circumstances, each circumstance is not only different but also perceived uniquely by the child. The other important factor for these issues to go unnoticed is that adult assume that the kid was born that way instead of acknowledging that their parenting, lack of attention and care, or the extreme demands and cruelty, are the reason for the children’s behavior, growth issues, and emotional/social problems.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: As a therapist, what types of clients' problem are most exhausting to work with?
Answer: I had a client that every week agreed to work harder next session, but every week he just talked and talked without really committing to do the exercises, to review our goals, to process the emotions he was experiencing, to name them, to stop or review his narrative, to read the articles I recommended, etc., etc. He finally told me that he didn’t believe in changing, that he had been successful being the way he was, and that he only liked having the routine of coming to therapy to talk about himself. “Do you think I am a narcissist” he asked me once :-) As a therapist, I find that working with clients who lack motivation to change or grow can be particularly challenging and exhausting. Many individuals seek therapy seeking validation, expecting someone else to solve their problems, or simply complying with external pressures. In these cases, it often feels like nothing sticks—interventions don't seem to make a lasting impact, and there's minimal improvement over time. It could be frustrating. I often remind my supervisees that therapy is most effective when both the therapist and the client are equally invested in the process. “Don’t work more than the client” I tell them. However, despite this understanding, I sometimes find myself putting a lot of effort to assist clients who may not tell me the reason they are not doing the work. It's disheartening when clients don’t take ownership of their journey in therapy, as progress requires active engagement and commitment from their side. While every client's journey is unique and complex, the most rewarding clients are those willing to collaborate actively, reflect on their experiences, and take steps towards personal growth and change. The therapist best reward is the improvement of their clients! That’s why we practice this difficult profession! In terms of problems, I don’t find problems difficult to work with. Every challenge is rewarding to certain extend because allows the therapist to learn more about a particular issue, or motivate us to learn something new about people or about ourselves. Exhausting? Regardless of the type of problem, again, what is the most tiring is to see no progress.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can a 3 year old remember a traumatic event?
Answer: We remember those instants where the brain recognizes there is something important to store for your survival. I can share an image I remember clearly from where I was 3. I was playing with my brother and I don’t remember what I did but he pushed me and I hit my leg with a corner of a table. There was an employee just few steps from us and when he saw me crying, he told me “come, I’ll massage you”. I still have the image of his face, and specially his eyes. I don’t think I’ll never forget that! You know why I remember it? Because I was able to detect an ill intention in the way he looked at me. Even as young as 3 or younger, even without understanding of the concepts, we are able to detect danger. It’s called neuroception, and it detects when there is threat. I told my mother what the employee said, she told my father, and they found out the guy had been drinking. My brain was able to distinguish the danger on the guy’s words. It was not a trauma because I didn’t allow him to touch me. It’s could have had a bigger impact on me if he had let him, and maybe other memories would have also been recorded as important but I’m sure I’d still remember the moment where he told me to approach him maybe as the most important. In general, no matter the age, we don’t remember all the parts of a traumatic event. When we are at risk, the brain focuses on the specific elements that are needed to monitor and disregards the rest. It’s called “tunnel vision” and it causes to only focus in particulars. Many people feel frustrated because they can’t remember most of what happened, but that’s because most elements were never stored. But yes, even young kids can store specific memories as relevant and recall them afterwards.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Did the person you used to be ever come back after you recovered from narcissistic abuse?
Answer: You are not the person you were yesterday, and hopefully, not the person you’ll be tomorrow. Everything changes all the time, and if we are engaged with life, we keep learning more and more to better live. We are adaptive beings. We need to learn from our experiences to be better prepared to face what life brings, from adversity to happiness. Every relationship influences how we’ll be in the next. A relationship with a narcissist will definitely affect how you see people, yourself, and the risks of trusting, loving, caring, and many other characteristics that were abused or dismissed by the narcissist. You will be “the same” in essence, but you’ll be different in terms of how you act and react to people and situations where you could be abused. Ideally, if you are a “recovered” person, you may be stronger, with better skills to set boundaries, recognize the intentions beneath the actions, and protect yourself. You can also recover the best qualities you had before the abuse, but now they will be much more in your awareness. If you give them the value they have, it’ll be more difficult for others to take them for granted. For example, if you were kind and innocent before the relationship with the narcissist, and the narcissist abused those characteristics, you may think that you won’t be kind and that you are definitely not innocent anymore, but that’s not necessarily true. You can now know the value of your kindness and continue being kind in a more selective way. Your innocence may have transformed into curiosity and acceptance as opposed to naiveté or inexperience. We are always the same at the core, but we are always morphing into some other level of consciousness. One of the main reasons for our existence is to learn. If we don’t learn, we don’t grow, and we are only surviving. So, hopefully, you will never go back to being the person that was identified as a prey of a narcissist.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is it possible for infants to be diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)?
Answer: It wouldn't be possible to diagnose a baby with a mental health condition like PTSD because they lack the language skills to express symptoms, and there are no definitive tests available for such young children. I think it’d be irresponsible to give a diagnosis to a baby. The DSM does have a section for "Posttraumatic Stress Disorder for Children 6 Years and Younger" which acknowledges the need for different criteria when diagnosing young children, but even this section is not directly applicable to diagnosing infants. Can infants have PTSD? That’s a different question. Or better yet, can babies be traumatized? The brains’ most important task is to keep us alive from the moment we are born. According to Stephen Porges, our system has a system called “neuroception” by which the nervous system detects cues of safety, danger, or life threat in the environment without involving conscious awareness. It is how the body maintains safety. So, even when babies have no idea what’s dangerous or safe, their brain could detect changes in their environment like unfamiliar or intense stimuli (e.g., loud sounds, sudden movements) which could be interpreted as potential danger, prompting a physiological response. There is also that Infants are highly attuned to their caregivers' emotional states and behaviors. If a caregiver displays signs of fear or distress, the infant can pick up on these cues and their brain will respond accordingly, trying to protect them by initiating the stress response. If what they perceive seems extremely dangerous, they could have an intense response that creates symptoms of PTSD. Mainly, we are born with a nervous system that is not regulated. This implies that if there are threatening events that distract the regular maturation of the system because it has to attend to risks, it’d be more difficult for that baby’s system to maintain equilibrium and regulation. That could actually mirror the reasons an adult develops PTSD. So, a baby can be traumatized because their system is so immature. The good news is that the developing brain is highly plastic, meaning it has a remarkable ability to adapt and heal. For the same reasons of survival, the brain will work on resolving and readjusting in order to continue doing its job of helping that body to grow and function as optimally as possible.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Could one love bomb a narcissist?
Answer: It’s sooo ironic that the term “love bombing” was first used by Sun Myung Moon, a cult leader and probably a narcissist. He used it to describe the affection and attention his followers received, obviously taking about it as a positive and desirable practice. It was not until psychologists noticed the ill intention behind the love bombing that the term became identified and defined as a psychological manipulation technique where an individual overwhelms their target with excessive affection, attention, and gifts to influence and control them. Nowadays, when you hear the term, it normally refers narcissistic abuse, cult indoctrination, and coercive control in intimate relationships. So, love bombing is something that narcissist do to control others. Are you asking if a narcissist could be controlled and manipulated by another narcissist? It’s not rare that narcissists get in relationships with other narcissists but you can correctly guess that they don’t last and that their interactions are full of power struggles. Each narcissist will attempt to assert dominance and control over the other and will get dirty to feel superior to the other. Since narcissists are skilled at manipulation and can use various tactics such as gaslighting, love bombing, and devaluation, they will obviously use those techniques to control the other. They will use the tactics that have proven effective with others, but when used against another narcissist, a very toxic relationship develops. Does a narcissist notice they are being love bombed? Probably, but so many of them lack self-awareness and reflection, that they may believe for a while that the partner (or other narcissist in relationship with them) may be giving all the affection, attention and praise because they deserve it. Once they realize it was manipulation, they may “want to kill” the other and may sharpen their manipulative techniques to “punish” the other. A narcissist with a higher level of self-awareness, might recognize love bombing tactics, or become suspicious of the tactic being similar to the one they use. They will take advantage of it, and allow the other to “manipulate” them to receive the benefits but knowing that it’ll not work to remove the control from them. So, yes, narcissist can be subjected to the same manipulative techniques they use.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How does childhood trauma affect the development of coping mechanisms in adulthood?
Answer: This is a very strange question but it’s very inviting. First, I can’t resist talking about “coping mechanisms”. The idea of coping mechanisms has roots in early 20th-century psychology and at this point most of those ideas are dated since they have evolved a lot. The term was popularized by psychoanalyst Anna Freud, who detailed various defense mechanisms. These defense mechanisms were seen as unconscious actions the ego uses to manage anxiety and conflict. In the mid-20th century, psychologist Richard Lazarus further developed the concept by distinguishing between problem-focused and emotion-focused coping in his work on stress and coping. Lazarus emphasized that coping mechanisms could be adaptive or maladaptive, depending on the context and effectiveness in reducing stress. In my opinion, all those ideas were important when mental disorders were perceived as genetic that needed to be managed by coping because they were considered incurable. That’s why therapy was so invested in teaching coping skills. But most of those ideas, particularly those that lack empirical support, have been revised or replaced by more scientifically grounded theories due to advances in neuroscience. The concept of neuroplasticity, which refers to the brain's ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections, has provided insights into how therapy and life experiences can bring about lasting changes in the brain, which makes it clear that instead of “coping”, we need to focus on healing. The goal in psychology and psychotherapy has shifted from merely coping to achieving overall well-being through various therapeutic interventions, lifestyle changes, reprograming the brain, and improving autonomic and emotional regulation. So, it's interesting that you ask if people with emotional issues after trauma will have problems coping. We all learn to cope when we have to. The brain's number one priority is to keep us alive, and it provides us with the tools to keep breathing. Let's say that breathing is a way to cope. Nowadays, instead of coping skills, especially when talking about trauma, we use the term "strategy." Our nervous system and our need to stay alive promote the development of survival strategies. We could say that trauma symptoms are part of those strategies. So, trauma makes us more skillful in terms of survival. It’s not optimal and may create dysfunction because these skills come at a significant cost to overall well-being and functioning, but we become very good at surviving because that’s what is really innate. Personality disorders for example, are people that develop so many survival strategies that they transform they innate traits and their personalities. So, the answer is NO, or YES, depending on what you are talking about. Trauma forces us to develop strategies to survive, and those strategies may cause so much distress, that we have to cope with those symptoms. The survival strategies are mostly maladaptive, and may push us to escape with the use of substances, aggression, or to shut down and disengage from society. Most of all, trauma causes us to lose tolerance. The dysregulation of our nervous system make life very difficult, keep us distressed, and pushes us to develop even more strategies or coping skills. But instead of coping, we need to address the maladaptation and aim to thrive instead of cope. But of course, you could call “coping” to skills such as compassion, tolerance, acceptance, relaxation, etc. Those coping skills are really affected by trauma because the person can’t seem to be able to achieve them. That’s again, due to the dysregulation and the survival strategies that, on top of everything else, distords perception and instill beleives of worthlessness, guilt, or shame.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why do kids have PTSD?
Answer: You may think that PTSD is something that soldiers experience, right? Many people connect PTSD with war or natural disasters. That’s how it became a recognized condition (and a diagnosis), but we have learned so much more since Vietnam, WWI, and WWII. Now we know that anyone can suffer from PTSD, regardless of age, race, gender, social status, education, or the specific event. We have learned that trauma has more to do with our subjective interpretation of the risk we confront than with the actual risk. Trauma is connected to fear and the way the brain interprets that emotion. For the brain, when we are afraid, it means we are at risk, and it must protect our lives. That’s why some soldiers don’t develop PTSD, while other individuals facing seemingly mild risks can become traumatized. Trauma therapy emphasizes restoring a sense of safety as soon as possible and guides clients to take steps to develop resilience and a strong prefrontal cortex (PFC). Or better yet, to develop resilience before anything threatening happens. A strong PFC will help us regulate the fear regardless of the event, and to keep us away from developing a debilitating disorder. A strong PFC and internal resources help us stay connected to the present, manage our fears, and make objective assessments of the dangers we encounter. Kids who are afraid of everything because they were raised surrounded by fear may develop PTSD more easily than those taught to protect themselves, to look for support, or to use their agency before they panic.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What causes a person to constantly dwell on the past and have difficulty moving on from certain things or people?
Answer: Your question has tormented people for decades, its answer long considered elusive. However, if we uncover the layers and apply recent neurobiological discoveries, we find that the key has been obvious since Darwin: most of our psychological struggles are connected to the principle of adaptation. We constantly dwell on the past and struggle to move on due to the fundamental nature of human adaptation, which involves continually predicting the future based on past experiences and remembering everything related to the risks and challenges of living. Adapting through remembering is basic principle of survival. That’s why our brains are wired to learn from emotionally significant memories, because they provide crucial information for survival and navigating future challenges. Negative events are remembered more easily for that reason. But why do we stay reviewing them? When get fixated on the past, it often indicates that our mind is trying to extract meaning or lessons from negative memories to avoid similar pain or mistakes in the future. This process is deeply rooted in our need to predict outcomes and prepare for potential scenarios. A reason we may stay stuck in the negative thoughts is based on another brain characteristic: habituation. The brain learns to automatically do an activity that the person practices often. If the person keep dwelling in some thoughts, the brain will trigger that activity without second thought because it helps the brain to save energy. It’s easier for the brain to always go to the same place as you become idle than not knowing what will be required from it every time. Also, our brain continuously seeks to update its internal model of the world. By reflecting on past events, especially those with strong emotional components, it tries to prepare for future situations by reviewing what went wrong, what could be done better, what other possibilities are necessary to confront the type of situations and actions that failed. If we review word by word our last argument, the brain has the hope it’ll be clear what to avoid next time to stop failure and suffering. It’s also the case that when we get so identified with our past, we may even build our identity around past events and relationships. Letting go of them can feel like losing a part of ourselves, causing us to cling to the past as a way to maintain continuity and a stable sense of who we are. It’s counterproductive and debilitating like many other habits we have, but without our reflective intervention, the brain makes this decisions based on saving brain energy and not on providing well-being. One other reason I have observed is that people that feel unresolved in terms of a failed relationship, job, activity, etc, feel the need to find a complete narrative of what happened before they can find peace and let go. Before reaching that point, revisiting past events and unresolved issues is what the mind do in an attempt to find closure. This can involve ruminating over what could have been done differently or longing for reconciliation or understanding. Just remember that the brain is not caring for your wellbeing. It’s only doing its tasks. It is YOU the one that has to care for your stability and enjoyment. Overcome your brain primitive tendencies if you want to move on; following the orders of a machine (brain = prediction machine) has proven deficient. It’s the reason most of our emotional problems.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Are super independent people actually suffering from unresolved trauma?
Answer: My daughter liked playing alone as soon as she was able to, and still like experiencing everything by herself. I could give you another 10 examples of how she was super independent from the moment she was born. This picture (of an older girl) kind of shows how my daughter used to caress her chick to sleep while sucking her thumb when she was months old. She doesn’t have or had any unresolved trauma! It disturbs me to see the tendency to pathologize the qualities of people. Do you know where it comes from? Not only from envy, but mainly from powerful people trying to maintain their status quo and impose social norms. It all started in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. During this time, there was a significant shift towards categorizing and diagnosing behaviors that deviated from societal norms or expectations. Doctors were powerful authorities that were also either very religious, or not religious at all but were respected and looked up as those that had the truth and the responsibility to spread it. Society norms had to be followed and doctors were doing their part to maintain control. As psychiatry emerged as a distinct field from medicine, there was a growing interest in understanding and categorizing behaviors that were considered abnormal or deviant. “Abnormal Behavior” was the term used to separate any behavior that deviated from what was considered typical or acceptable within a specific cultural or social context. This could include behaviors that caused distress to the individual or others, impaired functioning, or were statistically infrequent. That means that “laughing loud” could have been considered abnormal and a pathology if the group of people were quiet and spoke softly. Psychiatrists and psychologists began to develop diagnostic criteria for mental disorders, initially focusing on severe conditions but later expanding to include a broader range of behavioral and psychological issues. At some point, there were a lot of behavior considered abnormal, since we always have tails that separate from the norm. The concept of what constitutes "normal" behavior is inherently tied to cultural and societal norms and everything that doesn’t fall into that 80% deviates from what “everybody” do. But just think that what is considered abnormal in one culture or historical period may be normal or even valued in another. It’s really easy to pathologize behavior but it’s impossible to make generalizations. Th variability in our characteristics has led to ongoing debates about the universality of psychological concepts. Pathologizing all types of behavior like being “super independent” influences how society views and treats individuals exhibiting these behaviors. You question alone can lead to stigma and make people that are independent doubt their wellbeing, their temperament, or the “normalcy” of their personality. It’s unfair to make someone that is proud of their independence doubt their sanity, don’t you think? Having said that, being super independent may be, in some cases, not a sign of unresolved trauma, but of having had to develop self reliance as a way to survive if they grew up in an environment that was not supportive. That’s actually shows resilience instead of the opposite. But of course, life should be balanced, and if the super independent person doesn’t know how to receive help or support, that may be an indication that they may work on their trust and their capacity ask for help and to to take in whatever is given to them. It’s not unresolved trauma, but of a survival strategy taken to an extreme.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Would it be considered a traumatic experience if during childhood my parents did it knowing I was in the same bed as them? If so, what effects could that have?
Answer: To know if it could be considered a traumatic experience, we need to know: How old were you? How often did it happen? and most importantly? Were you scared? For something to be traumatic, the event or circumstance needs to be connected to risk, danger, or feeling threatened. Trauma is a phenomenon based of our innate protections to avoid damage or death, and these protections get activated because we experience emotions like fear that urges the brain to do something to protect us. The effects? It depends: If what your parents were doing seemed as if one of them was going to kill the other (like when one chokes the other during sex), I bet anyone would have gotten scared and probably traumatized. But if your parents were quiet and tender with each other, you maye have found it soothing and loving and may have not be afraid at all. There are also other elements to consider: If you were very young (1–3), you may have not even registered it, but if you were already a teenager, you most definitely noticed everything since you already had some information about what was happening and had a judgement about sex. If you were raised by liberal parents that taught you sex is part of love, it’d have less of an effect than if you were raised in a conservative environment and though of sex as taboo, sinful, wrong, disgusting, etc., then you may have had a very different reaction by witnessing it. Traumatizing? If it was traumatizing for you, you might experience typical consequences such as hyper-vigilance, where you're constantly on guard and alert for potential threats or dangers. This can lead to difficulties in relaxing or feeling safe in intimate situations. Additionally, trauma from early exposure to sexual situations could result in a profound lack of trust, not only in others but also in your own judgments and ability to discern safe versus unsafe situations. Fear of intimacy may arise as a consequence, stemming from the association of intimacy with the distressing experience of early exposure to sexual acts. This fear can manifest as avoidance of closeness, emotional withdrawal, or difficulty in sharing personal thoughts and feelings with others. Even if it wasn't traumatizing, it could still have negative effects. For instance, it might shape your attitudes toward sex and intimacy in ways that are not conducive to healthy relationships. You might struggle with boundaries, have difficulty understanding healthy sexual development, or face challenges in forming intimate connections later in life. Another important aspect is that children who are introduced to sex at a young age often experience premature sexual awakening, which can lead to several negative consequences. They may prematurely engage in sexual activities with peers, potentially involving other children who are not developmentally prepared for such experiences. Additionally, early exposure to sex can confuse children's understanding of love, leading them to seek emotional connection through sexual behavior. This confusion may contribute to a pattern of promiscuity later in life, as they equate sex with intimacy and affection. So, even if being in the same bed as your parents while they “did it” may not result in trauma, it can still impact your relationship with sexuality, whether positively or negatively. Hopefully, what you witnessed was an act of love that could have helped you develop a healthy understanding that sexuality is a natural part of human life, as long as it occurs at an appropriate age and within a mutually respectful, caring, consensual, and loving context.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is Hypervigilance a common experience for everyone? How can one cope with it when it occurs?
Answer: There are terms that are coined to describe specific dysfunctions or patterns of behavior associated with certain conditions, such as anxiety disorders or trauma. Hyper-vigilance specifically refers to an exaggerated state of alertness where individuals are constantly scanning their environment for potential threats or dangers. Sometimes these terms as used as generalizations without adhering to the real meaning of the word and concept but they shouldn’t. Hyper-vigilance is one of those terms that indicate a serious issue. Being hyper-vigilant is dysfunctional because it implies a persistent focus on finding potential threats or reasons to be worried, consuming significant amounts of the brain’s energy budget. This allocation can hinder other important cognitive functions from operating optimally and may be damaging your overall well-being. Therefore, the answer is NO, hyper-vigilance is not a common experience in healthy individuals. If it has become common for you, it suggests that your brain may be in survival mode or heading towards it, possibly due to experiencing something traumatic previously that you have not been able to resolve. If that’s the case, your brain is attempting to protect you from perceived danger that may not be happening. That’s very detrimental. If you live in a hyper-vigilant state, it's crucial not just to cope but to actively find ways to regulate your nervous system and reduce the activation of brain centers that perceive threat or danger and are causing you to be hyper-vigilant. Otherwise, your system will keep working ineffectively due to keeping a state of being excessively alert, and at some point, you may develop symptoms and eventually, a mental disorder.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why and how do men fall in love?
Answer: “Falling in love” is a vivid description of what some people experience when they lose their footing. The expression, originating from a sudden or unexpected shift into a deep interest, affection, and care for another person, implies a profound emotional change. When I see my clients fall in love, I observe that from a neurobiological standpoint, they seem to suffer from a temporary mental disruption and psychological “fever.” The cascade of hormones and neurotransmitters that flood the bloodstream all at once significantly alters our perception, behavior, and priorities. People’s view of reality suddenly distorts in a myopic way, where the object of their affection becomes perfect: the most beautiful, humorous, intelligent, and best in every way. Nothing and no one else matters, including themselves. They lose sleep, daydream, and feel heightened excitement (sympathetic hyper-activation), and even eating becomes either insignificant or an opportunity to celebrate life with their loved one. Because I love neurobiology, I’ve tried to understand why people experience this state. I found that Falling in love activates the brain's stress response system in a similar way that traumatic events do. This activation of the stress response trigger the release of stress hormones such as cortisol. So, the initial excitement and uncertainty of new love can have some negative effects on our daily function, since the brain may induce stress-like activation potentially contributing to, for example, lower serotonin levels. The focus and preoccupation with the beloved in early stages of love can be compared with hypervigilance and intrusive thoughts often observed in people who experience traumatization. There is a chemical explanation: Dopamine surges during the initial stages, fueling feelings of excitement, euphoria, and intense motivation directed towards the beloved. This explains the dreaminess, constant thinking about the other person, and the desire to spend every moment with them. Alongside dopamine, there is norepinephrine, a neurotransmitter that further intensifies feelings of arousal, energy, and focus. It contributes to the racing heart, sweaty palms, and sleeplessness that people falling in love often experience during the "new love" phase. Interestingly, serotonin levels can actually dip during this passionate love phase. This neurotransmitter is usually associated with feelings of well-being and contentment. The decrease in serotonin might contribute to the obsessive focus on the loved one and the feeling that nothing else matters. Obviously, the "bonding hormone" oxytocin plays a crucial role in falling in love but not initially. In later stages, oxytocin promotes feelings of attachment, trust, and calmness. It's released during physical touch and sex, which initially makes the person feel a strong emotional connection. While each neurotransmitter has its specific role, it's the combined effect of these chemicals that creates the intense and sometimes irrational feelings associated with new love. There is a concept in German called Gesamteffekt (gesamt = total, effekt = effect) that explains why the loved one seems perfect, why sleep and food become secondary, and why the world seems brighter. It refers to how various elements or influences combine to produce a particular psychological effect or outcome, in this case, “falling in love.” But like everything, these hormonal changes are temporary. Over time, dopamine and norepinephrine levels stabilize, and serotonin levels return to normal. Therefore, falling in love may be seen as a 'positive stressor' that still induces changes in brain chemistry and functioning, potentially causing the person to feel unwell, make poor decisions, lose objectivity, and heighten their expectations unrealistically. The end of that phase marks a point where the person may either feel disappointed, begin to see the beloved as imperfect, and fall out of love, or they may focus on the more long-term, attachment-based aspects of love fueled by oxytocin and satisfaction “staying in love.” These aspects are less chemically dependent and more psychologically/rational in understanding what a relationship entails. In short, men fall in love because there are chemical changes in their brain triggered by various factors, including emotional stimuli such as attraction, connection, and intimacy with another person. The stimuli could come from the other person fulfilling something desirable like looks, reciprocity, intelligence, or shared interests and values that resonate deeply with one's own. The more of these attributes are met, the higher the excitement, but also, the higher the probability of staying in love. So, in short, men fall in love because the initial encounters with someone that matches some of the person’s expectations activate brain regions associated with reward, pleasure, and motivation, leading to the release of all the chemicals I mentioned, causing a hyper-arousal state.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why do women find married men appealing?
Answer: In psychology, it’s recognized that attraction to unavailable partners, such as married men, is not uncommon and that there could be explained by several underlying emotional or psychological reasons. One common factor is a fear of commitment. For some individuals, becoming involved with someone who is already committed provides a sense of emotional safety and removes the pressure of having to fully commit themselves. This fear can be rooted in past relationship experiences or a general discomfort with intimacy. It can also be rooted in rebelliousness to the establishment, where marriage seems more like a trap than a joy, especially if the person comes from parents with a dysfunctional marriage. It could also be related to having an avoidance attachment style. These individuals value their independence highly. An unavailable partner provides the excitement of a relationship without the perceived threat of losing their autonomy. They can walk away easily if things get too intense. Sometimes, those with avoidance attachment may subconsciously believe they don't deserve a healthy, committed relationship. Unavailable partners reinforce this belief by keeping them at a distance. Low self-esteem can play a significant role too. People with low self-esteem like receiving validation and affirmation from others, and being involved with someone who is already in a committed relationship can provide a distorted sense of validation. The attention and affection received from a married partner may temporarily boost self-esteem, making them feel special, desired, and “better” than the other. Another reason is that being with a married men can sometimes involve complex dynamics of desire and fantasy. The forbidden nature of the relationship increases excitement and passion, creating an allure that stems from the thrill of breaking societal norms or experiencing something taboo. I read somewhere that there are studies that suggest that women may find men more attractive simply because other women find them attractive. A married man signifies he's already been "chosen" by another woman, which could potentially boost the perception of being a valuable partner. The logic may be flawed, but subconsciously, some women may think that a married man has, by definition, has been able to establish at least one relationship to the point of commitment. This might may mean that he possesses good communication skills, emotional intelligence, the ability to handle conflict, knows how to provide, etc - all desirable qualities in a partner. Lastly, I may add that married men often present an improved version of themselves during an affair, focusing on excitement and passion. This can be appealing compared to the perceived everyday routines and potential challenges of a single relationship. Besides that, there is something called the "Coolidge effect" which suggests an increase in arousal and sexual satisfaction with a new partner, which may be a reason to look for partners that are more experienced and freer to experiment sexually, and married men may be good candidates to achieve this. Remember that each one of us is different and may have different reasons to do whatever we do. It’s not right or possible to make generalizations. Our psyche is really complex.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What does retraumatization do to someone with BPD?
Answer: Retraumatization has similar underlying effects on individuals regardless of whether they have BPD or not. Do you think that suffering from BPD would make retraumatization different? Let’s explore if that’s the case. We know that specific manifestations and consequences of retraumatization vary depending on each person’s resilience, past experiences, intensity of the traumatic experiences, and other factors. Perhaps the most critical factor is whether the person has developed resources or if resources have been depleted due to unresolved trauma. In the case of BPD, most people develop the disorder because they were unable to develop resources in the first place. The most significant injury that a person with BPD suffers from relates to attachment; it may involve a failure to attach or attachment ruptures. Let's examine what it means to have these pains reactivated: If a person with BPD experienced both, a dysregulated system that never learned to regulate with the mother, and abandonment, they may repeatedly feel dumped, whether in reality or perceptually. This type of trauma is relived internally, even when no one is in fact abandoning them. They might feel abandoned, for example, if their partner takes 10 minutes longer than usual at the supermarket. While the situation may not seem retraumatizing, the person experiences the same type of hurt repeatedly, leading to further dysregulation and exacerbation of symptoms. So, to answer your question, we may say that retraumatization is a regular way to operate. They feel abandoned, alone, rejected, and dismissed repeatedly regardless of what’s happening, which is a way to make the pre-verbal past to be the way to perceive today. What does that do? It makes life harder and harder. That’s why it’s so important that they get treated. Otherwise, they continue having what they fear the most: more dysregulation, less control, and worse rejection.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How can a therapist have “unconditional positive regard” for someone? Therapists are human as well.
Answer: Many years ago, I had one of those therapists who let me talk endlessly while I lay on his couch. He always had his notebook at hand, and I assumed he was taking notes while I talked. However, one day I heard a click, and when I looked, I saw that he had fallen asleep and his pen had slipped from his hand. I then became more curious and I discovered that he was dozing off every single session. Maybe Carl Rogers had a similar experience that motivated him to develop the concept of unconditional positive regard as a reaction against the predominant psychoanalytic approach of his time (1950s). Psychoanalysis, particularly in its early forms, often focused on interpreting unconscious desires and conflicts seen as driving negative behaviors. With these ideas in mind, therapists perceived and treated clients as flawed or damaged individuals needing to be fixed. The technique or idea called for therapists to allow clients to talk for extended periods, session after session, aiming to uncover associations that could provide insights into the hidden contents of the subconscious. That’s probably why Rogers emphasized a client-centered or person-centered approach, prioritizing the client's subjective experiences, emotions, and self-perceptions. What he proposed was to stop assuming that the therapist knew more than the client themselves, and that the therapist had to be open to hearing the client's subjective experience without judgment. Rogers believed that everyone inherently wants to improve, and that therapy should support this natural tendency rather than pathologizing it. Unlike the psychoanalytic perspective, which sometimes portrayed clients as resistant to change or unaware of their own motivations, Rogers saw clients as capable of understanding themselves and making positive changes when provided with a supportive, nonjudgmental environment. I’m including this information about Rogers to make the point that he tried to bring balance by moving to the other extreme of what was happening in his time. I assume that’s why he used such an extreme term as “unconditional.” It seems to represent the opposite extreme of the pendulum. Unconditional positive regard refers to the therapist's ability to fully accept and support their client without judgment or evaluation, regardless of the client's thoughts, feelings, or behaviors. I don’t think that’s impossible. Maybe what is hard is to maintain it all the time and with complete authenticity. But it actually invites the therapist to be curious, to learn about human possibilities, and to grow. Let me give you an example: a conservative therapist starts working with a client whose lifestyle includes occasional sex and drug use. The therapist may have biases against casual sex and drug consumption, but they could authentically become curious about the client's experiences and relationship with that lifestyle before making judgments or assuming the client is wrong, which could jeopardize the therapeutic relationship. The lack of judgment can help the client lower their defenses and delve deeper into what motivates their actions. The therapist and client can learn much more about the potential harm in these activities, the client's own judgments about their behavior, and other insights. If the therapist brings their biases into the room, the client may never feel completely honest with the therapist or themselves. So, that openness from the therapist is what Rogers was asking for and that’s possible to do for all humans. The therapist may learn something new from that particular client without needing to change their thinking for everyone. Each client with similar behaviors may have different reasons and relationships with their actions, and maintaining this unconditional positive regard is what allows that diversity to manifest in therapy. How can therapists achieve this? By adopting a non-judgmental attitude, developing empathy, striving for genuineness, understanding that every person is unique and deserving of respect, and cultivating the capacity to be as present as possible. That’s very possible. The last part (being present) may be the most challenging but is also the most rewarding aspect of being a therapist. Practicing presence is the best way to develop wellbeing.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is the term for deriving pleasure from others' suffering and pain? What are the possible causes of this behavior?
Answer: I would call it "mental darkness." I believe a technical term exists, and many people would say that “sadism” is a good options, but the best explanation I've found, though not sounding scientific, is that their brain lacks light, and therefore, their mind is filled with darkness! Let me explain why I say this. We all experience envy and jealousy, for example, and we all have the capacity to be cruel, but that's different from enjoying seeing suffering and pain. Since we all have a primitive brain, primitive instincts, and primitive needs, it's not uncommon to experience momentary dark states. However, when these become the norm, It suggests a deeper issue where normal empathic responses and higher-order emotional connections, such as compassion and love, are diminished, and the person has fallen too deeply into their primitivism, disconnected from their humanity. This can occur when parts of the brain responsible for these emotions, including the prefrontal cortex and the mirror neuron system, are not functioning optimally. It may also indicate that the part of the brain responsible for feeling a sense of belonging may be working inadequately. If one only enjoys the suffering of those who "don’t belong" to their tribe, it's a partial disconnection. But if one enjoys everyone’s suffering, then even the emotional brain may be disconnected, with only the primitive brain running the show. In the case of partial dysfunction, when everyone is seen as an enemy, deriving pleasure from seeing enemies "defeated" occurs. Brain imaging studies show that regions activated during experiences of pleasure overlap with those activated during experiences of pain. Another reason is that these individuals lack empathy. Empathy has a neurobiological basis involving the mirror neuron system, which helps individuals simulate and understand the emotions of others and is connected to the sense of belonging I mentioned earlier. The development of empathy often begins in infancy and is shaped by early caregiving experiences. Children learn empathy through interactions with caregivers who demonstrate empathy themselves. Lack of nurturing or inconsistent caregiving in early childhood, or experiencing traumatic adversity, can be reasons why some people don’t develop empathic skills. It could also be the case that the person learns to produce dopamine by witnessing pain, as seen in activities like bullfights, dogfights, cockfights, or even boxing. Engaging in these activities can cause excitement, deriving pleasure from competition and enjoying seeing one fighter winning over the other. This production of dopamine can cause pleasure, and it could become linked to wanting and enjoying seeing the enemy in pain, especially if it means significant financial gain in betting. Lastly, the pleasure derived from seeing someone in pain may not be straightforward and can involve complex motivations or psychological defenses. It may serve to alleviate personal insecurities, assert dominance, or exert control over others when there is no other way to find solace. Still, these reasons are linked to poor activation of the prefrontal cortex and a low connection between brain centers and the body where vibration is perceived as movement, which is then translated as positive feelings. Normally, our minds are connected, and without this connection, we are alone, relying only on our primitive instincts for survival.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why do you think most relationships fail?
Answer: Expectations! As a couple’s therapist I have seen how people in committed relationship expect too much from the partner. There's often a belief that their partner should fulfill all their needs and make them happy, without considering their own responsibility for personal fulfillment. Growing up, I internalized the idea that investing in my own happiness was selfish. In my understanding, I was taught that being selfless, a good person, and making others happy would give me what I needed and lead to happiness and fulfillment. Now that I think about it, it seems that the idea is similar to heaven: if you are kind, selfless, humble, and make others happy, you’ll go to heaven. Similarly, my grandmother used to tell me that since I was such a good daughter and granddaughter, I was going to have a good husband. (She was soooo wrong!!! 🤣🥴🥲) But as I grew older, I realized that my grandma was raised herself and millions of people with the same ideas that many religions and philosophical perspectives promote: the idea of selflessness and the prioritization of others' happiness over one's own. Christianity, Buddhist sutras, confucianism, Islam, and even psychological approaches such as Humanism share that type of thinking. Catholicism emphasizes this to an extreme since if you act selfishly, it's considered a sin and you’ll be punished! I think that type of mentality contributes strongly to the failure and dissatisfaction of many relationships. This about how we are used to believe that we need our “other half” to be complete. I've learned through my work that successful relationships require both partners to be independently happy and fulfilled individuals. I encourage my clients to cultivate their own well-being and support their partners in doing the same. Fulfilled people make fulfilling relationships! When individuals rely solely on their partner for validation and fulfillment and think that they will receive “their reward” by giving and giving, they will most probably neglect their own needs and personal growth. This imbalance can lead to resentment, unmet expectations, and ultimately, relationship breakdowns. Those who feel incomplete without their partner often blame them for their dissatisfaction on unmet needs. The reality is that it's nearly impossible for one person to meet all the needs of another, especially since each one of us struggles to know what are needs are. There are other reasons, but managing expectations and learning to help yourself find satisfaction independently are good ingredients to avoid failing in a relationship.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Are narcissists sad inside?
Answer: Even when I had to deal with a good number of pwNPD in my life, I was never able to really know what was happening inside of their heads. Do they know they are lying? Or do they believe their lies? Do they suffer, are sad, or aware of their shame? etc. As I started learning, I was discovering some painful truths: they may not know, they may not be aware of how sad and miserable they actually are. A concept that helped me understand them better is “ego-syntonic.” Ego-syntonic is a characteristic normally found in pwNPD which means that their traits and behaviors align closely with their self-image and values. For example, a narcissist may view their inflated sense of self-importance, need for admiration, and lack of empathy as natural and appropriate aspects of their personality. These traits are integrated into their identity and perceived as acceptable or even desirable, reinforcing their self-image of superiority and entitlement. This alignment with their self-concept makes it challenging for narcissists to recognize or acknowledge the negative impact of their behavior on others. They may not only miss to see their behaviors as problematic but they develop pride and attachment to these behaviors since they serve to uphold their self-esteem and protect against feelings of inadequacy or vulnerability. There is another concept that help me knowing a little more about the experience of pwNPD. The concept of the "false self" was first formulated in the 1960s to describe the fabricated personalities individuals develop early in life due to inadequate parenting (often referred to as "mothering" in Winnicott's era), lack of empathy, and the infant's need to conform. It has been observed that those whose false self becomes pervasive—dominating their personality—are often unaware of the mask they wear, confusing it with their true self, especially if it formed in early childhood. This means individuals governed by the false self construct their self-concept around a defensive persona crafted to conceal their perceived defects, which they believe are unlovable or unworthy of acceptance. The hidden persona can cause significant psychological pain and inner conflict. Viewed through a trauma-focused lens, diverging from established psychoanalytic concepts, I use the term "hollow self" to describe an empty facade filled with survival mechanisms that avoid confronting painful realities or revealing their perceived defects. This may manifest as unintegrated emotional fragments. I liken it to a hologram of a person—superficially identical but lacking self-awareness, introspection, values, empathy, and the ability to engage with anything substantial due to its insubstantial nature. The hollow-self is what we see and name as narcissism. It’s purely mental and dissociated from the 'real' objectivity of the person; it’s only a projection of insecurities through a cluster of defenses that try to fit in and show worth that they ‘know’ isn’t there. But this hollow self, being mental, takes over the life and will of the person, blinding them from seeing their inner world. This includes most emotions that could bring them down, like sadness. I’ve been fortunate to work with several individuals with NPD and have confirmed that they live unaware of their inner emotional states. They have also shared with me that there are moments where they become aware of their sadness, their shame, their understanding of being undesirable, and selfish people. 'Heartless,' some say! So, yes, they are sad inside. They are also ashamed, empty, and insecure, even when most of the time, they are not aware of it.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How do you differentiate trauma and symptoms of PTSD?
Answer: Great question! Many people assume trauma is the event itself, but your question implies that trauma is the injury that manifests as symptoms, correct? And therefore, you wonder what is the difference between trauma and PTSD diagnosis. This is a common question that persists despite considerable discussion. Even with widespread attention, the definition of trauma remains unclear, and it’s not unusual to see professionals and even academics having these same doubts. That’s what I keep saying say that trauma is a phenomenon. I say that trauma is considered a phenomenon because it is observed, known to exist, but may not necessarily be fully understood or explained by current knowledge or theories. This is the exact definition of a phenomenon according to science. What we know and have been able to observe is that trauma includes a wide array of individual experiences and responses to distressing events connected to our survival instincts. As a phenomenon, trauma involves the event but also the unique ways in which individuals perceive, interpret, and respond to these events based on their personal histories, emotional resilience, and social contexts. We also know that trauma involves a lasting effect on our nervous system, our emotional responses, and our behavior. Interestingly, even before we could fully explain the phenomenon, we had already coined a name for the disorder it precipitates: PTSD. PTSD is a diagnosis that names the number of symptoms that typically appear following a threatening event. The diagnosis is only given if all the symptoms are present for a length of time. So, what many people refer to as trauma isn't always trauma. It has become common to label any experience of distress or misfortune as trauma, along with carrying some lingering effects from the experience. However, most of the time, these are simply part of life and the challenges inherent in being human. When we encounter something saddening or infuriating, it's natural for us to remember that event for a long time. This is how our system learns to navigate and survive, but it doesn't necessarily indicate that we are psychologically damaged. On the other hand, if we face an event that threatens our very existence, causing our system to enter crisis mode, we may develop more pronounced trauma symptoms. If these symptoms persist and accumulate, it may be considered that we have developed a trauma disorder. So, to address your question, trauma symptoms emerge during and after experiencing events that evoke feelings of fear, overwhelm, helplessness, and possibly hopelessness. The intensity and duration of these feelings correlate with the severity of the symptoms. If only a few symptoms persist for an extended period, it may indicate unresolved trauma. Persistent feelings of fear could suggest that your system is still struggling finding safety, which keeps traumatization running your system. If this process persists, symptoms can escalate until they meet the criteria for PTSD. This set of articles explain some of the myths around trauma:

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is it common for individuals with PTSD to avoid discussing their traumatic experiences or the root cause of their PTSD?
Answer: It's common to fear our emotional reactions, especially if they could be dramatic, even when the fear may be more damaging than the reaction itself. It’s also common to fear being judged! When I began my career as a therapist, I hesitated to disclose my profession because people often became reserved, fearing I would psychoanalyze them and uncover what was wrong with them. Then I learned to tell people right away that I was not a psychoanalyst, maybe even explaining my approach that was the opposite of assuming there was something wrong in people. My philosophy is that If you focus in what’s wrong, you’ll always find something wrong. But if you focus on what is right, you’ll always find something right. And finding what’s right may start a virtuous circle as opposed to the vicious circle of feeling inadequate. Psychology in general, over-pathologize our behavior. And we are always afraid about finding out we are not well, or sane, or “normal.” So, there are more than one reason people avoid talking about negative aspects of their lives. Let’s explore a couple: Talking about what went wrong in your life is opening the door to pathology! There is a simple reason to explain why people avoid discussing loaded material. You may have heard of the Window of Tolerance. It’s very practical way to explain how our system fluctuates from being active to be relaxed, and how both of those oscillations can go too high or down, causing problems in our responses and actions and dysregulation. When are system is out of the window, we loss tolerance to our own emotional responses, which increases the distress. You can read how to increase your tolerance here: So, crossing the affect tolerance threshold make us feel fearful because we know we lose control over what we say and do. Also, being outside the window feels overwhelming and confusing, or dissociative and confusing. Who wants to go there voluntarily? It’s wise not to go there unless you trust that there will be a good outcome if you do. Not only that, but many people cope with pain by convincing themselves of a good past, telling themselves they had a nice and joyful childhood, or wanting to believe their parents are/were great, or that there is nothing wrong with them. Facing the past may be taking the risk of finding dirt or stains in the beautiful picture they created. Again, it is worse to carry that fear than facing the reality that no childhood is perfect, that everyone suffers somehow, and that accepting not being perfect is relieving an healing. But since trauma is subjective, you may think they suffered from trauma while they may have not. There is always the possibility that people resolved their traumatization by focusing in the positives of their lives. Intuitively, we could help our system heal if we change the meaning we assign to our past. Trauma is more about the relationship we establish with the incidents than the incidents themselves. Lastly, remembering and reliving events that are connected to negative emotions or beliefs will make you feel bad, there is no way around. It could re-traumatize you, or make your daily life more difficult. Some people learn that it’s worse to do that (rehearsing the ugly) than to avoid remembering it. It’s only beneficial to remember and talk about painful past if there is a way to change the charge of the memory (reconsolidating it). Otherwise, better not contributing to make it stronger, more vivid, and more intrusive by “discussing” it! That’s why a seasoned trauma therapist pace the work until the client is ready and able to open the can of worms without negative consequences.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Do people's personalities change after they heal from trauma/PTSD/etc.?
Answer: It’s easy to confuse behavior with personality. While behavior can change frequently, our core personality traits tend to remain relatively stable throughout our lives. Let’s imagine you know someone who is funny, personable, articulate, clean, reliable, skillful, and sweet. These characteristics are likely to remain even after the person either experiences or heal from trauma. Once they heal, They may have the capacity to do more with their characteristics, the same they had, only better. Some individuals integrate certain symptoms of trauma into what appears to be their personality, such as aggression, disengagement, avoidance, cruelty, reactivity, impulsivity, or unpredictability. You may notice that my list sounds more like a list of symptoms than a list of inherent personality traits. True personality traits sound more like quiet instead of disengaged or boisterous instead of reactive. While core personality traits typically remain consistent, some trauma-related symptoms can fuse with an individual's personality. After healing, these integrated symptoms may diminish, resulting in a perception that the person has changed. They may seem now with less anxiety, impulsivity, avoidance, and other distressing behaviors they showed before. They may appear as an improved version of themselves after overcoming the distress of traumatization, but if you investigate deeper, their natural tendencies are still there. Some of maybe the most interesting changes may be seen in people that didn’t know how to draw boundaries and felt unimportant. When they heal, they may need more attention, become somehow more demanding, and will ask their space to be respected, which could seem very different from how they acted before. Traumatized people, especially those with a disorder, may not show (or know) who they really are because they had to adapt to their environment “to survive” which may have affected their behavior and their sense of self. But that person that now knows they need to be respected, always had the strength to ask that now show. As they navigate the new experience of feeling more whole, aspects of their personality may become more pronounced or shift in response to their circumstances for the better, at least for them.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can numbing an emotion be considered a form of dissociation?
Answer: The term “dissociation” has been excessively stigmatized. It's not just treated as taboo but almost like a curse or reserved for the most severe trauma cases. Many immediately associate it with multiple personalities. However, dissociation is a common experience for everyone, occurring in various ways multiple times a day. If you look up the definition of dissociation, it's typically described as a natural mental process where individuals temporarily disconnect from their thoughts, feelings, or surroundings. This can happen in response to intense emotions, stress, or the need to mentally step back from a situation. Daydreaming or getting lost in thought are mild forms of dissociation that many people experience. However, most people perceive dissociation as pathological, involving feelings of detachment from one's body or observing oneself from a distance. Yet, these experiences also occur during deep concentration, creative flow, or in response to overwhelming emotions from challenging life events. Dissociation is often more of a protective mechanism than a disorder; it allows our minds to adapt and cope with experiences or fatigue without indicating a psychological problem. Of course, dissociation can become dysfunctional. When viewed as a pathology, it disrupts a person's usual integration of thoughts, feelings, memories, or identity. In severe cases, this can manifest as: Dysregulation can be disruptive and a response to chronic stress or overwhelming experiences that are difficult to fully process or integrate into conscious awareness. To address your question, it's crucial to recognize that dissociative functions are often involuntary and not easily controlled or temporary. Dissociation is inherently protective, so attempting to dissociate from a specific emotion signals the brain that protection is needed, possibly leading to a disconnection from emotions altogether. Therefore, strictly speaking in terms of mental processes, “numbing an emotion” is not dissociation. Numbing can occur through alcohol use or distraction, but it doesn't equate to dissociation unless it arises as a defense mechanism against overwhelming feelings.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How often and why do people with BPD become hypersexual?
Answer: I have given a lot of thought to this intriguing, easily observable fact: pwBPD are very often hyper-sexual. Let me share some of these thoughts. First, it’s not just my personal experience but also a statistical fact that there is a correlation between BPD and sexual abuse. Estimates vary, but research suggests that between 40% to 71% of individuals with BPD report experiencing sexual abuse at some point in their lives. These findings intrigued me, prompting me to consider whether individuals with BPD already had attachment issues and were seeking a form of "love language," or if sexual abuse itself was a primary factor contributing to their instability, as much of the research suggests. What I've observed is a misinterpretation in how individuals with BPD perceive what qualifies as sexual. Many people with BPD I've worked with describe experiences that, upon closer examination, may not fit traditional definitions of sexual misconduct but involve a personal and sexual interpretation. For instance, someone with BPD might feel provoked or seduced when their mother casually enters their room in a nightgown, or if a coworker tells a joke with sexual undertones. These experiences are made personal and seen as sexual by the pwBPD even when many other people would never think that introducing a thermometer in the rectum of a sick child is sexual assault. I can't help but question whether these statistics are accurate or if they're influenced by a perception that overly emphasizes the sexual nature of certain interactions. What causes this distortion? Or why are they targets of molesters? One plausible explanation is that individuals with BPD may have witnessed sexual interactions early in life due to their hyper-vigilance, or they may have experienced heightened sensitivity to sexual pleasure at a young age, which could have awakened their sexuality prematurely. Since they were not able to process the experience, they give it a meaning that helps them feel better about themselves. In my years of working with pwBPD, I felt there was a correlation between people that are born with highly developed senses, and those that develop BPD. After some research, I found that there is indeed a recognized correlation between BPD and sensory hyper-sensitivity. Several studies have found that individuals with BPD tend to experience heightened sensory sensitivity compared to those without the disorder. Sensory hyper-sensitivity refers to an exaggerated response to sensory stimuli, such as sounds, touch, or visual input. Individuals with BPD may experience difficulty processing and regulating their emotional responses to sensory stimuli, which can contribute to the emotional instability often associated with the disorder. This sensory hyper-sensitivity makes me believe that they may have found sexual pleasure early in life, which, connected with their lack of trust, made them focus a lot on it, but misreading it.
