Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What are the reasons for seeking counselling/therapy if one has no issues?
Answer: Everyone has emotional issues! It's part of the human condition. All humans face emotional challenges and struggles to some degree as part of the shared experience of being human. Not only that, but our cultures don't exactly set any of us up for success in dealing with our emotional issues. We're taught to bury our emotions deep down, as if they're something to be ashamed of or scared to confront. From a young age, we're told to toughen up, to hide our vulnerabilities, and to pretend like everything's okay even when it's not. "Don't cry!" is a phrase every child has heard in their life. When we can't process emotions healthily, it often manifests in anxiety, depression, physical ailments and other mental/physical issues. That kind of upbringing affects us more than we think. It leaves us feeling disconnected from ourselves, unable to express how we truly feel, and it can seriously interfere with our relationships, present and future ones. That's how most of us have been taught to deal with emotions - by ignoring them! That's why I started saying we all have a reason to go to therapy. Therapy is like a school where we are explained all the fallacies we heard about ourselves and our emotional inner world, and unlearn those toxic and harming lessons. Therapy is where we learn to go deeper and deeper until we find our truth, convictions, values, and dreams. It equips us with vital emotional skills - self-awareness, self-compassion, assertiveness, regulation abilities - to then go after what we want in life. It's not just crisis treatment, but an empowering opportunity for profound growth.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How do I confirm that I love a person?
Answer: What type of love do you want to confirm? Romantic? Fraternal? Familial? Pragmatic? The list can go on. Upfront, I could tell you that if you really love a person, you then could live without them. Love is the opposite of ownership. For example, if you fall out of love because that person cheated on you, then you can be certain that your love was not the pure type. If you love a person for as long as that person fulfills your needs or expectations, then your love is pragmatic, grounded in conditions that can range from compatibility and convenience to companionship or financial support. I wish answers about love were straightforward or that we could find a device, like a thermometer, that could confirm we are in love and that our love is genuine, unconditional, pure, and lasting. But love is such a complicated phenomenon that we have not been able to agree on what it is. I’ll try to respond to your question, but let me talk a little about the maximum representation of love I have found in this human existence: Love in its most extensive manifestation is equivalent to limitless freedom, wisdom, beauty, and peace. This type of love has no object, which means that it flows without attaching to anyone or anything. Love is a force that feeds and builds the universe and each one of its elements, us included, and so, we sometimes can channel it. Some people say it’s always there but we lack the awareness. Others say that we only channel it when we become a clean vessel. When that force enters our system, everything looks, feels, sounds, tastes, and is better. Life becomes easier, more enjoyable, more fulfilling, brighter, shinier, greater. Can we channel that energy all the time? Hopefully! But we need to be so clear of all cravings, desires, and attachments, that it’s difficult to stay there permanently. That type of love I’m talking about is not biological but influences our biology big time. When we channel that energy, our brain lights up like a Christmas tree and produces all sorts of “feel-good” chemicals. We become healthier, more motivated, more energetic, more productive, more “alive.” We also turn out to be less demanding, less ambitious, less hungry, less attached to what we normally define as happiness. We become happier by accepting whatever it is. The inverse is also true. Our biology can influence our energetic body and clear the way to pure love. When we accept someone as they are, our brain produces all those feel-good stuff, and our channels open, facilitating the flow of the love force. That’s when we float and enjoy every second, assuming we are in love because of the relationship we are developing with certain people. We assign an object to the force we are experiencing, assuming they are the source. That type of openness is not caused by the person but by the chemicals that help us see everything beautiful and lower our guard. Our primitive circuits are nowhere active since the liking and accepting that new person makes us feel super safe. Safer than ever! As if misery will never be a possibility again, as long as we stay connected to that person. If that connection is just energetic, you can continue being in love and misery won’t come near you. But that’s not what normally happens. We immediately want to own that person, tie the knot so to speak, making sure they will never go anywhere else. But right there, as soon as we fear losing them, the channels close, the chemicals stop, and the primitive circuits make us feel at risk. And that amazing production of energy becomes a dark and all-absorbing black hole. What I could say is that we humans have the capacity to experience the very energy that creates us if we let go of all our human conditioning. If our humanity is bigger than our mind, then we get stuck on the miseries of attaching to a reality that is so limited. So, going back to your question, to confirm you love a person, you need to be certain that you could let them live their life as they please, that they can leave if they need to, that they can use their bodies as they find it necessary, and that you won’t close the flow of your great feelings if they don’t meet your expectations. Since that is almost impossible to do, what I suggest is to “love,” period. If you “love” as your regular mental state, you may not need to be with a person. You may enjoy the company of love, which could make your life easier and more beautiful than any person could. Then, you share that mental state with those you are with and continue working on accepting that you and they are human and that it is our condition to have needs. It is OK to practice conditional love. Your heart and soul could love unconditionally, but your daily activities, your body, and your brain need to work on meeting your needs to give you the opportunity to clean yourself of cravings. The better your needs are met, the less you will need, and the less you need, the more open to receiving the universe you will be. The bottom line is that it’s better to shift our perspective from seeking fulfillment solely through relationships to finding contentment within oneself. Once you are there, sharing that love with others will confirm that you love them ❤️

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What kind of person loves a borderline?
Answer: Anyone can fall in love with a pwBPD. They are not difficult to love. Think about it. They need you! Who doesn’t like to be needed? Also, if you get in contact with their inner child, they inspire compassion and promote playfulness. Who doesn’t like to keep feeling young? Most pwBPD can be wonderful companions, especially during the time they are not too attached. They are also great play-mates in many sports or activities that require power. If you were missing some playfulness in your life, they will make you feel like a teenager again! pwBPD are intelligent, prone to detail, very adaptable, creative, and most importantly, they are intense. Before you understand what their intensity is about, you may really enjoy their insight, their disposition for adventure, their wit, and what it seems to be a strong passion. Also, their intensity makes them great lovers. And let’s admit it! The way they idealize you is very enticing. At least for a while, the way they seem to see you, gives you confidence in yourself. They make you feel great, until they don’t! I think a better question could be What kind of person stays in love with BPD? Not difficult to fall in love with them, but kind of regular and expected to fall out of that love. Actually, many people leave a relationship with a pwBPD and still love them afterwards. It’s often a separation that becomes necessary to maintain sanity and self-preservation more than a lack of love, or worse yet, out of hatred. People that leave a pwNPD most of the time fear and hate them, while leaving a relationship with someone with BPD is difficult and heavy. Who stays? When the idealization ends and the devaluation starts, the cycle of push and pull never seems to end, The ones who either fall into the traps of a trauma bond, become co-dependent of their emotional turmoil, or have no options due to family ties or other obstacles, are the ones that may have no choice but to convince themselves they are still in love. Receiving devaluation comments is hurtful, especially after believing that they had seen the real you. The blaming, mood swings, impulsivity, violation of boundaries, secrecy, unpredictability, etc., end up affecting the way the partner perceives them, and the desire to stay with them dissipates. It’s hard for many to end a relationship with individuals with BPD, but it’s almost inevitable if the person with BPD does nothing to improve. Therefore, many partners who stay with them are normally those who can numb their emotions, deny their needs, and continue hoping for a better day.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can people who have experienced serious accidents be retraumatized by watching TV shows or movies depicting similar events? If so, what causes this reaction? Is it related to PTSD or another factor?
Answer: Watching a movie like this? If you watch a movie that depicts events that you find traumatizing without an option to close your eyes, you will certainly be retraumatized. I’m kind of kidding! Is it possible to be retraumatized by watching something similar to what happened to you? Everything is possible under the sun! And trauma is so subjective, than yes, it may be possible. Let’s see when. Some authors claim that we can get retraumatized very easily. I don’t completely agree. Even highly traumatized individuals have the capacity to recognize that a movie is not real. Also, everyone has the capacity to decide not to continue watching a movie if they notice that they are getting really upset and activated, don’t you think? Retraumatization happens when there is a reactivation of the survival circuits that will continue trying to keep us safe because the brain assumes we are in danger “again”. When someone gets retraumatized, there will be an exacerbation of trauma-related symptoms and distress in response to triggers or stressors. These triggers can vary widely, but in reference to your question, yes, many movies could depict scenes of something traumatic that you went through, and can make you feel so scared, that your brain may believe it’s happening again. But, as I said, if someone recognizes that the content of the show can be triggering, stop watching. What happens if the content is not similar to your traumatic experience but scares you? That’s a different story. If someone is already traumatized, lives hyper-vigilant and has distortions in perception that may see many events as dangerous, that person can have a trauma response out of insignificant events even if they are not related to their previous experiences. They may not notice they are getting scared, they may keep watching the movie, and their brain may confuse what’s happening with real danger. In those cases, we may not call it “re-traumatization” but the person’s symptoms may get worse. When we talk about traumatized individuals, we may not necessarily be referring to people with full blown PTSD or C-PTSD but with several of the symptoms. If they have a diagnosis, then it’s even easier to get scared, and therefore, re-activate the fear and survival circuits. A person that suffers from a trauma diagnosis like PTSD or C-PTSD lives in survival mode, and they are exposed to prolong the traumatization endlessly, which would be equivalent to say that they get re-traumatized all the time because they are very prone to feel anxiety, stress, fear, worry, etc., which is in itself, a way to make symptoms worse and to never recover a sense of agency and safety. That means that the “trauma” doesn’t get resolved, and instead, gets worse and worse. For those that have not developed a trauma disorder but has had traumatic experiences, a scary movie could be the catalyst to reactivate survival circuits and develop a trauma disorder. I explain that in this video: Just to be clear, it’s not about the content of the movie, but about the level of fear the person experiences. It doesn’t need to be a scary movie. It could be any movie

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can a person develop PTSD after being triggered, even if they were not previously diagnosed with the disorder?
Answer: The term “triggered” assumes that there has been some level of traumatization before. Also, someone can have post-traumatic symptoms without having full-blown PTSD. Many people store traumatic memories from traumatic events, which are connected to emotional responses without developing PTSD, but the traumatic memory can get activated and the emotions from the past can come back and make the person re-live the past as if it was happening again. That’d be considered “triggered.” “Being triggered” was originally used to describe the experiences of people who had been traumatized. It refers to a specific set of emotional and physiological responses that are activated after confronting or facing a “trigger,” which then connects the person with their past traumatic experiences. Triggers activate traumatic memories, meaning one’s personal damaging and threatening experiences, not the traumatic experiences of others or disturbing topics in general. Triggers then are very personal. Someone can get triggered by the color green even when most people find green to be calming. The phrase “go for it” can be a trigger for a particular person because they had a traumatic experience that was connected to that idea, etc. If the person goes through something dangerous that resembles the previous traumatic experience, the emotional reaction will get triggered and the previous symptoms can get exacerbated. If the person stays scared and feels hopeless, then they could develop PTSD.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What do therapists think when a client dissociates in a session?
Answer: Your question brings up a couple of issues. First, “dissociates” has several meanings, and when a therapist has one particular idea of what dissociating means, they may recognize that particular manifestation and may dismiss others. Let me tell you all the different ways someone can dissociate in session: Someone who shifts from one “personality” to another is dissociating (disconnecting parts). Someone who goes “blank” is dissociating (disconnecting from thoughts). Someone who is reliving the past and loses perspective of the present is dissociating (disconnecting from awareness). Someone who is thinking about something else and not engaging with what the therapist is saying is dissociating (disconnecting from the conversation). Someone who feels numb, hears the therapist's voice as muffled, starts losing sight of the edges of things, or feels like floating is dissociating (disconnecting from body/emotions). Someone who is “daydreaming” in session is dissociating (disconnecting from reality). Someone who suddenly feels disoriented, confused, and doesn't know where they are is dissociating (disconnecting from present/body/reality/identity). Which of these types of dissociation are you asking about? Remember that dissociation basically means that an individual experiences a disconnection or separation from their thoughts, feelings, memories, emotions, body, awareness, sense of identity, etc. It means that some brain functions go offline for either an instant, or for a while, but in general, dissociation is not permanent. Depending on the type of dissociation, in one extreme, some therapists may think, “I’m boring the client” or “the client is bored,” and in the other extreme, they may become scared and may not think because they know they have to immediately help the client get grounded to avoid further disconnection. The range is so big, that some therapists may not even notice it’s happening, or may think something else is happening before they realize the client is dissociating. Even clients may not notice. If the therapist notice, they will use an intervention or two to ground the client. Once the client gets grounded, the therapist may be curious about what triggered the dissociation to avoid triggering the client again or help regulate it. Second, it seems you assume therapists have negative thoughts about their clients reactions or behavior, right? That’s why you are asking? Because you think therapists are always judging their clients’ behaviors, thoughts, reactions, etc? They would be bad therapists if they do. Or maybe that’s what we think “analyst do, analyze us all the time? It’s not what most therapists do, specially trauma therapists. The “new” way to do therapy, is to be attuned and attentive to the needs of the client without judgment. I wonder if some clients are constantly questioning what’s in the therapist's head as if they suspect the therapist has a judgment or sees the client with a critical eye. I can tell you that most therapists don’t think much about why clients have certain reactions, especially if those reactions are connected to the client’s issues. What they think is in way to help clients suffer less from those reactions.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What kind of different mind games do narcissists play during a relationship with their partner?
Answer: I know a person who was married to someone with NPD, and she described some of the most incredible mind games. Let me give you some examples: She mentioned that her husband always told her that his family didn’t approve of her, saying they thought X, Y, and Z about her, always pointing at something she was insecure about. For instance, instead of telling her she was not pretty, he could say: “My mother still disapproves of marrying someone who can’t have beautiful children and would spoil our genetic wealth.” She was very religious, and being a good person was important to her, so he used phrases like “My grandmother has been warning me about you all along; she says I should be careful because it’s obvious you have darkness in your heart.” People say that narcissists use gaslighting and manipulation, but the type of mind games that narcissists can play on their partners go beyond that. People with NPD don’t want anyone to outshine them, but they also need people who help them shine. So, they may pick a person who can make them look good for several reasons: a beautiful person, a well-educated one, a wealthy one, etc., but they don’t want that person to be really confident because they may not stay in the relationship with them. Therefore, they need to undermine their partner's confidence. That’s a whole game on its own that can last years without the partner to know it’s intentional and well planned. They also need to feel they dominate the relationship, and they can be very punitive (silent treatment, withdrawal of affection, etc.) as a way to gain power, in addition to the typical love-bombing/devaluation. Undermining the partner’s feelings, thoughts, or experiences becomes a regular practice that the partner may internalize. A form of gaslighting is the well-known (but somewhat out of fashion) technique of "projection." The narcissist may accuse the partner of having the negative traits or behaviors that they themselves exhibit, such as accusing them of being selfish or unfaithful when in reality, they are the ones engaging in such behaviors. This technique is used to avoid taking responsibility for their actions and to blame the partner for any issues or conflicts. If the narcissist is caught in a lie, they might accuse the partner of being too suspicious or paranoid, deflecting attention from their own behavior. Another awful mind game they play is offering apologies or show resentment that are completely insincere, just to manipulate the partner into forgiving them without making genuine amends. They can also be great actors if that’s what is required for them not to take responsibility. I heard of a case where someone "felt sick" and threw up after being "accused" of lying. The partner really felt bad about making the spouse feel so bad about the accusation, only to discover that it was just "acting" since they found out that the spouse had been lying all along.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How dangerous, realistically, can a Cluster B personality disordered individual be?
Answer: A former client was married to a person with a Cluster B PD. I asked her if she ever felt in danger. She said with a smirk that she thought he was the safest guy she knew. She said that for 15 years, she was very confused about being with a person who seemed to completely dismiss her needs most of the time but could be so lovely and honest at other times., but that she never felt at risk. Unfortunately, she lived in this blinded state until one day she learned he had defrauded a couple of people and had legal and financial problems. That’s when she knew he had always hidden their money, had been using drugs for a while, had been fired from previous jobs, had several lovers, and had been blatantly lying all along about many things. That’s when she realized that she had no idea who her husband was and that she was at risk. That man put everyone at risk with his reckless behavior, his lack of care about consequences, etc. Many of the people around him, including his wife, had no idea he suffered from a Cluster B personality disorder. Some people say that ignorance is bliss, right? Many people have no idea they are dealing with someone suffering from a personality disorder, and therefore, they don’t feel they are at risk in any way. I know many people who are married to persons with BPD. Do they consider their spouses dangerous? Not really. Many of the BPD partners are not explicitly abusive. Their behavior and dysregulation may make the living situation unstable, but unless they are the type who threaten with suicide, they don’t put people at risk. Since our concept of what’s dangerous is subjective, many people may feel at risk when they are not, and some people who are at risk may not feel threatened. I know a person married to a pwBPD who has never felt afraid of the suicide threats. Histrionics may be the least dangerous of Cluster B, which doesn’t mean they can’t hurt people. They may engage in manipulative behavior to gain attention or approval, but this manipulation is generally more benign and less calculated than that seen in other personality disorders, like NPD or ASPD. What about pwNPD? Are narcissists dangerous? People who care none about the needs of others can become dangerous when they “use” others to their own benefit, even if it costs the other their reputation, their stability, their mental health. Like the parent who sexually abuses their children. They may not see themselves as putting them at risk, but exploiting them and making them feel used can make a child feel worthless. Depending on the level of manipulation and gaslighting, they can push a person to feel crazy or to do something they “would never do” like stealing, lying, or something else that can actually put them at risk. This disorder moves into dangerous areas like malignant or Machiavellian narcissism, which can include antisocial behavior, sadism, and a greater propensity for aggression and manipulation; those are definitely and objectively dangerous. How dangerous is a person with antisocial PD? This is where we get into the most dangerous of Cluster B. People with ASPD do not only disregard the needs of others but also disregard their rights! They engage in unlawful actions and exploitative behavior that easily pose physical, emotional, financial, and social risks. They not only manipulate but also deceive people and drive them into engaging in actions they despise or disapprove. People with ASPD are more likely to engage in behaviors that result in physical harm, criminal activity, and severe psychological trauma, which, in my opinion, qualify them as dangerous.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: After doing trauma processing each time in therapy, I have a hard time sleeping that night. Is this normal?
Answer: What a great question! You may say that you are “processing” trauma because your therapist probably told you that’s what you are doing? But, are you? Imagine a pipe full of water that has been accumulating for a while and it feel it could burst at any point. Then, you open the valve and allow all that accumulation to come out without having prepared a container to receive it and a way to store it. It could feel like this picture: Even if the amount of emotion will be much less, you still need to be prepared for it, and have an idea where it will end up. Many therapists learn a processing technique without having the previous knowledge of what trauma treatment requires. Trauma processing involves working through the feelings, memories, and physiological responses associated with a traumatic event to reduce its negative impact on your mental health and overall well-being. But before someone can process the emotions connected to fragments of memories, you need to be in a physically safe environment, free from ongoing threats or harm, you need to feel emotionally secure, which includes having a sense of stability in your daily life and relationships. Besides, you need to have achieved stabilization in your life, learned regulation skills, have develop tolerance to intense emotions, know hoe to handle them, and how to take in positive emotions and ideas. There are other important aspects but at least, those should be in place if processing could give results. Without those requisites, processing could become the activation of emotions and the physiological manifestations of those emotions. If you “open” fear, and you have no capacity to resolve it because you still feel vulnerable and don’t know how to deal with your response, your brain may interpret you are in danger, and activate your defenses. What you are describing may be connected to staying in a state of alert and hyper-activation and that’s why you may not be able to sleep. Other possibility is that your thoughts are racing and you don’t know how to stop them. In essence, you may not be really processing because you are not finding a better meaning or a resolution to your past experiences. Good processing should leave you more empowered, less afraid or anxious, calmer, and more hopeful. I know colleagues that process every session. I don’t believe in that approach. When I process with my clients, we do it one or 2 sessions and they find resolution. We the n work in some other aspect of the traumatization aftermath before I find another moment where processing becomes ready. Trauma therapy is a dance between resourcing, processing, reprograming, and recovering.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What causes people to forget their capabilities when they feel fearful and anxious?
Answer: Excellent question. I work with many people who complain about brain fog or feeling mentally sluggish. This often happens because the part of the brain responsible for mental agility receives less energy and therefore slows down. Let me explain. The brain has a specific energy budget. Regardless of how many functions it’s performing, it doesn’t receive more energy than if it’s only performing a few. When we feel fearful or anxious, certain brain circuits connected to risk prevention become highly active, consuming a large portion of this energy budget. These circuits sharpen the senses to look for danger or threats and start preparing the body to fight or escape, allocating energy to functions that are usually inactive. Because this energy is diverted to these circuits, it must be taken from other areas. Typically, the energy is taken from the prefrontal cortex, which is responsible for higher-order cognitive functions. This shift in energy allocation diminishes our cognitive capabilities, such as reasoning, remembering or storing new information, decision making, concentration, planning and organization, emotional regulation, and creative thinking.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What do therapists think about after a session?
Answer: Personally, I hardly have a minute to spare for a restroom break between sessions. Like many therapists, my schedule is packed, leaving little mental space for thinking in between. By the end of a day of sessions, mental fatigue sets in. On top of that, many therapists working in clinics may have to write a progress note about each client they saw that day. While this might seem like an opportune moment for thinking about clients, it's often necessary to draw a mental boundary to preserve our ability to function effectively the next day. I have the rule to focus on something else after a day of sessions. If what you want to know is whether your therapist thinks about you in between sessions, I’d say that must probably, they do. Clients are part of the therapist life, and it may be almost impossible not to keep them somehow present in our days. One client comes to mind when I see a show, another when I eat certain food, and another when I hear a joke or a word that they use. It’s also the case that we develop a secure attachment with them, which means that we carry certain confidence on our relationship. As the recently deceased Sue Johnson said: "We are wired for connection. The space between us is not an empty space, but a place of energy that holds our relationships and gives them meaning." So, our clients are guests of that place of energy that add meaning to the life of a therapist. Rest assure, you are indeed present in your therapist’s thoughts.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is a narcisist?
Answer: For decades, narcissists were perceived as arrogant individuals who held themselves in higher esteem than their actual position warranted. The term carried connotations of egotism and self-centeredness. However, there's a growing trend of overusing the term, often inappropriately labeling anyone with high self-esteem as a narcissist. A true narcissist exhibits an unwarranted sense of importance, using it to compete with and undermine others. They may hurt others to maintain their superiority without even noticing, and when noticed, denying their responsibility. When combined with a mental disorder, they may lose touch with reality, believing in the projection they've created, and becoming heartless. Distinguishing between real narcissism from being confident is a fair exercise because using the term has gone to far and pathologize many people that don’t hurt or exploit anyone. Feeling important isn't a flaw if there are valid reasons. We all want and need to feel important and that doesn’t make everyone a narcissist. Using arrogance to belittle others, or inflate achievements and exploit others, though, becomes a problem for many and for society. Narcissism is about manipulation and entitlement, not just confidence or pride. Narcissism is not the same as grandiose; narcissism involves projecting an image of grandeur where none or little exists. One of the worst characteristics of a true narcissist is the fact that they feel entitled to special treatment without regard for others' needs and without having worked on deserving what they feel entitled to. They may exploit situations for their own benefit, showing a lack of empathy or concern and demand getting what they need one way or another. Many people with narcissistic trait may develop narcissistic personality disorder (NPD), where individuals not only disregard others' needs but actively objectify and exploit them for personal gain. These individuals lack empathy and prioritize their own desires above all else, probably because they have deficits in their prefrontal cortex functionality that disconnect them from higher order experiences (leaving them without a connection to their heart). They may live to survive in a world where otherwise, will expose their incapacities. So, hard to say what a narcissist is because there is a whole spectrum, depending on who you ask. It comes from Greek mythology and the tale of Narcissus, a handsome young hunter known for his beauty and disdain for the love of others. One day, while walking by a pool of water, Narcissus saw his own reflection in the water and fell deeply in love with himself. Unable to tear himself away from his own image, Narcissus eventually died. From myth to the name of a mental disorder. According to the stoty, those that see themselves reflected as perfect and are unable to handle it realistically and objectively, so that their “reflection” consumes them, are narcissist. As with everything, before assigning a label, check for the intentions of the person, their level of dysfunction, their actions, and the consequences. The bad or exploitative intentions need to be considered not as an isolated event one day when they were in a bad place, but as a constant drive for their actions. If someone has the intention to make you feel small, is not really big, and their ego is huge, and they hurt people with their attitude and agendas, then it may be fair to call them narcissistic. I knew a person that put a disguised plan to diminish the self-esteem of a colleague until the colleague quit or was fired. It took four years of subtle but insidious comments, actions, traps, until the colleague fell into a depression, made a series of mistakes, and was fired. Four years!!! And day by day the intention never changed. That’s a narcissist.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is it possible for a person's personality to change as a result of trauma and anxiety?
Answer: A young woman I knew suffered from date-rape. She was open and funny before but after the event, she became suspicious of everyone. She felt that everyone around knew and that they though poorly of her afterwards. She also became suspicious of herself because she couldn’t understand why she still wanted to hang with guys and have sex. She became her worst judge and convinced herself she was a failure. Of course her personality changed. Not only one time, but several times in the years that took her to recover some of the shine she had before. Many things can change after trauma if we don’t resolve our fears. If a person develops a trauma syndrome, their personality and maybe their identity will change because their sense of self gets shattered. Trauma can alter the understanding of oneself, our relationships, and the meaning that the world around us. It’s common to struggle with self-doubt, guilt, or shame, question one’s actions or responses during the event, and not knowing what that says about ourselves. This self-questioning can erode self-esteem and confidence, further impacting our personality. As a result of these emotional and cognitive changes, individuals who have experienced trauma may find that their values, beliefs, and interests shift. This change can be particularly noticeable if they develop an aversion to activities, situations, or environments that, knowing or not-knowing, are reminders of the experience that made them feel at risk and defeated. They may avoid situations or events they once enjoyed, leading to a withdrawal from activities that previously formed a significant part of their identity and leaving them confused about their preferences, their likes and dislikes. Also, ongoing struggle with traumatic circumstances can lead to the development of new perspectives and strategies to conform or comply, such as avoidance, hypervigilance, or emotional numbing, which can further impact one's personality and how we engage with others. In essence, the combination of unresolved fears, altered self-perception, and survival strategies can change how a person thinks, feels, and acts, potentially resulting in a shift in their personality and identity.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can someone have BPD and be narcissistic?
Answer: I have still not met a person with BPD (pwBPD) without narcissistic traits. So, yes, individuals with BPD can exhibit narcissistic traits. However, this is different from meeting the criteria for both disorders. Narcissistic traits include a sense of entitlement, sensitivity to criticism, manipulative and exploitative behaviors, unstable relationships, a need for admiration, attention-seeking, arrogance, envy, a need to control, superficiality, fragile self-esteem, and exaggeration of achievements. Don’t you think that almost everyone has, to some extent, narcissistic traits? Who doesn’t like to be admired, or experience envy, or feel entitled to something? That’s even more pronounced in this era where everyone wants (and can) be famous overnight! Also, be proud of one’s achievements is something we normally judge as narcissistic. It’s hard to win with all the terms and judgments assigned to people that behave a little off from our expectations. That’s actually unfair! On the other hand, saying that someone with a personality disorder is not narcissistic is almost an oxymoron. People suffering from a personality that is not accepted or is perceived as a mental disorder don’t have too many choices but to develop some defenses, and narcissistic traits give them a sense of importance that may balance the pain of not being perceived as “normal.” Of course, I’m talking about traits only, and I’m also acknowledging that every disorder or pathology exists on a spectrum. Having some narcissistic traits (or being narcissistic) is not the same as suffering from Narcissistic Personality Disorder (NPD). Now, let’s examine what both personality disorders have in common from a neurobiological point of view:

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why do narcissists blame mostly everything on their partner or spouse?
Answer: A narcissist is a person that has separated so badly from their core that they become a mere hologram of the person they wish they were. This hollow self, a fragile construct of defenses, idealizations, and smoke screens, needs a relentless projection of infallibility. In their world, fault and failure are intolerable, not because they are beyond error, but because admitting any would shatter the carefully curated illusion of superiority they so desperately cling to. They blame everyone, not just the spouse or partner. Blaming others, especially those closest to them, serves two main purposes: First, it distracts others from seeing any of their imperfections, maintaining the facade of excellence and being in the offense and putting others on the defense. Secondly, it reinforces their self-image by diminishing those around them, keeping them as the perpetual scapegoats for their frustrations and failures. This externalization of blame is not merely a tactic but a necessity for the hollow self to persist. In essence, the narcissist's accusations are less about the actual faults of others and more about the existential threat of acknowledging their own. To admit to a mistake would be to confront the emptiness within, to see the hologram for what it truly is—a fleeting, insubstantial reflection of what they wish to be, rather than a solid, authentic self. Thus, in their universe, blame must always reside elsewhere, a constant testament to the supposed stupidity and smallness of those around them, making sure the illusion of their own grandiosity remains unchallenged.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: If a person with borderline personality disorder has a loving partner, can they heal faster?
Answer: If only!!! That sounds like wishful thinking. I hear a big risk in your question; the risk that the loving partner could quickly become co-dependent of the pwBPD emotional turmoil. It’s common to see that loving partners of pwBPD, on an effort to stabilize the partner's emotions, may start to prioritize their partner's needs above their own, neglecting self-care and personal boundaries. This dynamic can lead to an unhealthy reliance where the loving partner feels responsible for managing and mitigating emotional crises, promising never to give up, numbing their pain or frustration when they fail helping the person, ultimately feeding a cycle of dependency that is difficult to break. As the loving partner of someone with BPD becomes increasingly enmeshed in the emotional ups and downs, the relationship risks becoming unbalanced and emotionally exhausting. Of course, there are cases of pwBPD that are determined to improve for an important reason, and then, a loving relationship could potentially support and positively influence the healing process, but there needs to be a lot of awareness that the needs of the loving partner as also important and need to be attended.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is the normal behavior of a person who has been abused?
Answer: Every person has a unique set of conditions that rule their responses and behavior. One one extreme of the spectrum, there are people that have been abused that have a lot of tolerance and could react with compassion and have no changes in their behavior because they don’t take the abuse personally, know how to set boundaries, and resolve the issues before it affects them. In the other extreme, there are people that collapse and feel lost, unlovable, defeated, etc., after experiencing whatever they feel abusive. Strictly speaking, abuse has to do with behaviors that intentionally harm or manipulate another person, causing physical, emotional, psychological, or sexual harm. Abuse often involves a misuse of power and control over another individual. Still, I know many people that feel abused even if there is no intention to harm them. For example, micro-aggressions—subtle, often unintentional comments or actions that can be perceived as discriminatory or demeaning—are considered a form of abuse. Microaggressions come from a place of privilege and are regular practices to marginalize or belittle individuals from disadvantaged groups. Microaggressions can include remarks that make assumptions about someone's abilities, intelligence, or worth based on their race, gender, sexual orientation, or other aspects of their identity. These behaviors, though seemingly minor for those that practices them (and unintentional), can be considered a form of abuse and can accumulate over time causing big harm in the psyche of those that keep being the receiving end of them. There are other examples of behaviors that are considered as abusive by some, like white lies, keeping secrets, overprotection, excessive constructive criticism, well-meaning interference, etc. Perceived abuse occurs when actions or words, regardless of intent, make someone feel disrespected, marginalized, unsafe, fearful, or hurt. While the intention of many people may not be to cause harm at all, these actions can still lead to feelings of mistrust, exclusion, inadequacy, or control and can be considered by many as forms of abuse. My point here is that we are not sure what abusing other person means for that person. For some individuals, very few actions are abusive, while for others, many actions feel abusive. A boss telling the subordinate to dress up could feel like abuse, or at least as hurtful for some that will then will show shifts in their behavior, while some subordinates will be grateful for the attention and care of the boss pointed out they need to meet the standards. If the person is abused in the strict sense of the term, we also have to investigate what type of abuse occurred. Sexual abuse has a very specific type of sequela, different from those that were abused physically, or abused emotionally. In general, again, we have to consider the uniqueness of each of us. The way we respond to abuse can vary widely based on several factors, including our personality or traits, the severity and duration of the abuse, the support systems available, and whether they have received any therapeutic intervention. The common changes on behavior could be hyper-vigilance, avoidance, emotional distress, trust issues, and maybe self-medication and problems in relationships. For sexually abused people, you have to add guilt/shame, secrecy, self-esteem issues, and probably either avoiding sex, sexual pain, or an excess of interest in sex. For those that get physically abused, you’ll probably see either aggression or submissiveness,, physical pain or illnesses, depression, trust and self esteem issues, and withdrawal. Emotionally abused people may be anxious, with a low or damaged sense of self, extremes of perfectionism or over-compliance, fear of failure, and emotional instability.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What prevents a narcissist from achieving self-awareness?
Answer: Self-awareness takes time to develop. It starts at around 18 months to 2 years old, when children begin to recognize themselves in mirrors and understand that they are separate entities from others. It becomes more sophisticated, with a greater ability to reflect on one's own thoughts and feelings once we reach adolescence and it continues to develop as individuals encounter various life experiences and engage in introspective practices. Developing deeper levels of self-awareness can take years of intentional practice and reflection. Its development is directly connected to the development of the prefrontal cortex (PFC) is such that as the PFC matures, individuals become better at evaluating their actions and making thoughtful decisions, which are higher-order executive functions such as planning, decision-making, and impulse control. The maturation of the prefrontal cortex is connected to the development of self-awareness. As the PFC develops, individuals become better at self-regulation, emotional control, understanding, and reflective thinking, all of which are essential components of self-awareness. Personality disorders also develop over time. They frequently start developing in childhood or adolescence and become more apparent in late adolescence or early adulthood. NPD may start developing pretty early, once early experiences of praise combined with pressure to be the best, idealization of being superior, inconsistent parenting, and overindulgence, contribute to distortions on self-image, entitlements, and maladaptive patterns of thinking, feeling, and behaving. If we consider that the development of executive functions that play a role in the development of awareness are highjacked by the formation of the defenses that constitute a personality disorder, we then can see that those important functions will be compromised. In the case of the development of NPD, the individual's focus on maintaining an inflated self-image can prevent them from acknowledging their own flaws and understanding the impact of their behavior on others. This hijacking of executive functions by the formation of a “hollow” self that represent what the parents expected but lacks the substance or confidence of being it, meaning that the crucial skills needed for self-regulation, emotional control, social understanding, and reflective thinking are compromised. Over time, these deficiencies can solidify, making it difficult for the individual to develop a balanced and realistic self-concept and to engage in healthy interpersonal relationships because there are brain functions that got replaced. The hollow-self takes over and they get farther and farther away to connect with their core. Many other emotional conflict add to this disconnection. For example, realizing that they lack empathy may cause them to feel more insecure (and ashamed), which they will resolve by numbing the awareness of their lack of empathy and flaws. In this way, they can continue to function better in their perceived role of being superior, but they distance themselves more and more from self-awareness, accountability, and the belief that they are like everyone else. They have no choice but to keep making everyone, including themselves, believe in their superiority. You may like this article:

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is the worst thing about being loved by someone who has borderline personality disorder (BPD)?
Answer: One of the worst things is to discover that what you thought was love is not exactly that. Instead, your emotional relationship may be based on emotional scarcity and dependence. Individuals with BPD frequently view their partners as sources to fulfill their unmet needs and, more often than not, struggle to consider their partners' needs. This is not because they are unwilling to give, but because their emotional struggles push them to focus more on themselves than on others. Their emotional landscape is dominated by intense fear of abandonment and instability, making it difficult for them to maintain a balanced and reciprocal relationship. pwBPD don’t typically love in the romantic sense of reciprocity and equality. Their relationships tend to be imbalanced because their needs are so overwhelming that they often overshadow their partners' needs almost by definition. This is because the way they choose their partners often revolves around finding someone who can provide something they lack, whether it is emotional stability, financial support, social status, cultural experience, etc. So, what is the worst part? What initially feels exciting and intensely passionate can quickly turn into a nightmare. The initial idealization, where you are put on a pedestal, can swiftly turn into devaluation, where you are seen as worthless or inadequate. This drastic shift can be bewildering and hurtful. The exhilarating feeling that they need you more than anything can transform into a suffocating prison. Their neediness can become overwhelming, leading to a situation where you feel responsible for their emotional well-being, often at the expense of your own. In essence, the worst thing about being loved by someone with BPD is the volatility and unpredictability: from intense passion and idealization to harsh devaluation and emotional turmoil. This rollercoaster can leave you feeling drained, confused, and emotionally exhausted. As always, each person is different and not because some people get assigned a label, that means that we can know how they feel or who they are. Some people may argue that they have BPD and that able to love unconditionally. It may be the case that the label is wrong, that the definition of unconditional is partial, or that love means something else for them. Who really can say what love is? Maybe being loved by someone is enough to fell fulfilled, and to overcome the challenges of a relationship. Why focusing in finding “the worst”? Relationships as difficult. It’s not fair to assign labels when someone finds it harder than others to relate or to regulate because they didn’t have enough love as children.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What are the reasons behind people with PTSD having dramatic emotional reactions? What factors contribute to this type of reaction?
Answer: The word “dramatic” in your question may only partially refer to people with PTSD. Dramatic means that there is an intense display of emotions, but not every person with PTSD shows their overwhelming emotions or disproportionate reactions. In fact, a very disproportionate emotional reaction can cause a person to faint, which has nothing to do with wanting to be dramatic, but rather how severe their physiology responds to fear. The reason a person can have an intense reaction without much warning is that specific reminders or stimuli connected to a previous threatening situation can get triggered, even if the person can’t identify what it is. The emotions involved are typically very strong and may include feelings such as extreme anger, fear, sadness, panic, or despair. Even when some emotional reactions can look “dramatic” such as crying, yelling, shaking, sweating, or even physical aggression, some emotional reactions cause mutism, numbing, going blank, becoming immobilized, dissociating, or withdrawing completely from the situation. These reactions are not visible but are as intense as the obvious ones. So, maybe not dramatic, but definitely intense. Let’s see why. The autonomic nervous system (ANS) of people with PTSD has shifted from operating regularly to operating in survival mode. This means that the person's brain anticipates that if they encounter danger, they will not be able to survive, and therefore, will be trying to detect threats all the time. Besides the hyper-alertness, the nervous system will use its protective mechanisms in crisis mode if an event similar to a previous one that jeopardized the person's life happens again. That’s where the intensity comes from. The ANS branches will react much more severely than the time when the person confronted the risk because “survival mode” assumes the person almost died. Remember that PTSD unfolds from the presence of hopelessness and a defeat mentality. What you call dramatic is actually an exaggerated reaction that doesn’t match the level of risk the person is experiencing. That’s why to the people around, it seems out of place and many assume it is attention-seeking or manipulation. The reality is that the person with PTSD may feel excruciating emotional pain; some feel as if their life is leaving their body, as if they are falling into an abyss, or as if a monster is going to swallow them entirely. Understanding these reactions as intense rather than dramatic helps us recognize the impact of operating in crisis mode all the time. The more times we get triggered and have these type of reactions, the less tolerance we have and the higher the aggregation of negative emotions and lack of safety. The solution is to be present and make the effort to assess the real level of risk.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is the typical duration for neurofeedback to show results in treating PTSD/complex trauma?
Answer: There are many models and different types of devices, so the answer must be considered with caution. Results from one-size-fits-all systems are quite variable; they may work sometimes for some people and may be ineffective for others. Additionally, effects observed from these systems can be short-lived, potentially disappearing after a few months. A treatment that utilizes a reputable system and is administered by a professional that has good knowledge of both, the brain's functions and neurofeedback techniques, typically requires at least 20 sessions, and possibly up to 60. The efficacy of the treatment is also influenced by the frequency of the sessions: more frequent sessions can lead to faster and more significant improvements. For example, someone attending only two sessions per week might need 40 or more sessions, whereas someone attending five sessions per week could see substantial results after just 20 sessions. Following these initial improvements, an additional 10 to 20 sessions could be spaced out to consolidate the gains. The way individuals respond to neurofeedback can vary greatly depending on factors such as the person's history, the severity of symptoms, and overall mental health. Studies suggest that neurofeedback can be effective for PTSD/complex trauma, but outcomes are best when the treatment is part of a comprehensive therapeutic plan. I like doing “relational neurofeedback” to add the effect of the relationship to the results. Still, treatment doesn’t end after the NFB sessions. Trauma has to be approached from different angles and NFB is only in charge of the regulation of the nervous system. Emotions still need to be processed as well as other domains such as sense-of-self, memories, cognition, perception, etc. So, committing to long-term treatment and NFB follow-up sessions need to happen to sustain the improvements achieved through the initial NFB training. Also, maintenance phases are also recommended to help preserve the benefits of treatment over time.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can adults still have emotional scars from childhood trauma and abuse, even after seeking therapy and following recommended recovery methods?
Answer: Did you ever cut yourself as a child? Do you still have scars from when you were a kid? I assume you do. It’s very rare that someone reaches adulthood without a scar in their skin, right? But what about fractures. Those are more difficult to see if the person that suffered a fracture will always remember because there are often reminders when temperature changes, or when they stress the part were the fracture was. Do you think scars or healed fractures last until adulthood, even if the individual received medical treatment such as stitches, antibiotics, rest, or physiotherapy? Yes, they do! Sometimes scars make the area stronger, and sometimes the are becomes more vulnerable to open again. It depends where the cut was. Depending on the severity and depth of the injury, the scar may be more or less visible and permanent. Well, psychological scars function in a similar way. They persist! That doesn't mean they continue to cause severe distress or always require significant attention. They might hurt a little when recalling the events, or perhaps not at all, but our brains hold onto them as reminders to help prevent similar situations from happening again. Much like physical scars, the severity and depth of emotional injuries can make a person more vulnerable to experiencing similar harm in the future. Repeated occurrences can cause more severe consequences and long-lasting effects. If someone hurts you the same way you were hurt before, the pain will be not only double, but many times worse. The brain may stop trusting your judgement since you allowed yourself to be in danger again, and may react in more dramatic way to make sure your survive this time and that you don’t take chances again. If you go to therapy and resolve the hurt, then, even if it happens again, you may find it much easier to overcome the pain because you already assigned a different meaning to the experience.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What can cause symptoms of PTSD in individuals with no history of trauma or abuse?
Answer: Trauma is not an extreme event or circumstance. Who gets traumatized is very subjective. A person starts showing PTSD symptoms as soon as they feel hopeless about resolving a situation that is very important to them. So important that the brain assumes their life is at risk. What could be so important that feeling hopeless is considered dangerous? Imagine a pianist that hardly pays the bills thanks to their gigs. and they they starts having pain in their fingers and the doctors tells them they may have rheumatoid arthritis. They think there is no other way they can make money because they never did anything besides learning to play the piano. Hearing about an illness that is not fatal should not be so scary, but for that person, it may mean being evicted, and not finding the way to earn their living. We may all think that they may be able to do many other types of jobs to earn so money, but that’s the thing about trauma; when we feel scared, the brain puts all the energy in our survival mechanisms and our cognition fails to see even the most obvious solutions. When our system responds to that level of fear and defeat, the alterations manifest as symptoms. If the person doesn’t find a solution, the brain will continue assuming there is danger danger, which at some point will cause more permanent damage to the system and symptoms may get worse or stay as constant. That’s when the person may get the PTSD diagnosis. You don't need a history of traumatic experiences to become scared one day. Imagine living in a castle your entire life, and then being attacked and bitten by a huge rat while strolling in the gardens. This could likely cause severe PTSD, as you never had to develop resilience or thought you could be at risk. Your life was protected, and you never expected to feel vulnerable in your own castle. The less skills to overcome obstacles or challenges, the more susceptible you may be to PTSD.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: I have BPD. Why do I destroy everyone I love?
Answer: I’m sorry to say it like this, but do you notice even your question is self-referential? It’s interesting to see the difference between the content of your question where some may hear a tone of empathy for those you hurt, versus the form you ask the question, where may see how you make everything about yourself. It’s ironic, but the answer may be exactly there. People who are consistently self-referential tend to focus primarily on their own experiences, perspectives, and emotions, and may exclude or minimize others' experiences and feelings. When you are in pain, you may care about you and only you, and allow yourself to say or do things that will hurt others, and as you say, even destroy them. It may not be their goal to destroy others, but when a person that suffers from dysregulation feels attacked or triggered, whether the attack is real or just assumed, the pwBPD will lose control over their reactions and may actually want to end the possibility of having that person making them feel as horrible as they feel. What they experience in those moments when they become destructive is so intense that they feel the need to make whatever or whomever is hurting them to stop. They may not realize that the way they feel isn't necessarily caused by the other person but rather by the combination of a potentially distorted perception of the present and negatively charged memories from the past, combined with the level of activation of their dysregulated system. However, they perceive the person in front of them as being fully responsible for their feelings. The solution, in their mind, is to lash out at them, and even crush them if necessary. If the other person has known the person with BPD for a while, they may not be destroyed, but the relationship could certainly be damaged. Unfortunately, the person with BPD often loses what they need the most—having someone attending to their needs—due to the consequences of their disorder. It’s undoubtedly a challenging disorder for all involved. Despite this, people with BPD often find ways to stay afloat and, as depicted in the picture, may even seem unaware of the impact their behavior has on others and the relationship. You are being honest. You know that sometimes, your actions coming from the dysregulation “destroys” those you love. Have you ever acknowledge it with them?

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What do we call this condition in psychology where someone feels like they are stripped of their "self" and can you explain it?
Answer: You may be referring to depersonalization if what you feel is to be detached from your thoughts, feelings, sensations, or identity, or if you fee as if you were observing yourself from outside your body or that your thoughts and actions are not your own. This doesn’t last long. Normally, it comes and goes, or happen just once in a while, if ever again. If that’s not it, it may be that you are talking about having an unstable or non-developed sense of self, which may manifest as uncertainty about your values, goals, beliefs, or identity. This one feels as you describe it when you “fuse” yourself with another person and you feel that you are not you if you were separated from that person. This one is more permanent and feel regularly, as part of who the person is. The first one, depersonalization, happens as a consequence of high levels of stress or overwhelming experiences, where your brain’s processes keep you away from distressing emotions and physical pain. Certain substances, such as marijuana, hallucinogens, or dissociative drugs like ketamine, can induce depersonalization. The second one, an unstable sense of identity or a lack of sense of self, happens when children grow up in environments where their emotional needs are not consistently met and they may struggle to form a stable identity or a sense of who they are. It may be by adverse experiences like abuse, attachment issues, difficult life transitions or social adversity, or may be by cultural values where kids get assigned a specific role regardless of their personal preferences or inclinations.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is the difference between a psychopath and psychotic?
Answer: Similar words but very different issues. Psychopath used to be a diagnosis that now is part of Antisocial Personality Disorder. Psychosis is a symptoms instead of a diagnosis. In case you don’t know, a diagnosis is given when many symptoms are present for quite a while, because symptoms can come and go. Psychosis is actually a symptoms of several disorders but not in psychopathy. Psychosis has to do with disruptions in though processes that distort perception of reality, which can include hallucinations (perceiving things that aren't there) and delusions (believing in things that aren't true). A psychopath is a person that has many issues that are associated with antisocial personality disorder (ASPD). It’s a personality disorder, which means they have symptoms that reflect mainly on their behavior such as lack of empathy, remorse, and guilt, along with shallow emotions and a tendency to manipulate others for personal gain. They also show impulsive and irresponsible behavior, disregard social norms and laws, and have a diminished capacity for forming meaningful relationships. As I said, psychopaths are not psychotic.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is the difference between PTSD and severe anxiety or depression caused by trauma?
Answer: Severe anxiety and depression are possible symptoms of PTSD. You may have depression or anxiety without PTSD, but you can’t have PTSD without being depressed (low mood, sadness, and hopelessness) sometimes, or anxious (hyper-vigilant, excessive worry and fear) most of the time. There is not much more to say about this :-)

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How can emotional neglect manifest in adults?
Answer: I like your question because most people talk about abuse but ignore neglect or assume it’s the same. I like separating it from abuse because the type of hurt neglect leaves in a child may be very different from the one that abuse leaves. I’m going to consider that the adult that was neglected as a child has not found anyone that help them feel valuable to answer your question, because the hurt that neglect leaves could be resolved soon as the child grows older and find or develop a support network. Emotional neglect can manifest in adults in various ways, often with subtle but significant impacts on their emotional well-being and the way they relate to others. Unlike physical neglect, which may have visible signs, emotional neglect can be challenging to identify. Children experiencing emotional neglect may not even recognize it as such, and may not develop a victim mentality the way some children develop after abuse. The effects of emotional neglect can be diverse and may result from different factors, including voluntary or circumstantial situations, omission, or commission. While physical and medical neglect pose immediate risks to a child's life and can have the effect that the person develops a chronic illness due to the lack of attention, emotional neglect could cause long-term harm without overtly threatening the child's safety. Instead of triggering immediate physiological responses to stress, emotional neglect can lead to synaptic pruning (de-activating neurons that are not used) if it happens early in life, affecting brain connectivity and development. Emotionally neglected individuals often internalize feelings of insignificance or lack of value. They may struggle to understand and meet their own emotional needs and may develop difficulties in forming close relationships. This can lead to behaviors such as excessive people-pleasing, withdrawal, or fear of intimacy in adulthood. Emotional neglect can also affect the development of a healthy sense of self and identity. As always, not everyone is the same and the individual characteristics of the neglected child play an important role in how emotional neglect will manifest in adulthood. Some adults may exhibit dissociative tendencies, while others may struggle with developmental challenges. Some of them may like being alone, may have difficulty expressing or understanding their emotions, they may often escape people of situations where they could feel out-of-place, or they may become the most reliable person you ever met. There is another interesting aspect of emotionally neglected individuals. Since they didn’t have someone to teach them essential life skills or provide emotional nurturing, neglected children may develop a strong inclination towards self-reliance and independence. As a result, many neglected individuals become adept at learning on their own (autodidacts) and excel in various areas of their lives, particularly in their professional activities. That type of response to the neglect may still have psychological consequences in how they perceive themselves as not lovable, but could make them very confident professionally, or personally because they may be very competent in areas that are not job related. They may develop self-esteem around their abilities that could actually help them meet the right people to interact with. They may never be the most popular individuals, but they may be admired.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is the purpose of a therapy session without attachment or emotional connection?
Answer: Venting, maybe? I guess some people go to therapy just to have someone to talk to, without caring about connecting. It’s not uncommon at the beginning of the therapeutic relationship that there is no much connection, but if that continues for long, it may be that the client is not really committed to grow, doesn’t understand what therapy is about, or they may have emotional, psychological, or even cultural barriers that stop them from creating a healthy bond. I have had clients that talk without looking at me, and when they do, it’s as if I’m transparent or not in the room. They may still get something out of therapy, even if only at a cognitive level. I know it takes time to develop trust, but ideally some level of connection between client and therapist develops in order to get better results. There are people that are very guarded but have the capacity to develop some respect or confidence in the therapist. That could be enough. Attachment between client and therapist may be a different story. You can be in treatment for years without ever developing a complete bond of trust, safety, and empathy for your therapist. It takes to open emotionally, especially if the experience of being hurt in vulnerable moments. Also, clients may not care to empathize with the therapist since therapist disclose so little about themselves. That can keep them apart. Many clients develop emotional dependence that at some point could even be detrimental. It may be the experience of some individuals that suffered a lot after a break-up with a therapist, or that have been disappointed. But If you have the courage to go talk to a stranger about your difficulties, you are already gaining something. Venting with a therapist may take you to a much better place than just venting with anyone.
