I knew one client that dismissed every single thing I told him to do, which help me discovered his narcissistic trait. Once I did, I changed the strategy and he started to get better. If you are paying for a service, make the best of it. Otherwise, you are fooling yourself. Imagine you are going to a restaurant and you put all the food in a plastic bag but don’t tell the waiter. You pay but are still hungry. What benefit could you get from that? Tell the waiter you didn’t like the food, so they can suggest some other option that makes your hunger go away.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is the typical timeframe for PTSD symptoms to appear after experiencing trauma or danger?
Answer: Lisa lost her job at a time when she was full of debts. She felt utterly shocked and fearful about her future. Various emotions, such as fear, shame, guilt, and doubt, surged within her and quickly manifested as symptoms. She had nightmares about becoming homeless, avoided anything work-related, and became highly reactive and depressed. Weeks passed, and instead of proactively searching for jobs, she spent her days watching TV, avoiding people out of fear of being judged, and neglecting self-care. Her symptoms worsened with each passing day. By a stroke of luck, a friend from college reached out to her, inquiring about her well-being and mentioning that her company was looking for someone with Lisa's profile. She asked Lisa if she would be interested in an interview. In that moment, Lisa regained some of her energy, took better care of herself, and ultimately landed the job. Within a matter of days, her symptoms began to dissipate. According to the DSM, a diagnosis of PTSD doesn’t apply unless the individual has experienced the symptoms for at least 30 days, or 6 months with ‘delayed expression’. Some symptoms start appearing as soon as few hours, even minutes, after the traumatic event is over, or as the shock subsides, but they naturally decrease, also within hours, if the person recovers a sense of safety. Some symptoms are at their highest the week of the event. Some others start developing as the body keeps struggling on finding peace or safety. Research has found that most people (60 to 70%) get back to normal within a year after experiencing a traumatic event even without treatment, which speaks about our natural capacity to recover. Our brain will work on re-establishing whatever functions were disrupted and to regain balance on whatever had gone awry. Our brain operates better when everything works as it should. No interest on keeping us operating in crisis mode. The reason some people don’t bounce back is because they have no mental space to recover objectivity because the brain is consuming a lot of energy using the emergency programs. It uses them because the fear has not gone, and the person may feel helpless. The brain will continue struggling for as long as the person feels that way. More symptoms show up and their severity accumulates. The point where the symptoms become more permanent is when the individual reaches a sense of defeat and hopelessness. That’s when the brain will turn off some functions and take over the decision making to operate in survival mode from then on. Reaching that point means that the whole system has shifted gears, that the internal balance may have been lost, and that the new functionality has become the new baseline. Not optimal functioning but considered indispensable by the brain given that the person doesn’t feel capable to overcome the challenge. Symptoms may become more permanent even if some of them may be less obvious than just after the event.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can individuals who have experienced trauma heal and develop meaningful relationships?
Answer: Firstly, it's important to clarify that experiencing trauma doesn't necessarily mean one is ill or in need of healing. Your question is assuming that experiencing something traumatic makes you ill. That’s not always correct. Trauma is not the experience, but the series of elements that happen from when we experience something dangerous to the lasting effects on our functioning. Experiencing something traumatic is an inevitable part of life but could leave no consequences. Life is full of situations that pose danger, threat, and risk. It’s basically impossible not to confront something that puts ourselves at risk. But we are naturally resilient because of the same reason. We react to danger because we need to protect ourselves, and we count with amazing adaptive qualities in case the danger doesn’t go away. It does not go away!! Think of people that live in environments full of poisonous insects, predatory animals, dangerous snakes. Do you think they live in a house full of traps and don’t leave the house to avoid being killed? No, right? They learn how to spot them and either avoid them, catch them, or learn how to neutralize their effects. The same way, we adapt to the “danger” that an aggressive parent can present, by avoiding it (going to your room to read), assessing how bad it could be, learning to calm down them, or compartmentalize the worry/fear. NOT All Traumatic Experiences are Traumatizing. Many individuals that live with adversity, become used to it and don’t get affected because they use their natural resilience. Those that live in dangerous situations learn to manage them and may not be affected by them. How traumatizing an event or circumstance is depends on a subjective evaluation, which means is different for each person. What’s terrifying for one can be “normal” for another. Adversity doesn’t mean trauma. Exposure to adversity can increase the risk of experiencing long term dysfunction, but not always. Trauma Needs Resolution to Avoid Illness. When there are lasting effects after experiencing something traumatic, the responses need to be resolved. Mainly, we have to develop either confidence we will be OK, hope that we will be OK, or certainty that we will be able to handle the situation. If it is in the past, even more. Resolution means recovering confidence that even when what happened was “awful” and hurtful, we could find ways to feel safe in the future. If we do, sooner rather than later, our adaptive characteristics will help our system recover and we will go back to normal. Yes, something will stay as a reminder, like some memories and maybe some painful emotions the same way that scars could be seen as reminders of an injury and also of our healing capacities. If the emotional and physiological reactions after the event are not resolved, then that individual could develop a trauma disorder. Trauma disorders need to be healed. What does that mean? That the effects of our responses have become the new program our brain uses to see and navigate the world, and it needs to be re-programmed to go back to normal. The autonomic nervous system needs to recover equilibrium, our executive functions need to be reactivated, our perception needs to be corrected to have a more objective take on what’s dangerous and what’s safe, our emotional scripts need to be reviewed and reprogramed for our emotional reactions to fall inside a tolerable range, our sense of self need to be reinforced, our level of engagement needs to be revamped and maybe our social skills improved. The memories may need to be proceeded to avoid them be intrusive but some memories will remain because that’s how our brain learns to protect itself. You ask if the can have meaningful relationships. Of course they can! but they need to recover meaning about life by feeling safe, confident, hopeful, trusting, and enthusiastic about future possibilities. They have to understand that the past was just a lesson, and that there are many more lessons to be learned, and that now they may have better skills to manage whatever comes.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can someone grow up in a toxic, dysfunctional home without developing PTSD or other mental health issues? Is therapy necessary for someone who does not have PTSD or depression?
Answer: I know someone who grew up in a very dysfunctional and toxic home environment. Her parents struggled with substance abuse, constant arguments, and financial instability. When she was 8, they became homeless, and they didn’t get a home until her father became a drug dealer. Despite the chaos in her life, she found solace in reading and writing. Focusing on stories and learning helped her escape the turmoil around her and motivated her to set ambitious goals. Today, she's a successful lawyer who helps families struggling with addiction, and she's happily married. She went to therapy for a while but mainly to develop more resilience, and not because she had any diagnosed disorder. We all struggle emotionally one way or another, but not everyone is mentally or emotionally dysfunctional. We humans are remarkably resilient, and we have the capacity to learn coping mechanisms or to adapt effectively from an early age to navigate challenging circumstances without significant psychological consequences. Additionally, our natural healing capacities allow us to recover well, especially when our minds support the process. Regarding your second question, therapy is essential for those experiencing mental health issues, emotional difficulties, or relationship problems. However, it also serves as a means for personal growth, helping us gain self-awareness, improve communication skills and relationships with ourselves and others. Going to therapy is a sign of strength and self-awareness, demonstrating a willingness to take steps toward improving mental and emotional well-being

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What are some signs that a therapist may not have enough training or experience in treating trauma?
Answer: Let’s be real! A paradigm shift takes long time to adapt and trauma has brought up a very different lens to understand mental health. It seems we haven’t even grasped at the extent of what it means to see mental disorders using neurobiology. Trauma is a phenomenon clearly observable in our physiology and not only a construct like many others in psychology. For instance, trauma is very linked to emotions, and we haven’t even agreed on what an emotion is. There's a growing movement to view mental health through a neurobiological lens, recognizing its link to behavior. This shift requires ongoing discourse and adaptation within the therapy field. Even when there are multitude of therapists and organizations actively working to improve our understanding and treatment of trauma, it will take time to get to a point where everyone is certain on how to treat trauma effectively. That’s why it’s not easy to answer your question. There are many challenges in the field of trauma therapy. One is how difficult is to shift to the new approach. It requires to “forget” most of what therapists have learned and relearn it using a different lens. Another challenge is to call trauma to everything that is upsetting or emotionally challenging. It creates confusion and may foment to work on something unpleasant from the past that is not actually debilitating in the present, and ignoring other issues that may be more detrimental. Another problem in knowing which therapists are well trained is the extreme focus on one or two symptoms, mainly the event and the memories of it. Many modalities target memories as if it was the only issue. That comes from a more linear thinking instead of a systemic approach. So, a therapist may be very good at helping clients process traumatic memories but may be missing the regulation of the nervous system, the brain developmental issues, the lack of sense of self, or other domains that are also affected by traumatization. Unfortunately, our understanding of trauma is still poor. It makes it hard to have a good training in treating trauma if we are not sure what we are treating. Also, Who’s training trauma therapists? Many of the trauma modalities were invented by people that had limited understanding of what neurobiology keeps discovering, designing their interventions on the previous understanding of mental health. Also, many trainers come from very different schools of thought (like psychoanalysis) and they are training trauma therapist with their previous foundation. Unfortunately, many of us, including clinicians, trainers, supervisors, and clients, are getting information from blogs or articles online that are written with the primary goal of selling something, such as a course, a clinic, or a retreat. As a result, we are inundated with misinformation. Numerous individuals hastily enter the conversation about trauma, often with the intention of creating a brand based on their ability to use social media effectively, coin new terms, share information they find online, or even fabricate it. As more people repeat this incorrect or incomplete information, the more credible it appears. Even AI chats are now providing outdated and biased information with a limited understanding and lack of critical thinking. How could we know what type of information the therapist is getting? There is an interesting situation about “trauma therapists”. Furthermore, the overuse of the term "trauma" has diluted its meaning and made it challenging to discern who has sufficient trauma training. Trauma has lasting effects on the nervous system which causes emotional, psychological, and social issues. Therapists who fail to understand the neurobiology of traumatic experiences and the significance of a dysregulated nervous system may not be well equipped to treat all the issues. Trauma is not about being emotionally hurt but about suffering from not resolving a challenging situation. For example, if somebody criticizes us, it’s only traumatizing when we feel that the criticism can “kill” us or jeopardize our future. If not, our survival circuits don’t go crazy, and therefore, our system doesn’t get hurt. If we call trauma to every hurt, then we could go back to do therapy exactly as we were when therapy was about talking and talking about whatever “bad” had happened to us without really finding resolution.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is the reason behind your therapist's recommendation to try using EMDR techniques?
Answer: I’m going to speak from experience. Every time I receive a referral from another therapist recommending their client for EMDR, it's a client who has not made real progress with the other types of therapy they have tried. The therapist feels lost, tired, discouraged, or stuck, and suggests the modality that is in vogue. EMDR has become the aspirin of the therapy world. Or the Prozac. The idea that there is a magic pill that will take care of your problems in a short period of time has always been in our minds, and we keep trying to find magic cures. Not very far from now, everyone is going to be sent to try psychedelics. Another reason a therapist trained in EMDR might suggest using the modality is either because they just completed their training and need to practice in order to obtain their diploma, or because they believe in the modality and want to help the client process their traumatic memories. Some therapists, however, think that processing memories (sometimes not even traumatic ones) is the panacea. It is not. Processing certain memories that still linger in the present as disturbing realities is beneficial to remove their negative impact in the present, but it is not the only thing that disturbs traumatized people. Learning how to tolerate emotions and regulate their emotional reactions is still one of the most important pieces of healing from trauma, and not many EMDR therapists know how to do this. This article explains how you can help yourself achieving that goal before you enter into a routinary EMDR treatment: By the way, I’m an approved EMDR consultant and really like the modality and its potential, but I use it as needed. This means that I don’t use it as a default experience in every weekly session. I find that approach to be tiring and ultimately ineffective. EMDR should not be as the only way to treat trauma because it may lose its effectiveness and because it’s not indicated for many of the alterations that traumatized people present. On EMDR, t’s an art to choose the right target to be processed, the negative cognition that will be replaced, and the appropriate resolution that will effectively reconsolidate the memory. They are not random; they need to be well conceptualized and planned before the protocol can be applied and the memory to replaced.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Have you ever experienced trauma from negative feedback?
Answer: I know a colleague who was training in a new therapy modality that required trainees to conduct therapy sessions with each other in front of instructors and other trainees. The feedback during the “public” session was not very encouraging, with several interventions being criticized as ineffective. After a long session, my colleague stepped away to gather themselves in a nearby room. They overheard others commenting, "I don't think this person will ever be a good clinician." Another person remarked, "Not only that, but they can harm their clients! I wish there was a way to stop them from being a clinician." Following this negative feedback, my colleague struggled immensely., to the point of having panic attacks in the middle of their sessions, felt constant brain fog, found impossible to concentrate on what the clients where saying, etc. After few months, they decided to stop seeing clients and became really depressed. Would you consider my colleague's experience as trauma resulting from the negative feedback? I would say yes. They became extremely insecure due to the criticism, constantly worrying about their performance and the potential harm they could cause to their clients. Probably, the fear of having a damaged reputation could have also added to the lack of safety they were experiencing. That stress kept growing until they became symptoms. Unfortunately, they didn't address these issues in time, and the symptoms worsened to the point of incapacitating them in the long haul. Trauma is about losing the sense of safety and staying in that state long term. If my colleague had become proactive in “fixing” the problems they were having with the modality, for example, talking to the instructors and getting mentorship to overcome the challenges, or something to recover a sense of safety, they may not have ended up “ill”. What makes an event to be considered “trauma” is its permanence. If we intervene timely, we can recover our confidence, and our system will not suffer lasting consequences.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How can trauma be properly processed when it is still happening?
Answer: In theory, you can’t resolve trauma if it is still happening. Trauma is about feeling unsafe, and “processing” it means that you could notice that your fear and sense of unsafety are just in your past. That realization need to be experienced at every level, visceral, cognitive, and felt-sense, and physically, as real in the present (that you are actually safe) as it can be to resolve the trauma. How could you recover the sense of safety if you are still in danger? Processing trauma is a vital component of healing, as it involves making sense of the traumatic experience, integrating it into one's life narrative, and developing new strategies to manage whatever lasting effects are still lingering. If you are still in danger, you can’t make sense of the past because it’s the same as the present; you can’t integrate the “new” meaning into your narrative because your defeating narrative is based on what you are still experiencing. What you can actually do, is to develop coping mechanisms and new strategies to become stronger, and to be proactive in finding safety one way or another instead of trying to process the past. Those mechanisms or skills you could try to develop include learning how to regulate your nervous system to avoid further damage by continue getting triggered and retraumatized. If you are aware of what triggers you, you can create some mental space to get some distance from the traumatizing occurrences. Connecting with supportive individuals, such as family, friends, or support groups, can give you some space too, and a sense of belonging and validation during ongoing traumatization. Sharing experiences and receiving empathy from others can foster resilience and help you cope with the situation. But most of all, you have to work developing agency and confidence in order to stop whatever is hurting you. Your health depends on you finding a way to feel and be safe. I remember a client that went back to school to get a degree as the preparation to be able to leave the abusive relationship she was into. It may take time for you to find safety, but you have to start somewhere.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: If a child was always soothed and given attention constantly could this create a sort of neediness in them? They would never learn to self soothe and so they would be dependent on other people for that comfort. Anxious attachment style?
Answer: I recall those sorts of directives from certain childcare philosophies that advocate allowing babies to cry until they learn to calm themselves. It seems like an approach from another era, yet it persisted during my own child-rearing days. But there is always there a large amount of advice on what's best for children. I learned early on that each child is unique, with their own set of needs and preferences. It became clear to me that I needed to tailor my approach to parenting according to my children's individual needs, rather than adhering to a one-size-fits-all strategy. From the outset, it's evident that every child is distinct, even in the womb. Some fetuses are calm and still, while others are more energetic and restless. You can often discern early on whether a baby will be easily soothed or require more frequent attention. Still, all infants have a lot of needs and they expect someone to help them. In general, when we are born, almost every organ still needs to finish developing and maturing, and that means having pains that they can’t avoid. Their intestines, for example, are porous, which means that babies may be more susceptible to certain food allergies, intolerances, and gastrointestinal issues. Relevant to your question, lets remember that baby’s nervous system is immature and feels distress very easily. Without proper attention and attunement, the baby will be anxious and even probably, shut down. Contrary to the notion that constantly soothing a child might create neediness, attachment theory suggests that attuning to a baby's needs helps them developing trust and facilitates the development of a secure attachment. In this view, a baby who receives consistent soothing and attention is more likely to develop a secure attachment, feeling confident that their caregiver will respond to their needs. This can lead to less frequent requests for attention as the child becomes more secure in their environment, focusing instead on exploration and learning. Conversely, a baby who does not receive adequate soothing and attention may develop an anxious attachment, seeking constant reassurance and attention to fulfill their unmet needs.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Do individuals who have experienced trauma tend to talk about it more than others? If so, what motivates them to share this information with others?
Answer: What you are referring to is probably related to “trauma centrality.” Trauma centrality refers to the extent to which an individual's trauma experiences are central to their sense of identity and self-concept. It is about how big is the significance they attribute to what happened to them and how much it shapes their worldview, relationships, and life trajectory. In many of those cases, they may tend to think a lot about what happened to them, and therefore, it may be easy for them to talk about it. It’s their reference point from where they perceive other people experiences. But maybe they talk about their traumatic experiences as a way to seek emotional support and understanding from friends, family members, or support groups. Talking about their experiences may help them feel less alone and more supported in their healing journey. It could also be a way to seek sympathy and validation. This is a double edge sword. If they find support, and that support helps them feel safer, then sharing is helpful and beneficial. But if they only share to get sympathy, they could increase a feeling of victimhood that can actually be detrimental for their healing. You can read something about that negative aspect here: In the positive side of sharing often, sharing traumatic experiences and its aftermath can be a part of the subconscious process of making sense of the experience with the intention of integrating them into one's identity and life narrative. Talking about their experiences with traumatic events may help individuals make meaning of what happened and find a sense of closure or resolution, and a way to reclaim power and control over their story and experiences. There is also the case for people with extreme experiences that sometimes may be silenced by those that find them shameful, that speaking out is a way to refuse to be silenced or defined by their experiences, asserting their agency in shaping their own narrative. That could be really empowering for them but also for many others that would feel motivated to do the same. That offers a collective healing experience. Like with everything, it depends of the intention and level of awareness of those sharing. Without awareness and intention, talking about negative experiences may only make things worse.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What methods do therapists use to prevent being triggered by their clients while treating those with PTSD or complex trauma?
Answer: In an ideal world, therapists should have worked already to identify their triggers and resolved their trauma symptoms. If the therapist has worked on their issues, they could be completely “present” in sessions, without the interference of their own material. Having worked on their own personal struggles helps them maintain self-awareness and prevent unresolved issues from interfering with their work. Even in cases where the therapist has not finished working on their own issues, or when the client share unexpectedly highly upsetting material, the therapist should know how to practice self-regulation techniques and grounding exercises to manage their own emotional responses during therapy sessions. These techniques help them stay present and centered, even in the face of challenging material. BTW, the word “trigger” is used excessively as a synonymous of “reaction”. In a strict sense, we only get “triggered” when we live a circumstance that is very similar to a traumatic experience we previously had and that we have not resolved. It’s not common that the therapist has experienced something so similar to the client that it almost feels as reliving it. To understand better what being triggered means, you can read this article:

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why do certain individuals experience trauma even after seemingly insignificant incidents?
Answer: Do they? or do they say the have trauma without really knowing what it means? It’s not common for people to call trauma to whatever upset them, or to adversity in general. I recently posted this quote: That helps explaining that it’s inevitable living a good life without having had bruises or scars. The same way, it’s basically impossible to live life without some emotional upsets, highs and lows, problems in relationships, and hurts. As we engage with others and face the complexities of human existence, we inevitably encounter moments that challenge our sense of self, our relationships, and our understanding of the world. But not all emotional wounds are “trauma”, but rather, they are the inevitable consequences of living, loving, and learning. They are the markers of our human experience, reminding us of our vulnerability but also of our resilience. While some wounds may cut deeper than others, leaving lasting scars, not all of them are injuries that create lasting dysfunction. Trauma should only be used to name those lasting injuries that change our relationship with the world based of the possibility of not surviving. Challenges that leave wounds or scars offer us opportunities to grow, to build our capacity for empathy, and to find meaning in life's challenges. As we learn to tend to our emotional wounds with compassion and grace, we open the door to healing, transformation, and a deeper appreciation for the richness of our human journey. There's a prevailing tendency to label every adverse experience as trauma, leading to the belief that everyone is traumatized. This mindset can weaken our psyche and potentially cause more harm than the initial experience itself. This is what you're hinting at in your question – the notion that some individuals may develop symptoms or profound distress even after minor setbacks. The anticipation of being wounded diminishes our resilience, causing us to exhaust our strength and confidence in the face of future challenges, even when there's no real injury. It’s like bleeding out our power without even a cut.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How often does PSTD really mean Pseudo Traumatic Stress disorder?
Answer: According to Rosen & Taylor, Pseudo posttraumatic stress disorder (pseudo PTSD) describes instances where a patient's symptoms mimic those of the genuine PTSD without an underlying traumatic event. This issue of simulated or pseudo PTSD has been overlooked by numerous clinicians and researchers, who frequently accept a patient's reported symptoms at face value. They state that false presentations of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) can arise from diverse causes like malingering (“the intentional production of false or grossly exaggerated physical or psychological symptoms, motivated by external incentives such as avoiding military duty, avoiding work, obtaining financial compensation, evading criminal prosecution, or obtaining drugs”), somatization disorder (symptoms of physical distress may manifest as psychological symptoms, mimicking PTSD), dissociative disorders (symptoms of dissociation, such as amnesia or depersonalization, can be mistaken for PTSD symptoms), or psychotic disorders (psychotic symptoms, such as hallucinations or delusions, may lead to misinterpretation of experiences as traumatic events, resulting in PTSD-like symptoms). How often people get misdiagnosed with PTSD when they don’t have it? REALLY OFTEN. Probably more often than people getting the right diagnosis. A lot of people nowadays receive the PTSD diagnosis only based on the nature of the experience, or the narrative of the client. That’s maybe because people, clinicians included, don’t have a deep understanding of what trauma means and use the term very loosely. If someone says “I have a lot of trauma”, they take it face value without really understanding if there are lasting consequences in their nervous system or only few memories and a defeating narrative. I worked really hard in explaining what trauma involves and when to give someone a diagnosis to avoid making every client that has experienced adversity as a trauma client. You can check the book almost anywhere Traumatization and Its Aftermath.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can a person be emotionally attached to two people simultaneously? If so, how can one determine if they are experiencing this?
Answer: Your question sounds as if you are either talking about romantic bonds, or believing that attachment is something beyond a mental phenomenon. Attachment, particularly secure attachment, is primarily a mental state and hence, there are no boundaries on to how many people you attach. Emotional attachment refers to the connection and bond that get created between individuals, which can involve feelings of love, care, trust, and/or intimacy. It is not uncommon for people to develop emotional attachments to multiple individuals in their lives, such as friends, family members, or romantic partners. Attachment has to do with mental representations. The internal working models, which are mental representations or schemas of oneself, others, and relationships, develop or get formed from early childhood experiences. These mental models influence how we perceive, interpret, and respond to social interactions throughout our lives. A securely attached individual generally has a positive view of themselves and others, believing that they are worthy of love and care, and that others can be trusted and relied upon. This mental state allows them to form healthy, stable relationships characterized by open communication, mutual trust, and emotional intimacy. This means that the person may feel confident and secure attaching to many because the attachment doesn’t reduce their freedom or makes them dependent, both ways. Having emotional attachments to two or more people simultaneously is not necessarily a problem or cause for concern, as long as the relationships are healthy, respectful, and fulfilling for all parties involved. However, if you are experiencing confusion, conflict, or distress related to these emotional attachments, it may be helpful to learn more about what you are interpreting as being attached. If you are insecurely attached to many people, then it may become a problem because your relationships are creating stress and anxiety. The idea of attaching to others emotionally has to do with trust, freedom, reliance, and confidence, It feel safer to know that there are people you can count on if you need something, that not knowing there are people that can be there for you. A nive definition of attachment I read once is something like: “Attachment is "sharing mental space" with someone who also holds space for you” or something like that. It’s should not create conflict or responsibility.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How is trauma “stored” in the body?
Answer: The concept of "storing" trauma solely in the body is not entirely accurate. It makes a great “title” but that’s not how our system works. The phrase “the body keeps the score” refers to the fact that trauma can leave lasting impacts on both our physical and mental well-being. Trauma is not "stored" in the body in the conventional sense of physical storage like files in a computer. Instead, trauma leaves a lasting imprint on both the body and the brain, impacting the way we perceive and respond to the world around us. One key aspect of understanding how trauma manifests in the body is through the concept of emotions as flows of energy. Emotions are not just abstract feelings but actual physiological responses that travel from our organs to our brain via our nervous system, particularly through the vagus nerve, which is the longest nerve in the body. The brain plays a crucial role in processing and interpreting these emotional signals. It has neurons that receive information from our sensory organs (eyes, ears, etc.) and transmit it to the central nervous system, as well as neurons that send impulses from the central nervous system to our limbs and organs. When we experience trauma, the brain stores the memory of the traumatic event along with its emotional charge and leaves an imprint in the brain that will transform our perception of what’s dangerous versus safe. These changes can be triggered by sensory information similar to the original traumatic experience, whether it's from the senses or from gut feelings and the brain will use that information to make predictions about what could jeopardize the individual. You can read more about predictions here: When those triggers occur, the brain activates survival responses to react to the perceived danger, which can include physiological changes and motor activations. Some theories suggest that trauma is linked to interrupted actions during the traumatic event that need to be completed. For example, if an action like running away was interrupted during the trauma, the emotional charge associated with that action may get stored in the brain and in the muscles of the limbs that were not able to complete the action. When similar triggers occur, the body may "remember" the incomplete action and respond as if it needs to complete it for protection. The idea that the body stores the trauma also comes from the theory that trauma can also manifest in various physical symptoms and conditions. These may include chronic pain, gastrointestinal issues, autoimmune disorders, and even cardiovascular problems. The prolonged stress response associated with trauma can dysregulate the body's systems, leading to inflammation, hormonal imbalances, and other physiological disturbances. That’s also a way the body manifests the traumatization. In summary, trauma affects both the body and the brain, leading to lasting changes in how we perceive and respond to the world. While trauma is not strictly physically stored in the body like a tangible object, its impact is deeply ingrained in our physiological and psychological responses, influencing our behavior and well-being. Also, if trauma is said to injure our nervous system, and the nervous system is in charge of all the millions of nerves that run all along our body, the idea may suggest that all our body gets affected, right?

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Has anyone experienced severe nausea as a side effect from EMDR? If so, how long did it last and how did you manage it?
Answer: Personally, if one of my clients gets nausea during an EMDR session and it lasts, I’d probably stop processing because I’d read the nausea as a symptom of dysregulation, and the length as a sign of not having enough tolerance for it. Nausea can be a physiological response to emotional distress, which may be triggered by the intense emotions brought up during EMDR sessions but they should be manageable and tolerable. Since EMDR therapy involves revisiting traumatic memories or distressing experiences while simultaneously engaging in bilateral stimulation, the activation of the emotions can be overwhelming to the point of causing nausea. That may be an indicator that the EMDR is activating the stress response which may indicate a dissociative state. Nausea during EMDR therapy may be influenced by psychological factors, such as anxiety and fear. If the fear is too high, and the person loses the dual awareness—being in the past but still connected to the present—it may be better to assess for dissociation and for the level of tolerance. EMDR could be powerful but could also be detrimental. I don’t use it until I’m certain that the client is capable of tolerate extreme emotional activation and that knows how to regulate it if it happens. I also need to know that the client is well resourced. If the nausea last too long (more than few minutes), I’d ground the client into the present before I continue, if I even continue processing during that session.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can having a good relationship with a therapist speed up the healing process for trauma compared to just being in therapy alone?
Answer: Depends on the meaning and extension of what a "good relationship" is for each and both of you, and the expectations you have about the relationship with your therapist. In general terms, a good relationship entails both individuals feeling valued, appreciated, and accepted for who they are. In therapy, this is often referred to as "rapport," which also encompasses a sense of ease and comfort in communication, facilitating effective cooperation and collaboration. Rapport is crucial in therapeutic relationships, contributing to mutual understanding and benefit. Research suggests that good rapport between therapist and client could account for more that 60% of the success of treatment. However, the definition of a "good relationship" also includes emotional intimacy, connection, and physical affection. Problems with expectations may arise when one or both parties start feeling this type of connection, potentially hindering the therapeutic process. In a good relationship with any other person, both parties feel supported in pursuing their individual goals and aspirations, while also prioritizing each other's well-being and happiness. In therapy, however, the client should not be pursuing the therapist's goals or aspirations, which creates an imbalanced and potentially confusing dynamic. Instead, a good therapeutic relationship involves trust that the client will be accepted and cared for without needing to please the therapist. Overall, a good relationship fosters growth, happiness, and fulfillment for both individuals involved. However, in therapy, the focus is on establishing rapport to aid in the healing process. If a client does not feel connected, trusting, collaborative, and safe with their therapist, their healing may be compromised. Therapists are not merely sounding boards or passive listeners; they serve as witnesses to our struggles and allies in our ambitions, guiding our internal world toward a more effective and functional relationship with the external world. That’s why we need to trust them. We kind of put part of the success of our lives in their hands.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is post-traumatic growth a common experience for individuals after a traumatic event, even if it is not immediately apparent?
Answer: Interesting idea but reality is not as ideal! Laura had a car accident. She struggled to drive for five years afterward. She still experiences nightmares and panic attacks while driving. Peter also had a car accident but returned to driving immediately. However, he has become a neurotic driver, frequently cursing at others and blaming all drivers for being reckless. Jesse experienced a car accident, leading them to become more cautious while driving. They now respect all traffic signs, advocate for road safety measures, and raise awareness about the dangers of distracted driving. The accident taught Jesse valuable lessons about life's fragility and the importance of cherishing each moment. They have become more appreciative of their loved ones and prioritize spending quality time with them. Additionally, Jesse has developed a newfound sense of resilience and determination to overcome adversity. Which one do you think is “a common experience”? The three people had a very different “post-traumatic growth” (PTG) after experiencing the same type of traumatic event. Each one of us is different and have a different set of strengths to help us overcome adversity. We could say that only Jesse experienced lasting PTG. In general, after experiencing a traumatic event, the first priority for our body is to address the physiological changes that occur due to our natural reaction to perceived risk, danger, or threat. This process may take a couple of months if properly managed. When I say "processing," I refer to assessing the level of risk not just in what happened, but also in its implications for the present and future. Once this processing occurs and the individual finds a new, positive meaning in the experience, such as "I'm a survivor" or "I have a new lease on life," post-traumatic growth can begin to unfold. Although not everyone experiences post-traumatic growth, research suggests that many do, even if it's not immediately apparent, and even if they initially experience significant distress and struggle. This process is not linear; setbacks and periods of difficulty often accompany growth. In general, most individuals possess reflective capacities and can learn from their experiences, from which it’s fair to expect some gradual post-traumatic growth even if it takes months or even years to manifest fully. As most posttraumatic symptoms tend to fade within a year, subsequent growth involves developing new skills, strengthening relationships, and finding new meaning or purpose in life. Several factors can influence the likelihood of experiencing post-traumatic growth, including social support, personal resilience, and better strategies to deal with adversity and challenges. Individuals with a strong support network and the ability to find meaning in their experiences are more likely to experience growth. For those who develop PTSD, post-traumatic growth is often intertwined with the healing process. If they do not experience growth, it may indicate that the healing process from past traumatic experiences has not been fully resolved.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What are the differences between C-PTSD and BPD? Can someone have one without having the other?
Answer: C-PTSD is a very broad diagnosis that aims to encompass all possible trauma syndromes caused by prolonged or repeated traumatic circumstances or adversity at any age. BPD may be one of those syndromes, particularly caused by attachment ruptures or failure, resulting in a lack of bond with the caregiver and, consequently, a failure to learn how to regulate their nervous system. As you can see, BPD is very specific, while C-PTSD is quite generic and vague. Yes, someone can have one without the other, unless BPD is considered a type of C-PTSD, but there no official recognition of such distinction.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How can you tell when a client is having a flashback in the middle of the session?
Answer: I often feel that there is a lot of magical thinking or misconceptions around the concept of trauma and its symptoms. The regular flashback is more similar to a thought than to a psychotic break, which may them imperceptible and irrelevant. We may have flashbacks all the time without interfering with our lives, or we may have an intense every blue moon. They are normally triggered more than random. If a person is having a flashback, they probably feel intense emotions or may show emotional disturbances, but nothing stops them from sharing with the therapist what they are experiencing, unless it is one of those intrusive "memories" that don’t come with a visual. Identifying a flashback during a therapy session without the participation of the client can be challenging because flashbacks can present in many different ways for different individuals. That’s why in my book, I separate the regular flashbacks that have a connection with sensory pieces like images, smells, sounds, etc., from "backlashes" that are more emotional than sensorial. If a person is "re-living" a traumatic experience during a session, then the therapist can help the client identify if it’s coming from the past or if the experience is purely caused by the session. This could be done when a therapist has conceptualized the case correctly and can predict the type of events that can be disturbing the present perception by mixing it with past situations and reactions. I normally try to identify triggers early in treatment just to help both to be aware of possible intrusions. Flashbacks are typically triggered by stimuli or reminders that are associated with the traumatic event. These triggers can be external, such as a specific sight, sound, smell, or location, or internal, such as a thought, emotion, or bodily sensation. Backlashes are triggered by actions, words, or situations that make the person feel at the same level of danger as when they got traumatized. Let me give you a couple of examples: The client is in session and brings their legs up as in a startle response. The therapist notices and asks what happened. The client may say that they saw a shadow coming at them. The therapist may ask the client if they had some incidents with snakes, or any other animal, or something else coming from the floor that scares them. The client then may identify that a few months back they found a dead mouse under the sofa. That’s a typical flashback. Flashbacks could be just momentary images of something scary that may be impossible to be identified by the therapist unless the client mentions it. Flashbacks could also as the client feeling nausea all of a sudden, and neither they nor the therapist could know that the client is having a flashback to the new cologne the therapist is using which smells similar or the same as the one an abuser wore. The client may be able to identify that it was the smell, but they may not even be aware that’s the reason. Those flashbacks are not easy to identify as such. In the case of backlashes, it’s even harder. The therapist may say a phrase that “makes” the client feel ignored, dismissed, criticized, etc. The client may have a very strong reaction and may attribute the reaction to what just happened without any awareness that the feeling comes from having been ignored, dismissed, or criticized in the past, probably many times, and not from what the therapist said. If the therapist knows that’s in the history of the client, they may identify the backlash; otherwise, they may feel accused without understanding that part of the client’s reaction comes from trauma. Many of us can experience flashbacks or even backlashes without having PTSD. In some cases, internal factors such as stress, fatigue, or heightened emotional arousal may increase the likelihood of experiencing a flashback. But people with PTSD other trauma-related conditions may be more prone to experiencing flashbacks as a result of their underlying symptoms and sensitivities. For those clients, it’s even more important to spend some time listing triggers in their regular lives for them to develop awareness of what “activates” their brain into protectiveness. It's important for therapists to be attuned to many of the sensitivities and signs of activation (and not only flashbacks) to create a safe and supportive environment for the client to process their experience. If a therapist suspects that a client is experiencing a flashback, or of the client is able to recognize it, they should invited to share it. Then the therapist can gently guide the client back to the present moment, offer grounding techniques, and providing safety and reassurance.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is the difference between trauma bonds and codependency?
Answer: It may be difficult to identify the differences because many times, they appear together. They both involve unhealthy attachments between individuals but trauma bonds develop in situations of abuse, neglect, or other traumatizing experiences. The bond is driven by fear of further abuse or abandonment, rather than genuine affection but it is confused with love, or reasons to be together despite of difficulties or hurtful dynamic or behavior from the partner (or other person because it may not be necessarily a romantic relationship). Leaving the abuser may be challenging due to fear, manipulation, isolation tactics employed by the abuser, sense of loyalty, or because the emotional dependency has grown to an extreme of being lost without it. Codependency forms in relationships where one person's needs are unmet while and because they focus on meeting the needs of the other. The codependent feels responsible for solving others' problems, often neglecting their own well-being mostly due to the fact that they define their worth through caring for others, leading to unhealthy dependence and many times, resentment. One important difference is that trauma bonds involve a power imbalance with one person having control over the other, while codependency often involves a mutual unhealthy dynamic of enabling and caretaking. Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What are the types of emotional disturbance?
Answer: Your question is vague but I’ll try to respond to some interpretations of it. People also say that someone is “emotionally disturbed” when they have difficulties in managing their emotions, thoughts, or behaviors, which can negatively impact their quality of life and functioning. Calling someone “emotionally disturbed” is somewhat ambiguous and lacks a precise clinical definition. It's not a formally recognized diagnosis but instead, it's generally used way to describe someone that is confused, disoriented, and dysfunctional. In general, it’s subjective and can vary depending on cultural context, individual experiences, and perspectives. In EMDR for example, the therapist is trying to elicit emotional disturbance in the client before they start processing, which means that they are activating the negative emotions connected to the memory that is being targeted. That disturbance means that it’s not only cognitive but also somatic, as in bringing up emotions and their physiological manifestations. As summary, I guess people can use the term with different connotations. Hope the ones I’m giving you clarifies the fact that we need to be careful in how we use terms in psychology to avoid stigma, pathology, and confusion.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why is it that people always seem to find faults in their upbringing once they start going to therapy? It seems as if there is always a reason that parents are the cause of the problem.
Answer: I like blaming Freud for some of the issues we're dealing with in therapy today like the one you are mentioning in your question. I know it's not entirely fair, as he was a pioneer in the field, but his ideas have had a lasting impact on the way we approach mental health. I like blaming him because he popularized the idea of looking for someone to blame, especially the parents. We're still paying the consequences of some of his ideas that weren't entirely accurate. Freud defined therapy as a search for patterns and old memories as the foundation of healing. While early experiences are indeed important, Freud's theories sometimes overemphasized their influence, potentially neglecting the impact of present circumstances and individual agency. Psychoanalysis and other therapeutic techniques he introduced have been criticized for their length, cost, and potential for misinterpretations. Yet, his influence on psychotherapy is undeniable. We often still think of therapy as delving into what went wrong in childhood and hardly focus on strengths and positive experiences. Childhood is a period of learning; hence, children absorb many of the behaviors and attitudes that their caregivers or immediate family—often our parents—have. That we learn unhealthy behavior or negative emotions is not the parents' fault. That’s natural design. For good or bad, we need to acquire information to become full individuals, and that information comes from our immediate surroundings, experiences, and circumstances, and from what our parents learned themselves from theirs. Yes, we learn many bad things in childhood, and we experience and get many of the bad habits from our parents, whether they are aimed at us or not. Many of the adults who exhibit unhealthy behaviors are often told by therapists they come from experiences in their childhood as if they were victims, even if they were not victimized. Some therapists focus on finding the root cause in parental figures or the past, believing that understanding and blame can lead to a solution but using that tone of victimization. This has proven wrong. While it's natural to identify influences from our caregivers, it's equally important to focus on regulating our reactions, understanding the impact of our actions (or lack thereof), and taking responsibility for our behavior. We are the product of our experiences for sure, or “victims of our circumstances” as some say. This is especially true in childhood because that’s when most of our development occurs. But it’s important to differentiate between different types of influences and recognize who was victimized and who wasn’t. Many times, parents use their kids as waste baskets to dump their own issues; parents could be cruel, mean, aggressive, neglectful, sadistic, and many other negative characteristics that hurt and harm their children. Yes, it’s necessary to address that type of upbringing to resolve some of the consequences carried by the child all the way to adulthood. It’s also true that many times the parents are not prepared to be parents, have not resolved their emotional issues, and may hurt their kids unintentionally. Those cases should be treated differently than those that had no consideration towards the kid at all. All parents have flaws, and every childhood presents challenges and difficulties. It’s human nature. The tendency to attribute current behaviors to childhood experiences and seeking to find someone to blame is not useful or the solution to help people. It may give them the wrong impression and can detract from the importance of taking responsibility and finding solutions in the present to build a better future, and to develop strength and resilience. It’d be wonderful to imagine perfect parents, but perfection is not attainable for us humans. Furthermore, perfect lives would not make perfect people.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can therapists develop PTSD from listening to their clients' trauma? If so, what are some ways for them to cope with this condition?
Answer: There are 2 constructs normally used to name what therapists develop after listening to their clients’ histories of trauma, particularly if the stories are disturbing, graphic, or involve children: secondary traumatic stress (STS) or vicarious trauma (VT). They both have symptoms similar to those of PTSD, such as intrusive thoughts, emotional numbness, hypervigilance, and avoidance behaviors. For me, the difference is that the secondary trauma can make the therapist internalize the phobia, the avoidance, the fears, without direct understanding that the symptoms come from the clients. It’s more similar to contacting a virus from someone else and suffering the symptoms regardless. Vicarios traumatization has more to do with a loss of faith in humanity, a sense of personal vulnerability, and feelings of helplessness and hopelessness for seeing people going through so much pain. It is often considered a more long-term, cumulative effect of repeated exposure to clients' traumatic experiences. Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What distinguishes a therapist from a life coach? Which profession is more suitable for treating PTSD, and what are the reasons for this?
Answer: There are huge differences between coaches and therapist, specially in relationship with the level of understanding of the human psyche. They may seem similar since both can offer guidance, support, and strategies for personal growth and development, but there are several key differences between the two professions. A therapist is a licensed mental health professional who has completed extensive education and training in counseling, psychology, social work, or a related field according to clear guidelines ruled by official institutions such as State Department of Professions. Therapists are trained to address a wide range of mental health issues, including anxiety, depression, trauma, and relationship problems. They are trained to recognize diagnosing, and focus on treating and managing mental health conditions while improving overall emotional well-being. Therapists are allowed to train in various techniques and modalities, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy, psychodynamic therapy, or humanistic therapy, to help clients, and are required to keep actualizing their therapy skills by law. In comparison, life coaching is generally not regulated in the same way as therapy and other mental health professions. Unlike therapists, life coaches are not required to have specific education or training in mental health, and there is no formal certification or licensing process required to become a life coach. Instead, they focus on helping people achieve specific goals or overcome personal challenges. Therefore, life coaches are not suitable to treat PTSD. PTSD is a serious mental health condition that requires specialized treatment and support from a trained mental health professional. Therapists can diagnose PTSD, assess its severity, and tailor treatment plans based on individual needs. They can also manage co-occurring conditions like anxiety and depression, which often accompany PTSD. While life coaches can offer support and guidance, they lack the training and expertise to diagnose or treat mental health disorders like PTSD. Their focus primarily lies on personal growth and goal achievement, which while helpful, might not adequately address the complex needs of someone with PTSD.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is your experience with dissociation? I am confused if that is what I am going through. I don’t feel hunger, fullness, tiredness, hot/cold, pain. I don’t feel emotions at all and don’t feel medicines either.
Answer: Your description of symptoms sound serious, if you allow me to say it. It may be more serious than just dissociation. But let’s start by clarifying that dissociation has different manifestations. Dissociation is a spectrum of experiences where you disconnect from your thoughts, feelings, memories, or sense of identity. It can range from mild daydreaming to more severe forms like depersonalization (feeling detached from your body) or derealization (feeling like the world is unreal). Nowadays. dissociation is normally separated in 2 big branches: compartmentalization and detachment. Compartmentalization: Detachment: Some of the symptoms you mentioned could be associated with dissociation, such as emotional numbness, feeling disconnected from your body, and not feeling pain or other sensations like hunger, etc. However, other factors could also explain these symptoms, because you may have executive functions difficulties. It’s not possible to say with certainty what's happening to you without proper evaluation but what you are describing is extreme. We all have the capacity to notice what’s happening around and inside of us if we bring our attention to them. Without them, our life would be in danger, and that’s the opposite of what our brain is always trying to do. In order to survive, we need to know what’s happening. Hunger for example is a way for our brain to send us the signal that we need to eat (to survive), etc. Try bringing your attention to specific parts of your body, stay focused, and see if you can get something. Whatever you get, you will be reprogramming the dissociation, if that’s what you are suffering from.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is it okay to message your therapist on Facebook after they left the practice? She left without warning and I want to thank her and let her know how I’m doing.
Answer: You run some risks. They may not use FB often, and they may not respond, which probably will make you feel offended, neglected, or dismissed. Facebook is not safe. Facebook Messenger fails to meet all four HIPAA requirements and is not considered a HIPAA compliant telemedicine platform. Therefore, in theory, it should not be used by a therapist to communicate with clients. If you have not been a client for more than one or two years (depending on the state), you can connect with your ex-therapist, but still, your therapist may not feel comfortable doing so. You can take chances, but be aware that if you don’t hear back, you should not take it personally.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is a person with PTSD / C-PTSD personality like?
Answer: PTSD and C-PTSD normally impact a person's personality because of the way the individual’s brain processes and responds to stress and danger after developing the disorder. Since experiencing traumatic events impact a person's emotions, thoughts, and behaviors, they may change the way they see themselves and also, the way they feel others see them. Let me give you an example: Sarah has been a photographer since adolescence. She loved exploring new places, capturing unique moments with her camera, and spending time with friends and family. She was known for her infectious laughter and adventurous spirit. But then, driving towards a place where she was going to photograph people in a festival, she suffered a terrible car accident that sent her and another 2 people to the hospital. She developed PTSD. In the months after the accident, Sarah became withdrawn and reclusive. She found crowds overwhelming and avoided activities that directly or indirectly had to do with cars, driving, or loud noises. She couldn't bring herself to pick up her camera. Her relationships suffered as she struggled to connect and share her emotions. She felt as a failure and felt that her friends saw her as a menace. She also felt guilty for having injured other people. Sarah is an example of someone that suffered changes in her peosonality from open, curious, fun, and adventuresome, to closed, unavailable, and blue. But I can give you as many examples as people with PTSD or PTSD we can count. Some people go from peaceful to aggressive while others go from kind to mean, or from mean to shutdown, from loud to silent, etc. Traumatization or a trauma disorder impact how a person views the world and their relationships with others. Hence, they may develop a heightened sense of danger which leads to either avoid situations or people, social isolation and difficulty forming or maintaining relationship, or to aggression. It all depends on the peritraumatic mechanisms used, and the posttraumatic strategies the brain chooses to survive. If the person stays stuck in a parasympathetic driven strategy, they will seem quieter, disconnected, absent, submissive, aloof, lifeless, etc. But of their system is driven by a sympathetic strategy, they will become loud, aggressive, fearful, anxious, rageful, vindictive, etc. It’s not possible to put everyone in boxes. Every person reacts different to the struggle they feel internally. The graph I’m including here comes from my book Traumatization and Its Aftermath. I have a detailed description on each one of the 6 clearly different “personalities” that people can show as survival strategies after traumatization.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is it possible to live with someone who has post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) without developing it yourself? If not, what steps can be taken to prevent it from happening?
Answer: Your question make PTSD sound like a contagious disease. It is not! If you live with someone that makes you feel afraid to the extreme that you lose hope in having the capacity to ever be happy, or that you may die by staying with that person, as if your life is getting exhausted, then you can easily develop PTSD. The traumatic event is what starts the activation of processes that could end up injuring our system, but it is our response what keeps those processes running, and if we can’t find a healthy way to resolve that activation (i.e. developing a sense of being safe), then the system will end up shifting to operate in survival mode. That’s when the PTSD symptoms appear and continue. PTSD is the term psychiatry uses to name the maladaptation of the nervous system—changes in the way the brain processes threats and danger—after an individual loses the capacity to feel safe following an experience of threat. So, PTSD is caused by the meaning you assign to your experience. If for you, living with someone with PTSD is threatening, then you will send the signal to your brain that you are at risk, and then your brain will start the processes to help you survive. As you can see, if you develop PTSD it will have less to do with the other person’s struggle and more with your own ones.I t's true that you might be exposed to some risk factors because people with PTSD can be volatile but you can definitely take steps to mitigate that risk and maintain your own mental well-being. Also, the steps will have to do with the type of presentation the person with PTSD has. There are some individuals with PTSD that are aggressive and there are those that are super accommodating and harmless. It’s not possible to generalize about PTSD presentations. How could you prevent developing PTSD? Start by finding the ways to feel safe. For example, if you repeatedly hear about the traumatic event from the other person, or constantly witness their emotional distress can trigger your own stress response. Educating yourself about PTSD and its symptoms can help you empathize and respond effectively. You may really benefit from reading books like mine that explains the roots and manifestations at detail (Traumatization and Its Aftermath). Maintaining open communication with your partner about their triggers and needs can reduce misunderstandings and build trust and will keep your system regulated. Don't feel obligated to absorb all the burdens of those that struggle. I recommend to prioritize your own well-being and seek support when needed. If you keep regulated and safe, you’ll help the person with PTSD to co-regulate. If you feel at risk, the person with PTSD will increase their uneasy feelings, making the situation worse.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can you be bipolar without trauma?
Answer: Nowadays, it seems impossible not to link mental health issues to trauma, right? Well, Bipolar Disorder is one of the few that is largely separate from trauma. Experiencing traumatic events or living on a prolonged traumatization can obviously exacerbate Bipolar symptoms, but trauma is not the root cause of the disorder. Bipolar disorder is a mood disorder believed to have more to do with genetic and biological factors that only environmental. Trauma is an adaptation while Bipolar is an illness similar to having a small kidney. Genetic predisposition and abnormalities in brain chemistry are considered to be the most significant factors in the development of bipolar disorder. Of course, some people with Bipolar Disorder may have comorbid conditions and experiencing traumatic events or circumstances could be sometimes the reason people get diagnosed but it’s not what causes the illness. The fundamental understanding is that Bipolar Disorder has biological and genetic underpinnings, making it distinct from trauma-related disorders like PTSD.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Are there people who aren't affected by trauma? If so, why?
Answer: The question should be “Are there people who aren’t affected by extremely challenging events or adversity? or “Are there people who aren’t affected by being exposed to traumatic events? When you use the word “trauma” you are already implying they got affected. Trauma is not separated from its effects; the experience of a traumatic event and its consequences are intricately interconnected and inseparable. The traumatic event triggers a response, and this response, in turn, molds how the individual carries the experience throughout their life or for as long as they remain entangled with the past due to feelings of threat and danger. This can create a continuous cycle of traumatization, making it challenging to genuinely disengage the past traumatic experience from a sense of safety in the present. “Trauma” encompasses more than just an event; it refers to the enduring effects that persist long after the event has concluded. An experience qualifies as trauma when it leaves lasting imprints on a person's physical, emotional, cognitive, and social well-being. These effects can manifest in various ways, including symptoms of PTSD, anxiety, depression, chronic pain, or difficulties in relationships. Trauma is a complex phenomenon that emerges when multiple factors converge: a traumatic event (scary, shocking, or threatening), an intense response (activation of survival circuits), overwhelm (exceeding one's capacity to cope), hopelessness, and resulting damage. So, to respond to the question of how some people experience traumatic events and don’t get affected has to do with the way they respond and they relate to the experience. Taking the formula I just posted in the answer, if the person interrupts the sequence of the response, or if one or more of the factors in the formula are missing, the person will not feel the effects of the exposure and may not be consider the experience as trauma. If they can handle their response, their system will bounce back to normal functioning and their system will not get damaged. If they are able to tolerate the response without getting overwhelmed, they won’t have long lasting effects. If they don’t lose hope, they will be ok and they won’t have a long lasting injury.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Do PTSD flashbacks make you enter a super hypervigilant state, or do they cause disassociation from the present?
Answer: It's actually the other way around. Hypervigilance, which is a common symptom of PTSD, often contributes to the experience of flashbacks. The amygdala becomes hyperactive, constantly scanning for potential threats, which can trigger dreams or visual memories in an attempt to alert you to possible dangers. Flashbacks themselves do not directly cause dissociation. However, if a person becomes intensely frightened during a flashback, their brain may interpret the situation as overwhelming and resort to dissociation as a protective mechanism. This can result in a numbing of the body and a partial disconnection from awareness in an effort to prevent the person from experiencing extreme emotional pain. It's important to note that this extreme pain is related to the fear of reliving a past traumatic event, rather than an immediate threat. Therefore, if an individual recognizes that they are experiencing a flashback and can reestablish their connection with the present moment, they can often avoid dissociation.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: As someone who struggles with pathological lying due to C-PTSD, does acknowledging it after I lie help to stop lying?
Answer: Saying that you lie because you have C-PTSD might sound like a justification upfront, which implies you're already discounting the value of acknowledging it. It sounds to me like apologizing by saying 'I'm sorry, but...' and giving a reason for your actions. That doesn't constitute a genuine apology, right? However, I'll give you the benefit of the doubt, considering that lying can actually evolve into a habit driven by the need to “survive” your environment or what many call a coping mechanism. It may begin as a strategy to meet some of your needs or avoid punishment, but over time, it can become a purposeless habit that your brain learned and which eventually becomes detrimental. Some papers talk about pathological lying as a psychological condition in which an individual repeatedly tells lies or exaggerates the truth for no apparent or logical reason. Lying becomes pathological when is not done for personal gain or to avoid punishment, but rather because you feel a strong compulsion to lie, even when it can go against your best interest. It could become so habitual, that people who engage in pathological lying may have difficulty distinguishing between truth and falsehood, and they may not have an awareness of their behavior or its consequences. They may also experience anxiety, guilt, or shame about their lying, but feel unable to stop. Acknowledging the lie after the fact can be a helpful first step in addressing pathological lying, especially if done with the intention of improving one's behavior. However, healing from it is not that simple. The brain may have developed a program that pushes the person to lie or seek alternative truths automatically, and that program needs to be replaced with one that fosters honesty. A new habit, such as acknowledging the falsehood, must be practiced many times until it becomes the new default response, promoting truthfulness. Since you mentioned C-PTSD, acknowledging the lies can also serve as a starting point for identifying the reasons behind using the strategy of lying. This process allows for the examination of the past, recognizing it as such, and acknowledging that the current situation is different. It enables the development of healthier ways to manage emotional reactions.
