On top of the schools of thought, there are ethical codes that suggest therapy for therapists. But those are all recommendations and there are not rules for therapist being in therapy. You are asking what we think about it. Personally, I think therapist have the moral responsibility to maintain a level of regulation and deep awareness of emotional challenges to be effective as therapists. Once a therapist is having personal issues, they may fail to be completely in the moment to attend to their clients and they may fail to understand their concerns because their mental space may be clouded by their own concerns. In those moments, the therapist should be responsible to their clients but also to themselves, and resolve their issues to continue being fully available to their clients. They don’t need to be in therapy all the time, but they may be on and off when their situation presents difficult. Therapists are humans and they may struggle like many other, but they know better and should take care of themselves. If they don’t, it may mean that they either think too high of themselves, or too little. They may feel like they are above others, or they may feels as if their lives are to serve others and neglect their own needs. Those may be the extremes that therapists suffer from. Besides those, which is a problem at the core, therapists may have many other issues that could be resolved with few sessions of processing, which they know how to do.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Do people suffering from borderline personality disorder (BPD) want friends or companionship in their lives more than others?
Answer: Imagine a fetus feeling stressed and lonely in the womb. Then they are born and they find even more loneliness and difficulty regulating their discomfort, their hunger, their cold, their extra sensitivity to stimuli. Noises, voices, silence, etc., become threatening, and their distress escalates. Their needs are ignored and their system never learns to find peace and comfort. They feel so disturbed that they constantly fear dying. They don't know what dying is, of course, but their brain fears not having the basics needs met and puts pressure on their nervous system to keep them alive at the cost of developing a sense of who they are and finding a bond that makes them feel safe. More discomfort! The struggle to stay alive causes them to ignore and condone the neglect or bad treatment they suffer and pushes them to "attach" to whomever is around. To do that, their brain will ignore or minimize their needs to avoid more rejection or abandonment, disconnecting some functions, numbing their pain, and separating their mental models of the world into all good or all bad, putting them belonging to the all bad. Their lives depend on it! Internally, they feel like a burden, or worse yet, like someone who should not have been born. They develop all sorts of fears and start developing all sorts of defenses to avoid further rejection and to survive their environment. That probably continues until adulthood. All those survival strategies or adaptations are the ones that we identify as borderline personality disorders. An adaptation to having been rejected, neglected, and pushed into a perpetual dysregulation of intense highs and lows. Do you think they want friends or companionship more than others? Of course they do! They also fear getting too close because if it goes wrong, they will encounter more rejection, disorientation, and loneliness. They may feel as if they can’t handle more emotional pain. On top of that, they very often develop a dislike of themselves because of the way they are, react, and act. They may dislike themselves even more than how they were disliked when they were born. Hard to have a good life with that type of mental structure. Don't you think? It's a very tough adaptation that leaves them alone most of the time. Like having been born with a curse! I’m glad you asked the question and I hope you find some compassion in your heart fro them.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: If a woman retroactively withdraws consent to sexual intercourse, was she raped?
Answer: Even when it sounds as if consent can’t be retroactive, I want to imagine you are asking if someone can realize after having had sex that the sexual interaction she got into was not completely consensual. “COMPLETELY consensual” is a subject I teach and use to educate young (and not so young) individuals that have difficulty understanding if they consented or not to sex. Our sexuality is a very complex subject. I define it as: “Sexuality is a complex aspect of the human experience encompassing heightened sensory stimulation that fosters physical, emotional, and even spiritual connection between individuals. It involves the complex interplay of neurobiological, psychological, and sociocultural factors, shaping diverse expressions of desire with the pleasure of bonding and relating.” To make my answer short, to consent, all our different systems need to be in congruence with each other. We need Studies and public conversations have introduced the idea that REGRET is the key factor to know if the sexual interaction was consensual or not. That’s a very dangerous assumption. Many people experience regret after having sex not because of the other person did it non-consensually, but because the person’s system were not aligned. If your body is saying yes, and you say yes, and then you regret it because you are either ashamed or fearful of the consequences, or if you think you consented but you didn’t even know what you were getting into, you will regret it because your own reasons, and you can’t put all the blame in the other person and call it rape. We are not used to talk about sex with our partners, or even think about sex ourselves. We carry a set of assumptions and we go with them into sexual encounters blind about many of the consequences or characteristics of what sex involves. If you “withdraw” your consent, as in meaning you regretted it, you can’t call it rape, but you can learn about your reactions, about what you want and don’t want, about who and when you want to do it, and about the aspects that could have make you feel regret. That could help you feel agency next time.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is depersonalization caused from my anxiety and panic attacks?
Answer: When you are very anxious and even get to the point of a panic attack, the brain gets into a complicated cascade of reactions including disruption in the neurotransmitter systems, changes in brain regions involved in self-awareness, emotion processing, and sensory integration, and the production of cortisol among many of the alterations needed to respond to the situation your brain anticipates due to your anxious response. Anxiety and panic also trigger the release of endorphins and enkephalins, which are endogenous opioids (produced by our own body) with analgesic properties. These substances bind to opioid receptors in the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral tissues, modulating our perception of pain to providing a degree of pain relief. Anxiety may also influence the endocannabinoid system, affecting its operation which in normal circumstances contribute to the modulation of stress, anxiety, and pain perception. While these mechanisms provide a natural form of pain relief during stress, chronic or intense anxiety and panic attacks can lead to dysregulation of all these systems forzing the brain to disconnect many of its functions. Prolonged activation of stress responses may contribute to heightened disconnection from pain, and therefore, from our body which is very connected to our self-concept. So, yes, depersonalization is directly connected to anxiety and panic attacks unless is caused by the use of substances, sleep deprivation, or neurological disorders.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is it possible to be traumatised by something that wasn't life threatening at all?
Answer: Envision these two scenarios: I’m at home, and I see a mouse in my pantry. I startle but keep going. I may do some extreme cleaning and check for any space from where the mouse could have entered. I’m not traumatized. Now, I’m at my office, and I see a mouse running in front of my client and me. I scream in terror, my heart races, I feel sweaty, I hear my client’s narrative muffled, I panic. That night I can’t sleep, I have nightmares, I have difficulty concentrating, I startle much easier, I hear noises at home and at my office, I have this impulse to avoid my office, I see mice shadows everywhere, etc., etc. I am presenting symptoms of PTSD, and I may seem to have been traumatized by the event. What’s the difference? Neither of them is “life-threatening” per se since the mouse is not going to kill me, but my brain doesn’t identify whether the situation is dangerous or not. What the brain identifies to activate the survival circuits that may end up traumatizing me is my response. I know that a mouse in my pantry is harmless, but a mouse in my office can damage the perception of my clients of me, and my emotional system may feel threatened of losing my income, my reputation, the respect of my clients, etc. That possibility is what the brain anticipates as “life-threatening” and starts the survival mechanisms to protect me from perishing. Ridiculous, right? Yes, our more primitive functions are too much for the type of dangers we humans encounter in today’s world. Those mechanisms were designed to protect us from predators, and when we “panic,” the brain assumes a life-threatening situation. Hope I helped you understanding the meaning of life-threatening in relation to trauma. I have to add that to avoid staying traumatized to the point of developing PTSD, all I need to know is become aware of the exaggeration of my response, make sure there are no ways for mice to populate my office, tell myself that my profession is not jeopardize for the mouse I saw, and become more mindful of my reactions. I may need to talk about it with a professional to process my fears, and I’ll go back to normal. If I recover my sense of safety, the traumatization ends and my system goes back to baseline. I’d not succumb to my primitive brain’s reactions and become ill for nothing. It’s in my hands to revert and dominate my primordial tendencies.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: To people with experience in cptsd; How do you know if you’ve ‘just’ been triggered or if you have been retraumatized?
Answer: Talking about "retraumatization" implies an increase in the emotional negative charge, or valence, stored in your system related to a traumatic memory. When an event is perceived as life-threatening, the brain encodes fragments of that experience into long-term memory, linking them with an emotional response to serve as future warnings of potential harm. These emotionally charged memory fragments act as triggers, activating survival circuits and heightening reactivity, hyperalertness, and stress. Retraumatization occurs when the brain reevaluates a similar event as more dangerous than initially assessed, assigning a higher level of risk—a higher valence (more negative). This causes the trauma disorder symptoms to worsen since it intensifies startle responses, increases alertness to potential threats, and enhances the vividness of memories. The distinction between being "triggered" and experiencing retraumatization lies in one's capacity to assess the situation. If you have cultivated some resilience, you’ll get back to your regular state without retraumatization. Merely getting triggered may activate your system, but with the ability to evaluate the actual level of risk, retraumatization can be avoided. In fact, being triggered presents an opportunity to assess the genuine risk, process fears, and reconsolidate memories into more adaptive forms, ultimately reducing reactivity and associated symptoms.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is emotional trauma from being a pedestrian hit by a vehicle?
Answer: My brother was about 4 or 5 years old when he kicked his ball across the street without looking. He ran to get it without being careful, and a car hit him. He got thrown a few feet away from the car. Surprisingly, he got up right away and kept chasing his ball. The driver saw him running and left before my dad could talk to them. My brother had scraped knees and a bruised arm, but he didn't seem to care. He didn't even look shocked, probably because he was so focused on his ball that didn't realize the danger of what had happened. But my dad had a very different experience. He felt sick to his stomach and threw up right after the accident. He was sick the rest of the day, pale, cold, feeling absent, upset, disconcerted. From that day on he couldn't stop worrying about busy streets, about the dangers of going to the park, and being scared of cars in general. He had a tough time dealing with the shock, and it affected him for a long time. He developed PTSD symptoms that stayed in him for years. We could say that he suffered from secondary trauma. This story shows that what's traumatic for one person might not be for another. We might think that something is scary for everyone, but it's not the same for each of us. We all react differently to scary or dangerous things because we have different definitions or awareness of what danger means.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Which books should I read to become mentally tough, resilient, and thick-skinned in order to not get affected by anybody’s judgements or opinions about my life?
Answer: That’s a lot to ask! :-) Specially because resilient and think-skinned may be contradictory. let go one by one of your goals: To be mentally tough is associated with mental and emotional strength. It involves the ability to bounce back from adversity, setbacks, failures, or disappointments while maintaining a positive mindset. This mental toughness goes hand in hand with resilience. Mentally strong individuals see opportunities in adversity and are flexible and adaptable to changing circumstances. A helpful book on this topic is 'The Mental Toughness Handbook: A Step-By-Step Guide to Facing Life's Challenges' by Damon Zahariades. Being thick-skinned relates to the capacity to not be easily affected or hurt by criticism, negative feedback, or insults. In other words, someone with thick skin can withstand and endure negative comments or challenging situations without becoming overly sensitive or defensive. However, enduring doesn't necessarily mean forgiving or accepting. 'Endure' means to withstand, persist, or tolerate challenging or difficult situations. It's better to maintain sensitivity, understanding, and compassion toward others who may be suffering than to harden up. Compassion is a valuable quality as it can protect you without hardening your skin or your heart. Many people with thick skin may harbor resentment or use dissociation and compartmentalization to cope with negativity. What you truly want is not just to endure, but to let go, understand, empathize, and observe without becoming entangled in your emotional responses. Personally, I wouldn't refer to this as being thick-skinned. It may be pure semantics but wanted to offer an additional food for thought. By the way, for those seeking to develop mental strength, I recommend my book 'Traumatization and Its Aftermath,' which recently received the Best Psychology/Mental Health award at the 2023 Best Book Awards. In this book, you can learn how to harness the full potential of your brain functions to heal emotional wounds and build resilience.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Are BPDs more resilient than others?
Answer: That one is hard to generalize. Could we say that most BPD are resilient? Speaking out loud, if they had been resilient, they would have not developed a personality disorder, don’t you think? Are pwBPD more resilient as adults than others because of the way they have had to adapt? I may not call it resiliency. However, we might describe them not as resilient but as skillful, adaptable, and capable in many ways. People with BPD frequently grapple with feelings of emptiness, uncertainty about their identity, self-doubt, and emotional instability while craving connections with others. To navigate this complex internal landscape, they've had to develop a wide range of coping skills. It’s similar to a blind person that learns to “see” through what they touch, smell, and hear. They become better at “seeing” by developing other senses and sharpening them. Similarly, individuals with BPD become proficient at reading people's preferences and social cues, enabling them to mirror and blend in for acceptance. They learn how to leverage the strengths of others to compensate for their own limitations, creating attachments to fulfill what they lack. While they may excel in certain aspects of life, this doesn't necessarily make them resilient. So, yes, they may be more capable than most in certain aspects of life, but that doesn’t make them resilient. They are still vulnerable to rejection, to criticism, to stability. In the strictest sense of the term 'resilience' as the capacity to bounce back to a baseline state, individuals with BPD may appear resilient on the surface. They can go from extreme emotions to appearing as if nothing happened in a matter of moments. But that’s only in the exterior. Internally, they are never at baseline. They are always struggling with the way they feel or not feel, with their opposite desires, with their lack of motivation, etc. clashing desires, and a lack of motivation. Their seeming return to 'normal' is often driven by a need for approval and acceptance, masking persistent feelings of shame, resentment, and anger.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What does healing from bpd look like? Will someone with bpd who does the work in therapy ever be "normal"? What does a relationship with someone who has healed from bpd look like?
Answer: Someone that suffers the symptoms of BDP can heal by working on regulating their nervous system, developing tolerance, reducing the overreactivity, and achieve more stable and fulfilling interpersonal connections, with improved communication and boundaries. It’s difficult to say that someone is “normal”. We all have our peculiarities. What one family might consider normal could be unacceptable to another, and seem crazy to someone else. What you want is not “normalcy” but “functionality”. Most people who suffer from personality disorders are not fully functional, and those with BPD struggle, particularly in terms of relationships. The goal for anyone with that type of symptomatology is to have long-lasting and fulfilling relationships, including employment and stable living arrangements. Many people with BPD struggle to maintain long-term friendships, employment, or housing. They repeatedly put themselves in situations that provoke rejection, which is something they fear profoundly. If individuals with BPD develop emotional regulation, awareness, and mentalization (understanding what others think and feel), they could strengthen their sense of self, which leads to a more stable self-concept, which could mean less sensitivity to rejection, which could lead to less reactivity. A relationship with someone who has healed from BPD could be genuinely pleasant because they can retain characteristics that make them appealing, such as high creativity, intuition, passion, closeness, resourcefulness, and organization, without the unpredictability or the threat of extreme reactions.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why do all narcissists behave the same way in adulthood when their childhood experiences and abuse varied case by case?
Answer: what a great question!! Narcissism is classified as a personality disorder or adaptation because individuals adapt to their circumstances by influencing how their personality develops. Personality is formed through a complex interplay of genetic, environmental, social, and cultural factors, as well as the influence of relationships, experiences, temperament, education, and challenges. It typically develops over time, primarily during a person's formative years, and tends to remain relatively stable once established. Regardless of early childhood experiences, individuals often develop certain defenses that can follow distinct patterns. Narcissism is believed to have its roots in early childhood experiences, such as neglect, excessive praise, or abuse, which shape individuals into compensating with grandiose ideation, competitiveness, and a strong desire to be perceived as valuable. Some research suggests that narcissistic traits can develop as a defense against feelings of vulnerability and low self-esteem. You can read this answer to see how I explain it: Individuals who experience traumatic stress during childhood may develop various adaptations to their personality due to a unique combination of biological, neurological, temperamental, environmental, and circumstantial factors. Our sense of self, identity, and personality is shaped by the interplay of these complex factors, and they intersect to form different classifications of personality disorders. From my perspective, personality disorders share many common characteristics, but each one also possesses distinct features. In the case of narcissism, a common underlying vulnerability exists, often masked by feelings of grandiosity derived from a subjective and partial self-evaluation. Many full-blown narcissists exhibit charisma, charm, and intelligence, which they employ to navigate the world. This success in their persona further reinforces their belief in the protective image they have developed.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can you have PTSD after being shot?
Answer: You are kidding, right? PTSD is all about fearing for one's life, and being shot is undoubtedly one of the most life-threatening experiences one can endure. It'd be completely understandable and expected to exhibit symptoms of PTSD after such a traumatic event. That said, people react differently, and not everyone who goes through such an ordeal will develop the full-blown disorder. Resilient individuals might rebound from the experience, regaining a sense of safety after surviving it, and determining that the chances of being shot again are reduced. This type of mentality can be a key factor in resolving traumatization and avoiding long-lasting emotional injuries. However, it's important to note that this won't be the case for everyone. Many individuals will develop PTSD after being shot, and even if they return to normal within a year, they may continue to experience symptoms from time to time. Traumatic events impact us and can have long-lasting and complex manifestations, affecting people in various ways.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can therapy undo some of the damage done by PTSD?
Answer: Absolutely! Can you imagine if it didn't? As a trauma therapist, I've had the privilege of witnessing numerous cases of individuals who were once struggling with dysfunction and despair transform into engaged and joyful members of society. It's both remarkable and inspiring to see the positive changes that can occur with the right support and therapeutic interventions. Through my work, I've had the opportunity to help people transition from lives marked by misery and dysfunction to becoming active and valued members of their communities. I've seen clients rebuild connections with their families, rekindle relationships, improve their job situations, achieve promotions, and even embark on entirely new career paths. The possibilities for growth and transformation are endless. Millions of dollars are invested every year in research and clinical practices to gain a better understanding of trauma and develop interventions to address the damage it can inflict on individuals. This demonstrates the significant commitment of professionals and researchers to help those who have experienced trauma. It's crucial to recognize that the field of trauma psychology is relatively young, and the full extent of its impact on the nervous system and behavior is still unfolding. We're constantly learning more about the intricacies of trauma and its effects, and therapy plays a vital role in this evolving landscape. Therapy doesn't erase or change the past, but it empowers individuals to develop a healthier relationship with their past experiences and the resulting emotional scars. Through therapy, individuals can regain a sense of control and safety in their lives, allowing them to process their traumatic experiences and find more adaptive ways to cope with their aftermath. Trauma often leaves people feeling disempowered, fearful, and insecure. It can fundamentally alter one's perspective on life, causing them to view the world through a different lens. Therapy serves as a crucial tool in the journey of recovery, helping individuals restore what was lost due to trauma and regain a sense of hope and well-being. But don't linger in a mindset focused solely on what you've lost and how much of it you may or may not recover. While it's true that there will be losses that cannot be fully recovered and damage that may remain unfixable, the key to healing is to shift your perspective. Rather than dwelling on what's missing or irreparable, strive to become "whole" again by concentrating on the opportunities and resources available to you. Healing from PTSD is about embracing the potential for growth and transformation, even in the face of adversity, and to recover the joy for the subtleties of life and the confidence that there is good out there. Go for it!!

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is it called when a child with trauma grows to become someone who inflicts that very same trauma on others?
Answer: “Hurt people hurt people.” This quote is commonly used in the fields of psychology, therapy, and self-help, as well as in everyday conversation. It highlights the idea that individuals who have experienced traumatic events and emotional pain, and who are emotionally wounded, may, in turn, unintentionally or intentionally inflict pain on others. It underscores the cycle of hurt and how unresolved issues can lead to negative behaviors or actions towards others. That's why it is so important to address one's own emotional wounds and seek healing to prevent perpetuating harm to others. This phenomenon can be described in various ways, but a diagnosis may not be the best way to address it. I could say that we could call it a form of "learning." We learn the language with which our caregivers use to communicate with us. If they speak English, we learn English, if they speak “violent”, we learn “violent”, if they speak “abusive”, we learn “abusive”, etc. Alternatively, this process could be viewed as "adapting." In an abusive or aggressive environment, individuals may need to adapt to those circumstances, sometimes having to become aggressive to confront the aggression. In essence, the person may be hurting because they, too, got hurt. This succinctly summarizes the response to your question.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is it normal to form imaginary relationships because of stress disorders like PTSD and depression?
Answer: Let me start by clarifying what “normal” means. Normal is what a lot of people do in the same way. That many people do things the same way doesn’t not mean they are right or wrong. We may have the tendency to equate “abnormal” with wrong, but that’s not the case. So, I wonder if you are asking about having imaginary relationships to be common, or wrong. I don’t think it’s very common, but it is definitely not wrong. When someone is struggling emotionally with feelings like depression or loneliness, it becomes necessary to find strategies to feel less bad. That’s common. The type of strategies vary a lot. Imagination is a very powerful tool that can bring aliviation to emotional distress. Daydreaming, fantasizing, and imagination are typical cognitive processes that people engage in to varying degrees. These activities are a normal part of human thinking and can serve various purposes, such as problem-solving, creativity, and entertainment. Imaginary relationships could be helpful as long as they don’t become the only way to relate and they are not a substitute for real-life social connections. An excessive focus on imaginary relationships can lead to social isolation; excessive reliance on fantasy relationships may hinder individuals from addressing the underlying issues and can delay or impede the individual's progress in seeking treatment and support for their mental health issues. if someone is experiencing excessive and distressing daydreams and everything in life moves around the imaginary relationships to the point where it significantly impairs their daily functioning and their ability to distinguish between their inner world and external reality, it could be a sign of a different mental health concern, such as a dissociative disorder or other conditions. What distinguishes the healthy from the unhealthy are the consequences into being functioning or becoming dysfunctional and impairing.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is it better for a person with PTSD to stay alone in a home?
Answer: PTSD is such a vague diagnosis that it doesn’t really help us getting the picture of the person you are referring to. Still, isolation is never a solution even when being alone can reduce potential triggers and allow for self-regulation and self-care. Staying alone at home as a way to avoid life and social interactions can have negative consequences for individuals with PTSD, particularly if it becomes a long-term and isolating strategy. By staying home, what they are doing is avoiding life. Avoiding life, including social interactions and activities, is a symptom of PTSD. It screams fear and dysfunction. We need to do everything to remove symptoms as opposed to perpetuating them. While avoidance can provide temporary relief from distressing triggers, it often perpetuates the cycle of avoidance and worsens symptoms in the long run. Avoidance can lead to increased anxiety and heightened sensitivity to triggers, and debilitate us overall because we lose agency and motivation. Staying there, avoiding life, would be interpreted by the brain as defeat since it anticipates danger, staying in survival mode indefinitely. Being isolated at home can limit opportunities to practice and develop healthy skills for managing PTSD symptoms and to regain a sense of safety needed to heal. Interacting with others and engaging in various life activities can be removing the idea that everything is dangerous. Being alone for extended periods may result in difficulties managing emotions, increasing the perceptual distortions. So, NO, it’s not better to stay at home alone if you have PTSD. It’s better to dare facing life in order to find that there is so much out there to enjoy, and that there are many people that can offer you a sincere smile. Sometimes that’s all it takes to feel confident again.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What are the differences between CBT and DBT?
Answer: CBT = Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy DBT = Dialectical Behavior Therapy CBT, as its name indicates, is focused on our cognition, how we use our thoughts, and how our thoughts influence our actions. In contrast, DBT uses the term 'dialectical' to describe the integration of two seemingly opposing concepts or ideas into a balanced synthesis—specifically, the balance between acceptance and change. DBT was originally developed to assist individuals with highly dysregulated nervous systems, primarily those with borderline personality disorder (BPD). It aims to help them cope with the intensity of their reactions, which often lead to self-harm, suicidal ideation, suicidal threats, and overwhelming emotional pain. CBT is a versatile therapeutic approach that can benefit anyone. It’s designed to be short term and involves structured sessions with a focus on setting goals, identifying cognitive distortions, and developing strategies for change. On the other hand, DBT is a more demanding approach for the client. Its original design incorporates both individual and group sessions, along with well-defined exercises aimed at maintaining individuals' awareness of their reactions. Both modalities have their roots in behaviorism, meaning that their ultimate goal is behavior change. CBT achieves this through cognitive restructuring, while DBT combines acceptance and change strategies. While DBT is adept at addressing the root of the problem and managing intense emotional reactions, it is often viewed as a remedial rather than a curative approach.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is the inability to create relations, even with therapists, a cognitive deficit or personality deficit?
Answer: Believing that you are unable to create relationships may be a cognitive issue or a schema you have developed. You may refer to the fact that you face significant challenges in forming and maintaining relationships, but that doesn't mean you are incapable of doing it. It is not accurate to describe facing challenges in forming relationships as "an inability," even for neurodivergent people or individuals on the autism spectrum. Yes, it's true that many people find it very challenging to develop a relationship with another person because they suffer from social anxiety or have attachment issues that make them either too needy or too detached, or because they lack social skills and suffer from a lack of trust, etc. Still, that doesn't mean they would never be able to form a relationship. It's obvious, though, that past experiences, traumatic circumstances, or unresolved emotional issues can significantly affect our ability to form relationships. If someone had a relationship that hurt them badly, they may be afraid to be in another relationship because they want to avoid getting hurt again. It's also possible to suffer from a specific emotional issue that has, as a characteristic, the difficulty to socialize or engage socially. These could be personality traits such as: There are also more severe reasons to have difficulty forming relationships. People suffering from personality disorders may have this difficulty as part of their symptoms. For example, for BPD, maintaining relationships is by definition difficult because of high dependency, frequent conflicts rooted in feeling rejected, criticized, or abandoned. The idealization and devaluation are also on the way to seeing the person as a constant source, which breaks the relationship. People with schizoid personality disorder avoid social activities and interacting with others, don't desire or enjoy close relationships, even with family, and prefer to be alone. Why? From what we have learned lately, it may be based on trauma and the fear of people. Like with many other syndromes, the person who suffered an emotional injury adapts to the best of their possibilities to surviving without taking chances to get injured again. Many times that means isolating and avoiding people. But it’s always possible to overcome the challenges, to learn social skills, and to dare to find some connection. We are social beings and we need each other. Isolation is not good for our health.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is the hidden reason behind forgetting, because children forget, adults forget, and the old do forget?
Answer: Memory plays a very important role in our evolution and it contributes to our survival by helping us to adaptat. That’s its main role. This about it! To remember is to learn from past experiences on how to adaptation to our environment. If we remember which plants are safe to eat, where to find water, how to build shelters, and how to navigate our surroundings, we have higher chances to escape danger and stay alive. Some people think that those with better memory and learning abilities are more likely to thrive and pass on their genes, but that was more truth thousands of years ago when are lives were jeopardized every day. Now, with all our technology, we remember less because we have created devices that can remember for us while we use our brain power to continue creating. One of the most interesting characteristics of memory is that the more emotion there is, the more we will remember. If something scare us, or make us happy, or make us sick, we will not forget. For example, you may read many books and make homework and hardly remember the content of what you read. maybe you remember it until you take the test, but then it’ll hard for you to recall that information. But imagine that you are in class and the teacher asks you a question, you respond, and the teacher makes fun of you or says that you are wrong. You’ll probably remember that question for the rest of your life. This characteristic is also adaptive and in the name of survival. So, to answer your question, we forget mostly those things that are not relevant for our survival or to adapt to our surroundings. The brain is too busy with millions of tasks and it can’t afford to store everything that happens. That’d be a waste of energy and mental space. That’s why pieces of memory are stored as packages of things that are similar. The brain doesn’t store the image of every single glass you have used. It only stores a generic image of a glass to help you recognize a glass if you need to. So, in a way, you are forgetting already thousands of glasses as soon as you drink from one. But if you cut yourself with one that breaks, that glass will have a special place in your memory because the brain will store that particular one as dangerous. So, we forget everything that is similar to other experiences or things, and everything that is irrelevant for us to navigate our world. That’s the overall explanation of why we forget, but you are mentioning children, adults, and elderly. There are different reasons we store memories differently according to our age. Children's memory systems, especially in early childhood, are still developing. The brain structures and processes that support memory, such as the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, continue to mature throughout childhood and adolescence. Young children may not have fully developed memory systems to encode and retrieve information effectively. Also, children are constantly exposed to new experiences, information, and stimuli. Their attention is often focused on the present moment, and they may not yet have the cognitive capacity to process and store all the details of their experiences. Once our brain matures, we are able to remember a lot until there is a decline in our brain functions. Older people forget maybe because they focus less on what’s happening, and therefore, they store less information, or because they have their mind occupied with so many problems or remembrances that they miss the present, or because their brain starts declining and functions as remembering to adapt are less important. Some parts of the brain shrink or wrinkle the same way as our skin does. Changes in some structures make their functions deficient. In my opinion, forgetting is as adaptive as remembering. For example, if you forget you watch a movie, you can enjoy the movie again. Forgetting keeps life exciting! And of course, in terms of relationships, forgetting the wrongdoings of others makes your life easier and your relationships last.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Are we born to sin?
Answer: Wow!! what a question! Born to sin, and what else? Just to sin? I like thinking that when a concept is shared across cultures, times, and geography, they may be part of the “operating system” that comes with the human design. If a concept is not understood the same way by all, they we should question it. The term “sin” is not universal. It has the fundamental meaning of moral transgression or offense against religious or moral principles, mainly Abrahamic religions. Not all religions or philosophies incorporate the concept of "sin" into their belief systems. The idea of sin is particularly associated with certain monotheistic religions, such as Christianity and Islam, which emphasize a divine moral code and a relationship between the individual and a higher power. Hinduism and Buddhism frame wrongdoing differently. These traditions may focus on concepts like karma, dharma, and ethical conduct, but the terminology and understanding of moral transgressions differ from the concept of sin as understood in Abrahamic religions. Buddhism, for example, uses the idea of unwholesome actions or unskillful behavior and the clear message that there is no effect without a cause, and that that cause-effect diad follows certain laws. Positive actions lead to positive consequences (good karma), and negative actions lead to negative consequences (bad karma). They don’t have the idea that we violate the laws written by a superior being, but the violation of the natural balance by harming others or yourself. I prefer rephrase your question as Is it avoidable to harm others or ourselves? I’d say that it’s basically impossible to live without harming ourselves of others, which is different from saying that we are born to sin.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What are some reasons why people might not want to accept the truth even if it would be beneficial for them to do so?
Answer: Have you had someone telling you “I swear I didn’t say that!!” How often do you think that statement is true? Nobody will know. When we are emotionally affected, our sense of what’s real can change a lot. Our memory may store few words and decontextualize them from the whole conversation. Those few words then may be mixed with other conversations or with the interpretation that we give to those word, of course, adding the emotionality they carry for us. Accept the truth? what truth? Your? theirs? In an objective sense, the truth represents what actually happened or exists independent of individual perceptions or beliefs. It is the verifiable, unbiased reality of a situation but that type of truth needs to be scientifically proven and irrefutable, or maybe be recorded. Objective truth is more like 2+2=4, the official capital of France today (2023) is Paris, or that we need oxygen and water to survive. Besides objective truth, there is personal truth which includes by definition subjectivity. That “truth" includes an individual's understanding or interpretation of their own experiences, feelings, or beliefs. Personal truths may vary among individuals based on their unique perspectives. For example, “chocolate is delicious” is personal and not objective, even when most people love chocolate and find it delicious. So, again, I wonder what are you referring when saying that “people might not want to accept the truth even if it would be beneficial for them to do so.” It may be beneficial to them to believe that chocolate is delicious but they may not find it to be so. If they don’t want to believe that 2+2=4, then we are talking about something else, like complete ignorance, stubbornness, delusion, or that they hold unconventional views on the nature of reality or the validity of established mathematical principles. Being right is another topic that could seem similar to accepting the truth. Being right is something the ego will die for, even if they have to transform reality. But the ego is the less objective part of us, hence, the ego doesn’t care about what’s true for you. They just care about what’s true for them to be right, to feel better than you, to win. So, to respond your question, you have to understand that not everyone perceives reality the way you do.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Despite discarding me 9 months ago and wanting no contact, my BPD ex doesn't turn indiffferent but hoovers me in subtile, mixed but mostly negative ways. Why is she fighting, lying, smearing, stalking, pushing and pulling, blocking and unblocking me?
Answer: So many of my clients suffer from the irrationality of those situations. It drives them crazy, right? After the “no contact” period, you may want to start processing the loss when they send signals that it may not be over. Your expectations go up. Then, another fall, fight, goodbye, or simple silence. Your expectations go down. Mixed signals, the push-pull dynamics in relationships, the confusion, doubt, self-doubt, anger, sadness, etc., they create can have significant effects on the nervous system and overall well-being of the individuals involved, and on the brain's neurochemistry. When there's an expectation of positive interaction or validation, the brain often releases dopamine, a neurotransmitter associated with pleasure and reward. Anticipation of a positive outcome can elevate dopamine levels. When expectations are repeatedly crushed, and the anticipated reward is not received, there can be a withdrawal of dopamine which can lead to feelings of dissatisfaction and disappointment. Also, the unpredictability and emotional turmoil associated with push-pull dynamics can trigger the release of cortisol, the stress hormone, and elevated cortisol levels over time can contribute to chronic stress, anxiety, and dysregulation of the stress response system. Additionally, the production of serotonin, another neurotransmitter that plays a crucial role in mood regulation, can be disrupted due to the instability and emotional highs and lows in a push-pull relationship, potentially leading to mood swings and emotional dysregulation. The cycle of anticipation, positive expectations, followed by disappointment, can create a pattern that resembles addiction. The brain may release endorphins during positive moments, contributing to a sense of pleasure. However, the subsequent disappointment can lead to a "crash," similar to withdrawal in addiction which makes the person feel close and form a bond. Many times, that bond becomes a “trauma bond” due to the inconsistency and unpredictability which leads to insecurity and self-doubt, inhibiting regular production of neurotransmitters. You may have experienced that problem yourself, so, just imagine the chaos in the brain of your ex. The behaviors that may seem contradictory or confusing, such as pushing people away while also desperately trying to pull them back in, are also manifestations of what’s happening internally. Seeking validation and reassurance can become a compulsive behavior to alleviate the fear of abandonment, leading to fluctuations in dopamine levels associated with the anticipation of validation. When the validation is not received or if there's a perceived threat of abandonment, there can be a drop in dopamine levels, contributing to feelings of disappointment, emotional pain, and distress. Serotonin dysregulation is associated with impulsivity and emotional dysregulation. Many individuals with BPD suffer from the intense and rapidly changing emotions in a push-pull dynamic linked to disruptions in serotonin levels. The push-pull dynamic, with its alternating between seeking closeness and pushing others away, can contribute to disruptions in the normal release of oxytocin during positive interactions. The release of endorphins during positive moments and a subsequent crash during negative ones create a cycle where the individual seeks to recreate positive emotional states. In short, your ex got attached, an attachment that may have felt grounding and stabilizing. Losing it leaves them in constant turbulence, and reaching out to you may be equivalent to self-medication. It’s better than self-cutting or entertaining suicidal thoughts, you know! Of course, it bothers you, but when someone is dysregulated, others become less important, and alleviating the pain of feeling all over the place becomes their main goal. Remember that one of the main characteristics of BPD is suffering from disorganized attachment, where an individual displays inconsistent and often contradictory strategies for dealing with stress, seeking comfort, and forming relationships. I’m sorry you are going through it. Rest assured that as soon as your ex finds the next person to get romantically involved with, you won’t hear back from her.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Therapists, what are your thoughts on complex trauma? I was hit, locked outside and thrown in a freezing cold showers as a kid when I threw bad tantrums. I suffer with severe anxiety and shame from this.
Answer: I kind of agree with David. It sounds that your memories are very specific and could be easily targeted for processing. Still, to respond to your question about complex trauma, before trying to process those memories, it’d be important to assess for dysregulation since you are suffering from anxiety. The shame in itself, needs to be treated and EMDR doesn’t work for that. It could actually cause more shame. I have a whole section on shame in my book as one of the main internal traumatizing agents. Complex trauma is as real as it can be. And Developmental trauma is too. If your caregiver was “cruel” and you lived in fear and shame, your system may be more affected than just having some disturbing memories. You may live in survival mode, and you may have many more manifestations in your physiology besides anxiety. And your psyche may be compromised to the level of distorting the meaning of your interactions. When a child lives in fear, their brain development gets compromised and there may be small alteration that need to be attended because with time, and if the abusive behavior was prolonged for many years, it could have put you at risk of crashing of your nervous system. If it hasn’t, intervening can stop that from happening and from developing a trauma disorder with long-lasting consequences. Hopefully, you may only need to become aware of your fears, gain management and dissolution of your anxiety, and recover confidence in your self.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: I feel like everyone thinks EMDR is the magical cure for trauma. Am I the only one who doesn’t like it and didn’t feel like it did anything?
Answer: There are no magical cures for mental health in general and EMDR is not the exception. But managing expectations is extremely important to get results because if you get disappointed or lack hope, you won’t engage at the level its required for your brain to believe and heal. Trust plays an important role while healing from trauma. Trust in general, and trust in the process in particular. The brain find its way into resolution and healing but it needs to be prepared and guided. There are 3 elements participating in a successful EMDR processing: EMDR is amazing if all the elements are in place. Still, it is amazing TO PROCESS traumatic memories. It doesn’t help regulating the nervous system, which is one of the main problems of traumatized people. Trauma treatment has at least 3 phases, and memory processing is only one of them. It can resolve all the issues that we develop after traumatization.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: I switched therapists because I became attached to her. I let her know in an email afterwards. She said I made the right decision. What does that even mean?
Answer: Did you want to hear you made a mistake? Or did you want her to show her pain? The answer you are looking for can’t come from someone that has no idea what your relationship was like. What I can tell you is that your question sounds as if you were bothered by her reaction. Since you are mentioning that you were attached to her, I can imagine you wished her to be attached to you too. When she didn’t show missing you, you got upset, or at least surprised. I don’t blsm you. I’d have been too. I have observed that basically everyone has a part that likes to be missed and desired even from people we don’t want to missed or desired by. So, I can assume that that part of you is asking the question. A part that has the doubt of whether the therapist didn’t value having you, and didn’t “suffer” when you left. She should, right? Even when we don’t know the real context, I can tell you that your therapist was doing her job at validating your decision and applauding your agency. A good therapist, even of felt pain for your termination, should not show it or mention it. Some experienced ones know how to do it in a way that is subtle. But think about it! It have been an error to tell you that you made the wrong decision. You were already gone and had already found another therapist. It was done! I think that her best option was to approve your decision and let you move on, which you had already done.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Will a relationship between 2 people with BPD work? In my opinion, its either diamonds in the sky . or its crashing from the sky for short periods anyway s
Answer: When two individuals with a tendency to feel very intensely live together, the dynamics of the relationship logically, will be intense and challenging. If someone is emotionally expressive with excessive and strong reactions to many situations, have low tolerance, and is prone to seek attention or validation—which are characteristics that many pwBPD—, relationships are not easy. If both sides of the relationship are equally reactive, the relationship could be explosive. When two people with BPD traits live together, the household may have a heightened emotional atmosphere with frequent displays of strong emotions. This could lead to passionate moments but also more frequent conflicts. The relationship may experience frequent ups and downs, with both individuals riding emotional highs and lows and the intensity of these fluctuations can make communication and understanding very challenging. Therefore, conflicts may escalate quickly and disagreements might become more difficult to resolve. On a positive note, both individuals may share a deep emotional understanding because they know how the other feels and how difficult is not to react the way they do. That could help them to connect on a profound level, as they can relate to each other's emotional experiences and pain, which could facilitate them to stay together for longer, which is such an essential reason they become over-reactive. Another positive, is that is that if they both channel their high energy into a common interest, they might engage in creative endeavors together. Their passion and expressiveness could lead to artistic collaboration or shared projects. There will be challenges, of course, since both partners may have a strong need for validation and attention. While they may provide emotional support to each other, there's also the risk of competing for attention and get into something that I call “victim competition” where both fight about who is more hurt than the other, who had it worse than the other, who should be receiving more in that moment. Another challenge may be making good decision, since they both may doubt their judgment, may be impulsive in their choices, and they both may have strong opinions and emotions about various aspects of their lives and neither would like to compromise. Living in an emotionally charged environment can be exhausting. Both individuals may need to develop coping strategies to manage stress and prevent burnout, Their relationship might experience cycles of intense intimacy followed by periods of emotional distance which, well managed and with good boundaries, could help them to maintain a healthy dynamic.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What are the signs your partner doesn't love you anymore?
Answer: One of my clients recently experienced distress when their ex removed them from their social media accounts, interpreting it as a sign that their partner had stopped loving them. Another client faced heartbreak upon discovering their partner's infidelity. Yet another felt romantically abandoned when their partner chose to get drunk rather than be together. In these three cases, the partners hadn't necessarily ceased to love their partner; instead, they were prioritizing themselves. The one that removed the partner from social media struggled with emotional stability. The second was engaged in a sexual affair but remained deeply in love with the partner and valued family highly. The third, dealing with stress at work and recent failures, sought solace in alcohol, making decisions to cope with personal struggles rather than lacking love for their partner. Still, even when the actions could potentially be considered signaling a lack of love, they might be responses to personal struggles, unmet needs, or weaknesses. Only the individuals involved truly know what it means to stop loving their partner. Certainly, we can identify behaviors that may indicate a disconnection from a loved one, such as decreased communication, reduced tolerance and affection, avoidance of intimacy or connection, physical and emotional absence, increased criticism, disinterest in the partner's life/achievements/needs, or a general sense of indifference or apathy. In such cases, it may be crucial to rejuvenate the relationship or prioritize reconnection before assuming lack of love. In a broader sense, I often emphasize that enduring romantic love involves a significant element of acceptance. Once there's a clear lack of acceptance, love may be supplanted by something else. While it's easy to feel love at the beginning of a relationship, sustaining it requires ongoing care, similar to the care that a delicate flower needs.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can a human with low empathy be a good psychologist?
Answer: Can a person with atrophied vocal cords be a good singer? Can someone with flat feet be a good dancer? Similarly, lack of empathy is a deficiency in the capacity to connect with others, and psychology is fundamentally about understanding others. To be fair, let's consider psychologists who are not primarily involved in clinical practice. Psychologists who solely teach may not require as much empathy as those engaged in counseling. Researchers, marketers, or psychologists who utilize cognitive understanding of human behavior for suggestions, assessments, plans, projects, etc., may not need empathy to the same extent. However, for psychologists dealing with people face-to-face and involved in clinical work—treating individuals with psychological disorders, emotional difficulties, and mental health issues, providing therapy and support—empathy is a crucial component. While knowledge is essential, the ability to understand and share the feelings of others is equally vital. I firmly believe in the uniqueness of each individual. If a clinician is unable to recognize the individuality of each client, their effectiveness in treatment may be compromised. While we share many traits, the number of combinations and manifestations is endless. Customizing treatment is key to achieving healing and stability.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why do people feel lonely?
Answer: Great question. People experience loneliness regardless of how much company they have, and that feeling, loneliness, could be as painful as toothache or a heartbreak. I have observed that many “lonely” people suffer also from fibromyalgia! Just get how painful it seems that the pain gets trapped in the nerves. Loneliness is not necessarily real but a subjective experience. It is a complex emotional state that can result from various factors, including social, psychological, and environmental aspects. Apparently, there studies that suggest there are neurobiological factors that contribute to and influence the feeling of loneliness. First of all, we as mammals, are social beings. We are designed to survive in packs, and therefor, being among others promote the feeling of safety. So, if we don’t feel safe, we get a feeling of not being protected which translates as loneliness. That normally is joined by a feeling of lack of trust on others, which increases the pain. The brain has specific networks associated with social behavior and connection. Differences in the functioning of those brain regions may be linked to feelings of loneliness. Those areas need the production of some neurotransmitters (mainly oxytocin and serotonin) for developing social bonding and well-being. The lack of production of the neurotransmitters may contribute to feelings of isolation because there is a deficiency in creating connections, feeling connected, and empathizing with those around. The lack of production of those neurotransmitters is sometimes associated with a high production of cortisol that is produced when we are stressed. When we are anxious, we may lose the capacity to connect as well. We humans may feel lonely for several other reasons, for example lack of confidence. Low self-esteem or negative self-perception may cause to struggle with forming and maintaining social connections, which then causes us to develop a feeling of loneliness. It is possible to eliminate psychological loneliness not only with physical company. We can feel very accompanied if we develop mental connection with others including God, birds, flowers, women is despair, etc., etc. We don’t need to be with them; we just need to carry them in our mental space.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How do you dissociate?
Answer: The other day I was in a party and a person that I adore arrived, and when I tried to introduce them to another friend, I couldn’t remember their name. Horrible! It’s not that I didn’t know the name, it was that my brain was too busy with all the excitement of the party that it couldn’t assist me and I just went blank. But I also have a favorite type of dissociation: when I go very deep in a meditation, I experience a sense of freedom and liberation, as I’m floating out of my body and feel all the expansiveness of the world. The other day I went up, up, up, and saw all my community as a bright and beautiful light coming out of each one of them but as a whole. The entire concept of dissociation holds immense significance within the realm of psychology and in a very unspoken way in the real of spirituality. Dissociation as defined in psychology is characterized by the separation of interconnected realms of experience. Which meditators and spiritual people aim to achieve. Psychedelics are using this exact same characteristic to help people heal. Under the umbrella of dissociation there is vast array of diverse manifestations, processes, and experiences that encapsulate the essence of "disconnecting." It involves a disconnection between various aspects of consciousness, memory, identity, or perception. Dissociation can manifest on a continuum, ranging from mild episodes of spacing out to more severe and clinically significant dissociative disorders. I know that the act of dissociating when not voluntary can feel horrendous, but I also know that we can develop the skill of dissociating in our advantage, like when we dissociate from pain.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why do people have to go through trauma?
Answer: It sounds like you're assuming that trauma is inevitable. It's not! Of course, it all depends on how you're using the term. 'Trauma' means a wound or injury, and there are many people who never get emotionally injured. Trauma can be considered a phenomenon because it is observable and happens as part of who we are. In its extensive understanding, trauma is connected to danger or threat and, therefore, the need to survive. Since I'm not sure what meaning you're giving to the word trauma, I'll rephrase your question using the different ways the word 'trauma' is used: I could give you more examples, but what I want to make clear is that trying to survive is natural; resisting it makes things worse. Getting injured is avoidable! Experiencing adversity is unavoidable, yes, but getting hurt from them is completely preventable. Trauma means long-lasting negative consequences. Not everyone suffers from long-lasting injuries after going through adversity." I wrote a book to explain in a very detailed way all these questions. I really want people to feel safe and this type of assumptions (that we all have to go through trauma) make us feel scared and in danger. That’s what’s dangerous for our mental health. Hope you can read my book (Traumatization and Its Aftermath) and feel safer.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Since we got engaged in June, the number of episodes my fiancé with BPD has increased to almost one a month where before it was 3-6 months. Is this normal?
Answer: In general, because of the attachment issues of pwBPD, they “invest” a lot of time and effort to secure a relationship. During that time, they feel that they give more than what they get, and that they have had no control in the relationship. Once they “secure” the relationship (as in getting engaged), they then want to exercise control for more than one reason: If your partner is or has been in therapy, it’d be good that they talk about it with their therapist. It is unavoidable but they need to recognize that something big is happening inside. I know people that leave therapy in these particular instances because they fear being discovered in their inadequacy and dysfunction. Remember that they carry a lot of shamed, and feeling childishly, entitled, and impulsive (specially if they have done a lot of work in getting better) make them feel ashamed again, and triggered for reasons they may not understand. Most of the time they lack mentalization and they don’t know what others think. They then expect the worse, blame others, and hide. They may hide in their reactivity, anger, and feistiness when in reality they want to hide to avoid being seen as damaged. In general, there are many moments (like the one you are mentioning) that can trigger a more exaggerated response in a pwBPD, causing more erratic and unpredictable behavior, like the death of the mother or attachment figure, the birth of a child that will take away the attention of the partner, or even success. When they get a promotion at work and a raise, they may become so full of themselves (something that they rarely experience) that they may not know how to behave and become erratic and arrogant. That’s what not knowing who you are causes. To answer your question, yes it is “normal” that they get more dysregulated when their status quo changes, but it should be managed to bring them back to a more average reactivity. Otherwise, it could easily escalate and lose control. And then, after marriage, it could get worse and you may feel sorry you finally signed the deal.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How does dissociation develop?
Answer: The entire concept of dissociation holds immense significance within the realm of psychology. Dissociation is characterized by the separation of interconnected realms of experience. Scholars have observed a direct correlation between the intensity of the response to a traumatic event and the extent of dissociation experienced. Furthermore, the more profound the dissociation, the more acute the symptoms of trauma-related disorders. The intricate exploration of dissociation could easily fill the pages of an entire book, as it has emerged as a pivotal player in the realm of psychopathology, closely intertwined with the effects of traumatization. Its association with conditions like DID (formerly known as Multiple Personality Disorder) has elevated its prominence. The body of literature that covers it has grown so much that I think it should be regarded as an umbrella term at this point because dissociation, like trauma, is not just one thing. Under the use of the term dissociation there is huge amount of diverse manifestations, processes, and experiences that encapsulate the essence of "disconnecting." It involves a disconnection between various aspects of consciousness, memory, identity, or perception that can manifest on a continuum, ranging from mild episodes of spacing out to more severe and clinically significant dissociative disorders. Dissociation often occurs in response to overwhelming stress, trauma, or distressing experiences. Dissociation occurring during traumatic events, particularly within the immobilization phase, is referred to as peritraumatic dissociation. It naturally emerges as an implicit byproduct of survival mechanisms. This dissociation may persist as a symptom, or it may resolve once the individual's autonomic regulation returns to baseline. While this scenario is relatively straightforward to envision, a more intriguing question arises: can we apply the term 'peritraumatic' to situations where traumatic incidents occur not as isolated events, but rather recurrently over extended periods, spanning years? In cases where a continuous state of stress prolongs the experience of traumatization, the survival protections could be turned on and off as the sense of dread is experienced over and over—until the neural circuits get disconnected more permanently. Eventually, this recurrent activation may lead to more enduring disconnections. Consequently, dissociation may evolve into a habitual manifestation within an individual's 'personality,' particularly in the case of a child enduring an inescapably unsafe environment, where disconnecting from the present serves as an adaptive strategy (such as in cases of incest). Before someone develops a trauma disorder, they may experience dissociation, which makes them more likely to have dissociative experiences in the future. This is more than just a coincidence. When someone is immobilized, their part of the system in charge of producing numbing agents kicks in (analgesia). This can cause them to disconnect from their thoughts and feelings. This is because their body is trying to protect them from the overwhelming experience of the trauma. After developing a trauma disorder, the person will experience a number of dissociative symptoms, such as emotional detachment, memory problems, and a sense of time distortion. Dissociation can become a way of life for those living on survival mode, and it can take a lot of energy to maintain. This can lead to problems with brain function, as the brain is not able to get enough energy for all the processes involved, hence, decreasing the activation of certain brain functions to harmful levels and the extreme of eventually making them unavailable. That person then lives “dissociated.” I explain this in detail in my book Traumatization and Its Aftermath (Chapter six). I have written a couple of articles that talk about dissociation:

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How can you effectively stop caring about what others think?
Answer: The problem is not caring but obsessing about what others think and living life dependent on their opinions rather than what's enjoyable. Perhaps it's the fear of being discovered as fake. Caring about what others think is inherent in us as social beings. We are mammals, and mammals live in groups. To survive, we need others because without them, we would perish. Even if someone learns to manage and provide for themselves, emotionally, we won't. Isolation debilitates our sense of self to the extreme, leading to illness and despair. This despair may not be obvious but can diminish motivation for living. Socialization, companionship, and social interactions are essential for mental and emotional health. Loneliness and segregation have negative effects on our well-being. Bonding among humans reduces stress and promotes the production of healthy chemicals that help us feel satisfied, joyful, motivated, and engaged. However, we have become more motivated to pretend to be happy than to actually be happy. That's why we obsess about how others perceive us because deep down, we know we are faking it. The less fake we are, the less important others' opinions become. The more we separate from being truthful, authentic, and real, the more our "hollow self" grows and drifts from our core. The part that cares much more about others is what we normally call the "ego." I don't use the term often because it may be confusing. Instead, I call it the "hollow self" because it's a construction we use to project an image of who we want others to see, not who we truly believe we are. It's similar to a hologram of us: it looks great and acts confident, but it lacks substance, is full of defenses and insecurities, and is easy to wound. The more we try to seem perfect, the farther we get from accepting and honoring our shortcomings, our humanity. You asked how we could effectively stop caring about what others think. Well, we need to dissolve the hollow self by noticing it, accepting our flaws, and seeking more recognition and acceptance from ourselves. Waiting for others to give us validation and recognition is what weakens our sense of self. We need to continue working on building it until it doesn't need external feedback because it's content.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is it possible for someone to have no imagination?
Answer: As a general rule, NO, it’s not possible. But there is always cases that break the rule, right? If you have a functioning brain, then you have imagination. You may lack visual imagination but you can imagine without visions or images. Some people, very few, lack the capacity to imagine other senses, but even the ones suffering from a disorder (aphantasia) can imagine stories, music, etc. For example, they are still able to imagine a plot and the characters on it and their actions in detail, or they can imagine a piece of music by thinking about the melody, harmony, and rhythm. Imagining is a form of thinking but in the abstract and using memory as opposed to senses. Imagination is a fundamental cognitive ability that allows individuals to create mental images, ideas, and concepts that are not directly tied to their immediate sensory experiences. It plays a crucial role in creativity, problem-solving, planning, and abstract thinking. If a person lacks cognitive abilities, maybe due to a brain injury, then they may lack that brain functionality of imagination. But in those cases, lacking imagination may be the least of their deficiencies. Imagine that!!

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Who agrees and who doesn't with this quote, “Trauma explains behavior. It does not excuse behavior.”?
Answer: Excuse = a reason or explanation put forward to defend or justify a fault or offense. If we apply that definition of “excuse” to your question, you are asking if it is acceptable or not that a traumatized person (someone suffering from a trauma disorder) uses their condition to defend or justify their behavior. Traumatization alters the functioning of our nervous system causing us to react in ways we don’t choose. Dysregulation, a key component of suffering from a trauma disorder, is characterised by the lack of tolerance to certain actions (such as criticism) and by the exaggerated and disproportionate reactions towards stimuli that may seem insignificant compared to how they take it. Could we excuse someone for reacting in such ways? We could understand it but they can use the argument of their dysregulation to be excused for the damage they can cause. You know what’s funny? Most people that suffer from dysregulation don’t even mention it. What’s more common to see is that many individuals use “trauma” as a way to excuse themselves from suffering the consequences of their actions and reactions, and develop a victim mentality. It’s not our fault to become reactive after traumatization but it’s our responsibility to work on re-establishing balance for our nervous system to stop interfering with our behavior. I’m seriously concerned about the practice of calling trauma to whatever sad, difficult, hurtful, or challenging we experience. It’s like calling depressed to whomever cries. or calling dissociated to whoever is forgetful or distracted. If we do that, then everyone could use their “labels” or belief of being “damaged” to treat others poorly, to avoid accountability, to disengage from the responsibility to act in way than don’t hurt others (or themselves). So, Trauma explains behavior and we could justify people that lack control over their actions for their reactions, but they can’t defend themselves or ask to be excused. If they are able to acknowledge that their behavior is extreme, they could start exercise dominion over it. If they can’t even acknowledge that their behavior is hurtful, then the problem is bigger. You may be dealing with the hollow-self, an empty shelf that protects the weak and fragile sense of self but creating smoke curtains.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is CODEPENDENCY in a relationship the same as having DEPENDENT PERSONALITY DISORDER?
Answer: Codependency is not a disorder; it could be considered a trait, a behavioral patter, or a tendency. You could say, if you please, that it may be a symptom. A personality disorder instead, is a whole set of symptoms. Are you asking if codependency a symptom of DPD? Let’s investigate. DPD is a recognized personality disorder (listed in the DSM-5), characterized by a pervasive and chronic pattern of dependence on others to meet emotional need or to make decisions. The pwDPD lacks agency or the believe that they are able to thrive on their own; they feel extremely incompetent and are convinced that nobody else is going to want them if they are left by either a partner or by their caregivers. The codependent instead, make the decision to remove the priority from themselves and give it to others. They trust they don’t need much and that giving makes them happy. The codependent is not completely defeated because they find joy in enduring adversity, which build up leverages on resilience. pwDPD are defeated in general, and lack resilience. That’s why they developed, overtime, a more permanent disorder.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Are there any benefits of going through narcissistic abuse, or is it only destructive?
Answer: Positive individuals make the best out of adversity. Your question may indicate you are one of those lucky individuals. We all know that narcissistic abuse is a deeply painful and destructive experience, and it can have severe emotional, psychological, and even physical consequences for the individuals who endure it. Most people here may be disturbed and may get upset with the idea of finding any benefit from being abused in general, but especially by a narcissist. Abused people may react with questions like: Is there a benefit of having a hand amputated? Or of being poisoned? Or from being denied the opportunity to enjoy life? The obvious answer is NO! And that’s how many people feel after narcissistic abuse. That they were deprived of something they may never be able to have. There is no benefit from that. But again, some individuals may have the capacity to find certain positive outcomes or personal growth on adversity. We could say that some benefits may be to increase resilience (what doesn’t kill you, makes you stronger), develop a much deeper self-awareness by getting a better understanding of themselves, their boundaries, and their needs, and even developing empathy and compassion for others that go through similar experiences, or worse. They may be more careful choosing their next partner, for sure, if you want to call that “a benefit”. Again, with a constructive sense of justice and a very positive attitude, you can find great qualities and value on excrement. These are just few examples of quotes that promote that type of positive mentality:

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why can't the narcissist understand the pain he caused me? Doesn't he know what he has done? Or is it to evade responsibility?
