Answer: They can understand that they cause pain but they may find so many justifications that they manage to not care. Do they know what they have done? Depending on the angle they see it. Do they evade responsibility? yes, always. Let’s go question by question you are asking: Why can’t the narcissist understand the pain they cause? You are assuming they can’t. That’s probably a wrong assumption. pwNPD almost never lack intelligence. They can logically grasp the consequences of their actions. However, their intelligence can be used to construct elaborate explanations and justifications that, in their eyes, excuse their behavior. Their actions are driven by unmet needs, and since they prioritize themselves (due to a lack of empathy) or consider themselves superior (grandiosity and entitlement), they often prioritize their own gains, even if it comes at the expense of others. Do they know what they have done? Many individuals with personality disorders have a distorted perception of reality. While they may witness the same events as others, they assign different meanings to them, resulting in a disconnect. They understand what they do, but it carries a different significance for them. Let me give you an example. Imagine you live in a French speaking country and that you grew up not using bad words. Then you move to an English speaking country and learn some bad words in English. You may use them, you know they are bad words, but they will never have the same “force” or emotional significance for you that those words have for native English speakers. The English bad words will continue being foreign to you even if you use them because you have no connection with their weight. It’s something like that! I’m not saying that they are not trying to insult you when they use the bad words. They put the energy of insulting but they may argue that it doesn’t count because they don’t truly grasp the full meaning of those words. Do they evade responsibility? Always!! They lack self-respect and they live hiding they defectiveness and insecurities (such as knowing they don’t care about others, they don’t have deep feelings, etc.), and they feel unfulfilled, dissatisfied, incomplete. That’s why their false-self (which I call hollow-self) gets so inflated. This leads them to develop tactics to get what they want. That’s part of what developed the disordered “personality.” So, once they become skilful at manipulating, denying, projecting, blaming, and gaslighting, they lose even more respect for themselves and the need to “survive” and win becomes paramount. That vicious circle causes them to evade commitment, accountability, or acceptance of the consequences of their actions.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: As a therapist, have you ever had a client start seeing you again a year or more after having previously finished therapy sessions with them? What was that like?
Answer: Have you stopped seeing a friend or a relative for a year or more? what’s like when you meet again? I bet that many times it feels like no time has passed, right? and just in few occasions, it may feel awkward, as if you have disconnected and don’t know where to start or how to reconnect. I have had many clients coming back after they had left. When a client comes back is very probable there was a very good connection between the tow of you, and hence, it’d feel as if no time has passed. It’d also depend on how or why the previous work ended. If the client left with a bad feeling, they may come back to find resolution. It happens. And then, as a therapist, you may feel grateful to have the opportunity to do repair work. Many times clients leave without giving us the opportunity to finish an intervention, to amend a mistake, to correct a bad day. When they come back and give you the opportunity, it feels like a victory for both. But if the client stopped therapy for a good reason, having them back means that they learned the value of working on themselves, the importance of self-care, and the beauty of growing emotionally. As a therapist, you also feel very satisfied and happy not only to see them coming back to you, but to see the evolution of the work. It feels amazing!

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can a trauma bond form after just 1 date?
Answer: Good question even if it doesn’t sound like. For many, it may seem like it. Let’s see why. Trauma bonds form over time in situations where there is repeated exposure to an abusive or traumatic relationship where one person exerts control and power over the other. A full-fledged trauma bond requires a prolonged and repetitive exposure to abuse, manipulation, and intermittent reinforcement of positive behaviors. Of course, there could always be a case that breaks the rule, or an interpretation that makes it seem possible. Reality is that even people can experience intense emotional reactions to negative or traumatic events even in short interactions, that doesn’t mean they have already developed a trauma bond to that specific abuser. Still, in cases where all the signs of a trauma bond are present after just few interactions, we could say that the person may have been accustomed to be part of a trauma bond that got transferred to the next partner if the previous trauma bond was not dissolved. But that, more than a trauma bond, could indicate a co-dependent tendency that may end up as a trauma bond overtime.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Do people with BPD choose partners that abuse them?
Answer: The answer is not a straightforward "yes" or a resounding "no," but I think you are very close to exposing a cruel and sad reality. Individuals with BPD, in one way or another, may end up being abused or, at the very least, feeling abused. Their most basic relational needs have never been met, and they will eternally seek a connection that, ultimately, they also fear. There is no doubt that people with BPD have specific vulnerabilities that could encourage, promote, or even necessitate some tough treatment. Even therapists sometimes hold the conception that to treat BPD, they need to apply "tough love." I don't agree with that idea at all, but several schools of thought teach it. BPD is rooted in rejection, criticism, detachment, and other types of adversity that place those who develop the disorder in a very dependent and weak position. Their Achilles' heel is failed relationships, and therefore, the more rejection they experience, the weaker their self-esteem and their capacity to find good partners become. They either befriend or enter into partnerships with troubled people or have to compromise, perpetuating the feeling of being rejected, inadequate, and so on. To answer your question, it's not that they choose abusers. Most partners they choose are actually nice people with a tendency to take care of others but pwBPD may become more childlike than a partner, which compels the other person to establish very strict boundaries, rules, contracts, and even punishments to manage the volatility and reactivity that create so much confusion, hurt, and chaos. Most people in a relationship with someone who has BPD suffer as well. They love the person but feel incapable of predicting what will happen next, what might trigger an outburst, a fight, a disappearance, or a hurtful and impulsive decision. The unpredictability causes stress, and it's only natural to feel the impulse to "control" the person with BPD, which is a significant mistake and can lead to breakups followed by the fear of abandonment which may turn into abusive behaviors.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can a narcissist fall in love?
Answer: Narcissists can fall in need more than fall in love! In general, individuals with narcissistic traits may struggle with forming healthy, deep, and lasting emotional connections because their self-centeredness and need for admiration can make it challenging for them to truly empathize with and prioritize the needs and feelings of others. If we are talking about NPD, then the answer is that they don’t compute “love” the way other people do. From my experience “reading” brain activity through the EEG (electroencephalogram) and it interpretation through the QEEG, and my direct observation of the thought and emotional patterns of many individuals, I have been able to detect that people with a full blown personality disorder lack important activation in sections of the cortex that have been identified as love centers (among them, the ventral tegmental area (VTA), medial insula, anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), nucleus accumbens (NAC), caudate nucleus, hypothalamus, Orbitofrontal Cortex (OFC), Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex (dlPFC), and Medial Prefrontal Cortex (mPFC)). When some of those areas, specially those located in the PFC, lack activation, the person can’t “understand” love in its full extent. They though, can get emotionally attached to others in a way that seems emotionally dependent, and which many people could consider “love.” There is a saying in Spanish “El que te quiere, te maltrata” which translates as: The one who loves you mistreats you. That saying comes from that type of emotional dependency. People may get attached to a level of madness but it’s not love, but possessiveness. pwNPD feels as if they own the person they “love” and they may feel desperate with that idea of losing one of their most valuable possessions. That, of course, until they find a replacement, and then the move into discarding. They may verbalize “I don’t love you anymore” but really meaning “I don’t need you anymore, and I found a better ‘model’ than you.” The same way they would deal with a car or an iphone. Do they love their car when they first buy it? They would say so, but that’s not love. Hope you get the difference.

Question: It is said that acceptance is essential to healing from a trauma bond, but what is the essential belief that the victim must accept?
Answer: Acceptance is a “one-fits-all” kind of term because there is a clear “maxima” in psychology that explains that once a person stops struggling and gets to the point of acceptance, the struggle subsides and the person finds peace. But I don’t think it can be applied straight forward or “essential to healing from a trauma bond” in a simple way. Actually, one of the problems of a trauma bond is that the abused “accepts” the abuse. I think that what’s essential is awareness. Awareness of that the dynamics and treatment are abusive; awareness that your vulnerabilities and shortcomings (such as low self-esteem, lack of self worth, dissociative tendencies, etc) may have driven you into the trauma bond; awareness that you may be dependant on the abuser; awareness that you need help because you are stuck in a situation that keeps debilitating you. Having awareness of those issues is not the same as accepting them. The one thing that may be essential to accept is that the trauma bonded individual is not to blame for the abuse.

Question: How long does it take to realize trauma bonding?
Answer: Knowing that you are trauma-bonded is almost an oxymoron. Trauma-bonded individuals are almost by default unaware (or have limited awareness) of the abusive and debilitating nature of their relationship. Trauma bonding often involves a strong emotional connection with an abusive or manipulative individual, which can lead the person experiencing it to rationalize, minimize, and justify the abusive behaviors. It can also be the case that the person is afraid of the consequences of acknowledging the abuse, such as further harm or retaliation from the abuser. This fear can keep them from recognizing the situation. So, to realize that you are trauma bonded, you have to become well-informed about the concept, which is one of the reasons you are here, asking and reading about it, right? Then, it may be necessary to have a strong support system that helps you identify and address your unhealthy attachment among the several steps you need to take. If people are not informed and are even oblivious to the “trauma bond” concept, it may take a very long time to recognize it, particularly if they lack awareness of the negative dynamics of their relationship, have become numb to the abuse, or are in a situation where manipulation and control are pervasive (which cloud their judgment and make it difficult to recognize the abuse). I think it’s fair to say that the more severe the abuse, the longer it may take to realize the trauma bond, especially if the person comes from a background of abuse, lack of safety, and if they have low self-esteem and a weak sense of self. As the abusers use manipulation tactics to keep the person in the relationship and succeed, the trauma-bonded person will keep debilitating and becoming less confident about being able to thrive outside the relationship. To get out of that horrible place, the trauma-bonded individual needs to exercise self-reflection, get educated, and, in most cases, seek assistance from a therapist or counselor who specializes in trauma and relational dynamics to develop awareness, rebuild the strength needed to stop the abuse and find a way out. It’s not automatic or fast because trauma bond is a survival strategy and removing defenses too fast decompensates the person’s stability. That sometimes is worse. Question: Does my narcissistic mom really not remember the traumatic events that happened in my childhood?
Answer: Interesting question but it’s vague. Did the “traumatic events” happened to you only? Was she just a witness? Or did she caused you to feel shocked, hurt, overwhelmed, and hopeless? I’m going to assume that what you are referring to as “traumatic events” are related to your mother hurting you and I’m going to assume that she suffers from NPD. Otherwise it’d be too difficult to respond. I know people that receive sentences like: “You ruined my life,” “I wish I had never had you,” “You were a mistake,” or “I don’t want you near my dead bed” and then deny they did say or even thought like that. Is that what you are referring to? People with NPD tend to deny or minimize the consequences of their actions as a way to protect themselves from acknowledging their wrongdoing or facing feelings of guilt. Denial can also serve to maintain a self-image of being blameless and superior. But also, pwNPD may have a distorted perception of events due to their self-centered nature and the disconnection with parts of their PFC. They might only remember events from their own perspective, downplaying or disregarding the impact of their actions on others which makes it that your mother may remember certain events but chooses to selectively remember or ignore the aspects that are uncomfortable for her to acknowledge or distorting the meaning of what she did. If your mother is like that, you’ll never know if she is only denying the events, if she distorts reality, or if she didn’t event registered the incidents because she compartmentalizes reality and is too busy about how she feels and disregards what other feel. Question: Can we make a pwBPD agree to respect our boundaries, and do they respect them?
Answer: Can a person that suffers from BPD agree on something? Can they respect boundaries? Because how difficult it is for them to regulate their emotional responses and due to the impulsivity, they may find it very difficult to respect the boundaries of others, or respect their words/agreements. Because they don’t have a strong sense of self, they hardly trust themselves. So, agreeing on something seems challenging. Because of the splitting, they may agree with you the good you but in the moment you become the bad you, they don’t see how they could commit. Because of the distortions in their perception, they may shift perceptions of themselves and others, which can influence how they perceive boundaries. A boundary that seemed acceptable one moment might feel intrusive the next due to rapidly changing feelings and thoughts. Because they don’t trust their judgment, they may be confused about what they agreed on. They carry a lot of shame for knowing they can’t hold to their intentions, so, they know they can’t trust themselves because they know they have little control over their reactions. That’s why many of them prefer not to make commitments or promises. In short, even if they agree on something, and they may respect boundaries in occasions, that doesn’t mean they will continue doing so. Boundaries need to be renegotiated, clarified, reminded, and modified in order to continue having them respected. Please don’t be surprised and/or punitive if they don’t.

Question: Are random flashbacks a way for the brain to heal?
Answer: Nope! Flashbacks may be evidence that the person was shocked or that a charged emotion was experienced but it could be the only symptom after the experience. They are preventive more than remedial. Flashbacks are intrusive pieces of a memory from incidents that had an emotional impact on you. Many times they come from incidents that are not even traumatic. They are the fragment of an emotional event that is stored connected with the emotional valence you experienced. These fragments are stored that way to make them more rapidly available. I’d even dare to say that there could be “positive flashbacks” that remind us of positively emotionally charged memories. Imagine memories of your baby giving their first step, or your wedding, or carrying your first pet. You can see images of that event when seeing someone’s baby, wedding, pet. But that was a stretch. Normally, the term “flashback”is used in connection with PTSD and traumatic events and they are considered sudden and vivid reliving emotional state the person was in during a traumatic event, with or without necessarily having a clear memory of the event itself. Their purpose is to remind you of possible threat, or of something worth having in mind as dangerous. While emotional flashbacks are commonly associated with PTSD and C-PTSD, they can also occur in people who have experienced other types of distressing life events or highly emotional moments that are then stored as important. They come without announcement if the brain encounters that the experience you are going through needs a warning. The flashback come to alert you of the possibility of facing a threat or an event that can shock you again. I like saying that our brain is extremely efficient but dumb at the same time. In order to avoid distress, brings distress. To avoid facing threat, brings anxiety and fear, which then activate the survival circuits that create further traumatization. In my book Traumatization and Its Aftermath (Routledge, 2023) I describe flashbacks in detail in all their variations and include hints on how to eliminate them.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: In EMDR, under what circumstances do clients share “out loud” the worst parts of their traumatic memories and when does the client only go there only in their mind? Isn’t putting into language traumatic memories essential for integration and healing?
Answer: I heard Bessel van der Kolk saying among a small group of clinicians that a large percentage of what therapists ask the client is for their own curiosity and not in the benefit of the client. I think this happens in many cases (not all), but it’s especially true during EMDR processing. In my experience, the more "internal" the person is, the better the processing goes. If the therapist asks too many questions about what’s happening in the client's mind, the client may lose some of that internal richness. EMDR is a modality that, even when many don’t want to accept it, is highly influenced by hypnosis. For better results, the client should be in a semi-trance state where they have more access to their subconscious and to the pieces of memories that need to be integrated, reconsolidated, and interpreted. If they feel obliged to report what they are seeing and experiencing, they may leave that state of semi-trance to be "present" in their narration to the clinician. This may also "invite" the ego to participate, tainting the report with drama, victimhood, or even cognitive interpretations that will derail the processing into a different type of intervention. That’s why I suggest my EMDR supervisees not to ask too much, and be explicit with the client about how disclosing everything that is happening is not necessary. Just enough information for the therapist to know (more or less) what’s going on and to be able to continue directing the process towards resolution. So, saying "out loud" the worst part of their traumatic memories may be an invitation for aberrations or exaggerations. But maybe, in some cases, that’s what the client needs before they can release all the anguish and pain they have carried. That’s why therapy in general, and EMDR in particular, needs to be individualized. Only the good connection, trust, and clinical understanding between the therapist and the client would decide whether the client should be loud or quiet during processing, and whether the client is using loudness to gain sympathy, as a characterological sign, or as the way they need before resolution. In summary, putting words to memories is not essential for integration or healing.

Question: Can PTSD get worse over time?
Answer: Yes, it can if it’s not resolved. One of the most important characteristics of having developed PTSD is the loss of internal equilibrium and the shift into operating in survival mode. Those two changes can make everything go wrong until we either feel out-of-control emotionally, or we fall physically ill. If the traumatic event that caused PTSD was mild, or if the person is resilient or finds ways to feel safe again, PTSD’s symptoms fade away gradually, but if the person doesn’t find the way to recover a sense of safety, the symptoms could gradually increase. Traumatization is the struggle for survival that our nervous system gets into after we experience shock, adversity, threat, etc. But traumatization can be running in the background for ever, and will continue wrecking havoc. I explain this at length in my book Traumatization and Its Aftermath.

Question: If the sense of self has not been properly developed in childhood (i.e., some individuals with personality disorders/adaptations), what are the best ways to develop it as an adult, so that one can stop perpetually seeking a sense of self in others?
Answer: I remember a woman that took her 4 year old child to the doctor because he was not talking. The doctor asks the child “what’s your name” and the mother mutters “tell the doctor your are Carlitos”, then the doctor asks “how old are you Carlitos” and the mother says “tell the doctor you are four years old”. After a few more questions with the same dynamic the doctor looks at the mom and says “That’s why your son doesn’t talk! Because you don’t let him talk!” I know a mother that cut the son’s hair until he was an adult who never even questioned whether he likes his haircut or not. I know individuals that were convinced by someone that they had bad taste, or were not good at certain tasks, who then chose to rely in the taste or abilities of others. I also know women from a conservative cultural background with strict gender roles and expectations for women to prioritize family and traditional roles over personal ambitions. They may never explore their talents because they are “programed” to follow a certain path. Those are just few examples. There are many other reasons kids don’t develop a full sense of self. Parents could be very impository in terms of what’s better or correct for them and kids never question their own. But it’s clear that not having a well developed sense of self doesn’t imply suffering from a personality disorder/adaptation by default even when several people with personality disorders lack a sense of self. To answer your question, there are several ways to develop a sense of self regardless of why they didn’t. In general terms, developing a robust sense of self in adulthood, to alleviate the perpetual seeking of validation from others, involves a process of introspection. Of course, engaging in therapeutic support offers an easy way to address underlying issues and unravel patterns that obstructs self-identity. It’s useful start by identifying, setting, and respecting personal boundaries, which helps safeguarding identity while mindfully exploring thoughts and emotions. Embracing personal growth activities aligned with individual passions fosters self-discovery. Practicing self-compassion and positive self-talk aids in countering negative self-perceptions. Cultivating relationships based on genuine acceptance reduces the reliance on external validation. Choosing autonomously, guided by intrinsic values, strengthens self-definition. A more self-assured sense of self emerges through patience, persistence, and gradual change that include the space to assess one’s preferences, views, values, desires, needs, etc. Seeking support from individuals who value one’s individuality, and gradually asserting one’s own identity in the face of different norms and expectations culminates the effort of finding and accepting one’s own voice and sense of Self. I full explanation on how the Self forms is in my book Traumatization and Its Aftermath (Routledge, 2023)

Question: How did you break the trauma bond when you were addicted to the narc?
Answer: At the peak of my trauma bonding, I could make anyone believe that what I was feeling was love! I think I even thought it was at the level of unconditional love!! Reality was that I wasn't addicted to the narcissist; I was addicted to the stress hormones flooding my blood. The anxiety provoked by the instability of my relationship kept my nervous system fighting to avoid collapsing into nothingness. It was not easy to accept that I was tied to a person who was both the source of my distress and the temporary relief from it. I didn’t know about this particular phenomenon that often arises in the presence of an abuser, where the cycles of affection and harm create a deeply confusing and addictive emotional pattern. This bond is not simply a product of love or affection but a result of the unpredictable mixture of pain and comfort that abusers provide. It's been many years of no contact, and I still wonder how much of it was genuine love and how much was just the trauma bond. I question this because even when I know trauma bond is based on survival and coping, I can still vividly recall the initial positive feelings I had for that man, specially the caring and attentive person I initially knew. But those positive feelings gradually faded, replaced by intense anxiety triggered by his dismissiveness, cruelty, lack of empathy, and manipulative words and actions. I held onto those positive emotions because they were the only way I could still experience "feel good" chemicals like serotonin, dopamine, and even oxytocin. Believing I was in love served as a shield against losing hope and motivation, preventing me from tumbling into despair and hopelessness. Still, I believe I wasn't just convincing myself it was love; I was genuinely opening my heart to feel love for that man, or simply to feel love. I needed those positive qualities to infuse into my system in order to maintain my footing and to build resilience. I discovered that love doesn’t need an object to feed ourselves. What I can see now is that instead of admitting I was enduring emotional abuse, I was concealing myself behind the "noble" notion of wanting to help him become a better person! Rather than terming his actions and conduct as abusive, I unknowingly painted them as his personal suffering and believed he required me to heal, overcome his struggle, and become the person I idealized. How did I break free from that terrible cycle? In a period when hardly anyone discussed trauma bonding and emotional abuse was frequently linked to children, I experimented with various approaches. Domestic violence was the glaring warning sign for adults, yet since I hadn't encountered physical abuse, I struggled to find strategies that aligned with my circumstances. The phrase "relationships aren't easy" crossed my path often, but a genuine understanding of the agony emotional abuse can cause was lacking, as well as an awareness of how incapacitating and damaging it can be to endure the actions of a person with Narcissistic Personality Disorder. So, I devised a few tricks to shield myself from falling back into the narcissist's claws. I remember snapping a picture of him in one of those moments when he was being abusive; his face twisted into a "beast" with fiery eyes, enlarged pores, and a gaping mouth. I enlarged the image and placed it on my night table. I also recorded some of his manipulative phrases and listened to them whenever I felt vulnerable and tempted to give him another chance. I jotted down some of these phrases on cards and positioned them around my home – spots tied to "pleasant" memories, like a perfume bottle he had given me or the sofa where we used to be intimate. These tactics helped rouse me from my slumber and I started realizing that most of my "love" was an illusion, a sentiment that didn't belong to him. The positive feeling I had protected so strongly connected to him were needed to make me stronger, not to be squandered on futile hopes of recovery. I realized that “my love” belonged to me and that I was not going to allow anyone to take that from me. He had taken away enough! I confronted the reality that what was left in our relationship bore no resemblance to what I thought I had initially. Joy had vanished, satisfaction had warped into anguish, admiration had twisted into fear, and attraction had soured into disgust. What I had dubbed love was truly a fervent attempt to deny my own failings – my blindness, the emotional reliance I had nurtured, the depletion of resources I had allowed, and the fragility shadowing my heart. Calling it love was a bid to infuse vitality into the destitution plaguing my heart, relationships, perspective, and life itself! I recovered “love” and used it to give myself the comfort I so badly needed. Love just needs space to flow and fill our system with hope and healing chemicals. I developed a lot of compassion for myself, and I broke the chains of the trauma bond. My book Traumatization and Its Aftermath expand on this subject and my experience

Question: Will therapy help a narcissist if they’re self aware? Can you be in a relationship with one if they’re in therapy?
Answer: People with NPD typically do not willingly seek therapy. They may be compelled by circumstances or the demands of others, rendering therapy remedial and often less effective. However, if the individual you're referring to as a "narcissist" displays only certain traits and possesses self-awareness along with a genuine commitment to personal growth and change, therapy can indeed yield benefits. Individuals who can recognize their narcissistic tendencies and engage in self-reflection should not be classified as full-fledged narcissists. While they might encounter emotional and social challenges, labeling such individuals as "narcissists" would not be accurate if they sincerely wish to address their issues. Central to this discussion is the concept of self-reflection. What distinguishes a functional, healthy person from a dysfunctional one lies in the robust activation of their executive functions—the higher-level cognitive processes enabling individuals to regulate their thoughts, actions, and emotions for goal attainment and adaptive behavior. Self-reflection involves the capacity to thoughtfully and introspectively examine one's thoughts, emotions, behaviors, and experiences, and become accountable for them. Crucially, awareness stands as a pivotal executive function. Possessing awareness empowers individuals to be present and impartially observe themselves, thereby developing an objective understanding of their shortcomings and the consequences of their actions. Initiating self-reflection necessitates being mindful of thoughts, feelings, and actions, while also acknowledging their impact on others. This entails paying attention to internal experiences and maintaining a truthful stance regarding one's thoughts and emotions. It's important to note that individuals demonstrating such qualities should not be hastily labeled as "narcissists" since they seem to possess empathy and concern for others and not solely focused on their needs and how to use others to have them met. Moreover, if someone exhibiting self-reflective capabilities actively engages in therapy, it reflects a sincere desire to better themselves and grow. In light of this, the opportunity to improve and evolve should be extended to those who genuinely seek it. After all, why should we withhold support from individuals who aspire to enhance themselves and their well-being? If the individual you are contemplating entering a relationship with displays these positive traits, why wouldn't you consider giving it a chance? However, if the reason you are labeling the person as a narcissist stems from traits such as abusive behavior, lack of empathy, neglect of your needs, absence of consideration and attention, violence, dismissiveness, or any other trait that places you in jeopardy or makes you feel diminished and threatened, then being in a relationship with that person is not advisable, irrespective of whether they are undergoing therapy or not. Many people go to therapy solely to enhance their self-esteem or to feel better about themselves rather than seeking genuine personal growth or improvement.

Question: Is it gaslighting when saying "it’s not my fault you feel that way"?
Answer: Gaslighting is among those terms that can inadvertently promote a victim mentality and contribute to stigmatizing our capacity for resilience. Moreover, it has the potential to pathologize behaviors that might not necessarily warrant such classification due to the prevalent use of the term. Many innocuous phases or interactions could be mistaken for abuse, manipulation, or psychological harm when labeled as "gaslighting." In a general context, we employ the term "gaslighting" when a person employs it as a deliberate strategy with the intent of causing another individual to doubt their own perceptions, memories, or sanity. This is often done subtly and over an extended period. Gaslighting constitutes a form of emotional abuse. I explained emotional abuse in this post: Hence, to address your question, we would need to know whether the individual who used the statement "it's not my fault you feel that way" did so with the deliberate intent to manipulate, confuse, weaken, or undermine your personal power for their own gain, before we can accurately classify it as "gaslighting." Question: Do you think it could be true that all addicts are suffering from childhood trauma?
Answer: Have you ever enjoyed a glass (or two) of an alcoholic beverage (or another addictive substance) that brought about feelings of euphoria? Did you find it appealing? Do you feel compelled to recreate that experience? Most likely, you do. Many addictive substances (opioids, stimulants, or even certain behaviors like gambling) can have similar effects on the brain's reward system and neurotransmitter release, particularly dopamine. Addictive substances impact the brain's reward system by triggering the increased release of various neurotransmitters, including dopamine. These neurotransmitters are closely linked with feelings of pleasure and reinforcement. This phenomenon generates a pleasurable sensation and fosters a desire to relive the experience, which can contribute to the development of addictive behavior. Not only that! Consider that our brain is highly efficient in multitasking, constantly juggling numerous functions every second. If the brain perceives that certain functions can be delegated to other mechanisms, it may reduce its effort in those areas. If the addictive substance becomes the means through which the brain experiences pleasure or disinhibition, it might cease seeking alternative pathways to generate these sensations. Consequently, the brain diminishes its dopamine production, relying on the addictive substance to initiate this process. This mechanism is a crucial reason behind the addictive nature of these substances. The brain becomes dependent on them to enable the individual to encounter the positive effects associated with the reward and motivational systems. That happens to all of us! And anyone of us can become addicted regardless of whether we suffered from abuse, neglect, or other types of adversity because addiction is an inherent characteristic of the interplay of the substance and the brain. Other factors also contribute to the development of addiction. If the child suffered a lot of traumatization and depleted their resilience and internal resources, or there are other factors like genetics, addictive substances in the environment or addicted parents, and individual vulnerability, the kid may be more prone to develop of addiction. So, to respond to your question, while traumatization during childhood can increase vulnerability to addiction for some individuals, it's not the sole determinant. Addiction is influenced by a combination of factors, and some people may develop addiction without a history of trauma.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How do childhood experiences impact adult mental health?
Answer: Think about it this way: How does the language your parents speak at home impact your language development? Not only will you speak the language your parents use at home, but your tongue will also develop the specific flexibility required to pronounce words like them, your brain will develop circuits that follow the grammatical structure of that language, you will accumulate words, one by one, to identify objects, people, actions, moods, and more. You will learn to use not only the words but also the body language that accompanies each one, and your emotions will follow a “script” on how to act or respond when experiencing specific emotions according to what you saw as a child. These pictures show you some examples of what I’m trying to convey: It was difficult to chose the pictures because not everyone adopts the same posture or attitude when sad, happy, angry, or friendly. The way you express your emotions is typically developed in childhood, primarily influenced by what you observe at home and, secondarily, by your experiences at school, on TV, or through social media. Mental health is intricately connected to how you manage your emotional system. That’s why your childhood experiences impact your mental health. Your parents' emotional responses and beliefs shape your emotional brain, influencing the intensity of your emotions, your emotional reactions, and your beliefs about them. If you are unable to express your emotions authentically, you may begin to alter your natural responses and adopt what is accepted or tolerated. What you witness as the norm for how people relate to each other during childhood becomes the template for your own relational patterns. If you observe abuse, you are likely to learn either the "language" of the abuser or the language of the abused, and so on. In addition to the "language" you acquire, childhood experiences contribute to shaping various other aspects, such as your identity and self-esteem, your emotional regulation, your cognitive abilities, your behavioral patterns, and ultimately, your personality. For this second part, consider your body: if you engage in exercise and cultivate healthy habits during childhood, your body will develop healthily. Conversely, growing up with a sedentary lifestyle, isolation, and unhealthy eating habits can lead to a predisposition for illnesses that become more apparent as you age. The good news is that growth never truly ceases! We continue to learn and develop new neural pathways, habits, and even languages. We have the capacity to modify unhealthy "grammar" or vocabulary, introduce new words, expand our knowledge, and adapt to new circumstances. But, of course, our childhood experiences lay the foundation for our future emotional well-being, which can be either nurturing or toxic.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What do victims of narcissistic abuse all have in common?
Answer: Before the abuse or after? Before becoming victims of narcissistic abuse, let's explore the characteristics that narcissists find attractive when choosing their victims. Abusers deliberately exploit vulnerabilities, and they are drawn to individuals with qualities such as high empathy, emotional sensitivity, compassion, low self-esteem, a history of adversity (especially abuse), naivete, and a tendency to prioritize the needs of others. Additionally, narcissists may be attracted to people with specific achievements or qualities that reflect positively on themselves or elevate their status. Being naive is significant for narcissists because individuals without much experience with narcissism may not anticipate what to expect, and it can take several years of manipulation and abuse before the naive victim realizes the reality of the situation. While you only mentioned "narcissistic abuse" in your question, many times people are victims of narcissistic use, which can have similar consequences. Being used may not be immediately recognized as harmful, but it can cause significant damage, especially if endured for an extended period. These types of relationships are prevalent in professional settings and not just limited to familiar relationships. When individuals realize they are victims of narcissistic abuse or use, they may experience a profound sense of vulnerability and weakening. Their existing vulnerabilities may intensify, leading to increased insecurity, sensitivity, shame, and disappointment. They might harbor confusion, doubts, and regrets, feeling let down by themselves for not recognizing the abuse earlier and for unwittingly playing a role in the manipulation. After escaping narcissistic abuse or use, individuals may go through a phase of victimhood as they seek validation for their suffering they have endured, and the losses they have to face. They will require substantial support to reclaim what was lost or come to terms with the things they will never regain. Once they have completely moved beyond the narcissistic abuse, survivors may gradually awaken to their strength. With perseverance and healing, they can regain self-esteem and the resources they lost. They may become a tremendous source of support for others, having gained resilience, tolerance, stronger boundaries, self-awareness, and various other attributes through their experiences. While narcissistic abuse is an incredibly distressing experience that nobody should endure, it can lead individuals to develop resilience and other positive qualities. Survivors often undergo personal growth, gain a deeper understanding of themselves and humanity, and foster healthier relationships with both themselves and others. The freedom attained from leaving an abusive situation and the insight gained are valuable assets that contribute to a more fulfilling life and better relationships with oneself and others.

Question: As a therapist, what things do you notice in PTSD patients? Can you tell from session 1 that's what they have? Is it a problem if they won't speak to you?
Answer: As a therapist, I avoid giving a diagnosis during session 1. Instead, I focus on understanding the client's emotional state, their perceptions of their situation, and why they seek help. From there, I build a therapeutic approach tailored to their needs. In clinical or insurance settings, therapists are often trained to provide a diagnosis early on. Common diagnoses include Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD), and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). Adjustment Disorder is also used, but insurance may be hesitant to cover extended treatment, assuming it should resolve quickly and hence, some clinicians avoid it. Some therapists may settle for a disclosed diagnosis without further exploration. However, the reality is that diagnosing PTSD requires multiple sessions to ensure the person is dealing with long-lasting damage to their nervous system and other functions. Many therapists tend to diagnose PTSD once they learn the client experienced a traumatic event, such as domestic violence, rape, car crashes, or the death of a close relative. It's worth noting that while the death of a close relative can be extremely painful, it may not be considered traumatic by default. In any case, it's not solely the event that marks PTSD; many people do not suffer from it even if their lives were jeopardized. Before giving a diagnosis, therapists must thoroughly investigate if all the symptoms listed in the DSM are present and if they significantly impair the person's functioning. The symptoms to look for include: Still, they are not easy to discover because the client may not even be aware of all the symptoms and their manifestations, or they may be hesitant to share until they have developed trust in the therapist.
