Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: I have C-PTSD from childhood sexual trauma, which resurfaced as an adult. I'm feeling a lot of shame. I was shamed as a child too. What do you feel shame about?
Answer: This is a difficult subject, and I will do my best to discuss it sensitively, but it's possible that some of you may feel upset. I've been teaching this subject for several years, and I understand that it's not easy to grasp the two main ideas surrounding sex and shame. The first one is that when we talking about sexuality, our body doesn’t necessarily synchronizes with our mind. The body reacts to the erogenous stimulation regardless of the thoughts, values, or even fear. Our primitive brain responds with sexual arousal even if we are deeply submerged on emotional pain. When investigating in this topic, it is very shocking to learn that kids that get molested before they have cognition of the inappropriateness of it, may enjoy the touch, the attention, the care they receive. Many kids learn to receive love through sexual games and through the special “treatment” they get from the molester. They don’t feel bad until they become aware of what they got into and that’s when the shame comes to hunt them. They feel defective, guilty, damaged, etc., which are feelings that the brain takes as signs of the need to hide from being perceived in their “sins”. The shame is actually what traumatizes the system because once the awareness hits, the person feels lost, confused, at risk. The second one, when the molestation (or sexual abuse) happens when the person is already aware of the severity of the act is that many people feel sexual pleasure while being sexually attacked. The brain knows that the person is in danger because of the fear, and in order to avoid more damage, lubricates the woman’s sexual part and irrigates blood to the genitals (male & female). People could even experience an orgasm during rape! That makes the person that was abused feel as if they had participated on the act, as if they can’t complain because they “enjoyed” it. That’s when the shame takes over. That’s a clear example of what I’m referring to when I say that the body and the mind disconnect. The body does its task while the mind dissociates from the pain of the event. If you were shamed as a child for other reasons, then your system may have learned to hide and feel as if you don’t deserve much. When you add to that the information we gather nowadays about the damage caused by sexual abuse, your system can become conflicted—struggling between wanting to talk and not talk, feel and not feel—which creates fragmentation of your psyche. I'm an advocate of allowing individuals who have experienced molestation to express themselves freely without feeling the pressure to meet society's or social media's expectations. It's important to recognize that while some people may be traumatized by the experience, many are not. Unfortunately, many individuals feel shame thinking there is something wrong with them, while others may feel ashamed for not experiencing guilt about the incident. Therapists should approach these situations with an open mind, ready to listen to the story of the person who was molested without immediately labeling or judging them. It's possible that they may not feel guilty or ashamed, they may not consider themselves victims, or they may experience a combination of these emotions simultaneously. Each person's experience is unique, and it's crucial to respect their feelings and perspectives without imposing preconceived notions upon them.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Will therapists warn their client that they are being abused by someone around them if it happens and the client doesn't notice it, or they won't say anything and wait for the client to realize it on their own?
Answer: To get an idea if there is a standard practice regarding this important subject, I asked several of my supervisees before responding to your question. I was surprised to find that their initial answers were that they wouldn’t warn the client! Many of them said they would wait until the client realized it on their own, as you are asking. However, this is not my opinion, and I'll tell you why. After an interesting discussion, I learned that many of the clinicians I supervise were afraid of upsetting their clients, which was probably the main reason they didn’t want to say anything. Some therapists fear losing the client if they address issues that may sound like a “judgment,” and they consider labeling someone as “abusive” to be seen as judgmental. Additionally, they expressed concerns about having only part of the story and how that might impact their ability to accurately assess the situation. To me, it is clear that putting the expectation on the abused client to realize they are being abused is not in line with the trauma lens. This realization gave me the opportunity to continue building up on what trauma therapy is versus ‘traditional’ therapy. Through the trauma lens, we understand that people often become numb to their pain when abused, making it nearly impossible for them to come to that realization without some guidance. Certain functions of their brain become disconnected as part of their adaptation to the pain of being hurt. They may try to justify the abuse using cognition alone or dissociate from the reality they live in, feeling nothing. Additionally, some abused individuals develop a trauma bond, making it extremely difficult for them to accept that they are being hurt, and they may even blame themselves. That’s what traumatization is about! If we, as clinicians, don't say anything, we may become bystanders, which some authors consider to be a type of moral guilt Of course, the “truth” needs to be delivered slowly and kindly because numbing or dissociating are defenses and we can’t remove defenses abruptly; there is a risk of decompensation or confusion if the person feels all in a sudden “naked” and “discovered” in their ignorance or permissiveness. So, something I do, is for example, recommend an article where they can see their own situation reflected on the reading. Other thing that I do is to bring the PFC activation with role-play, empty-chair, or some exercises that allow them to take distance and see the situation played out without having it “on their face”. But sometimes the abusive situation may require immediate assistance and the therapist can’t wait until the interventions work. So, the way to proceed is with psycheducation, a lot of questions that bring more awareness, and a conversation about risk and safety. The therapist may need to help the person make plans or even have a conversation about “mandatory reporting”. As always, it depends on the situation, the type of abuse, the severity of it, and the type of resources (or lack of) the client has.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can you get PTSD from siblings abandonment?
Answer: You could develop PTSD from almost everything that jeopardizes your life or your integrity. But we don’t unless we stay in a state of fear, helplessness and defeat. People may be afraid of their shadow and live hypervigilant to when the shadow will destroy them. They develop PTSD and maintain their symptomatology alive for as long as they stay afraid of their shadow and believing that the shadow is more powerful than them. If you depended of your sibling and if you think that the fact the your sibling abandoned you puts your future in danger, and that you won’t be able to survive without your sibling, then you could easily develop PTSD. But you won’t develop PTSD merely for the pain of the departure of your sibling even if the pain is huge.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Are highly sensitive people more likely to develop C/PTSD?
Answer: The concept of “Highly Sensitive People” HSP has a little of myth, a little of science, and a little of magic. The myth started developing in the 70s around the concept of the “indigo Children.” It was suggested that certain children are born with special or ‘supernatural’ traits and abilities, making them more spiritually evolved, empathic, and sensitive to the world around them. The term "Indigo" comes from the belief that these children possess an indigo-colored aura. The idea of Indigo children is not scientifically supported or recognized by mainstream psychology or science, but it gained a lot of attention because many parents needed to understand their kids and the proponents of the Indigo children claimed they could observe certain traits or characteristics in their children that could be pointed as weaknesses. The movement recognized certain attributes often explained as deficits in personality, temperament, and cognitive development as strengths. I think this got the attention of the scientific community which found that many kids are born with heightened sensory responses. Psychologists Elaine N. Aron and Arthur Aron coined and developed the concept of HSP in the 1990s. They stated that HSP tend to process sensory information more deeply and thoroughly than the general population. For example, they have a heightened awareness of sensory stimuli, such as sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures. They often notice subtleties that others might overlook, which can make certain environments or situations overwhelming or overstimulating. They are also more attuned to their emotions and the emotions of others and tend to feel things deeply and may be more affected by emotionally charged situations or experiences. What’s interesting is that they are considered as having a high level of empathy and compassion that helps them readily sense the feelings and needs of others, making them great listeners and supportive friends, which was one of the main attributes of the Indigo Kids. But since HSP was developed by psychologist, they had to pathologize them. even when they didn’t define it as a disorder, but rather, as a personality trait. They say that HSP can become easily overwhelmed in noisy or crowded environments, or in situations with intense emotions, and that they may need more downtime to recharge after such experiences. What I call magic is the fact that there are people that are extremely attuned to others which makes them more selfless. They seem to be more advanced in their perception and intuition, they value what’s more important and deep, they reject violence, etc., which make them kind of being that don’t belong to this plane of existence. They commonly feel misunderstood, rejected, bullied, and treated as weak. They are pushed by the parents to become tougher without valuing their “beauty”. Actually, many HSP end up developing mental disorders because the lack of understanding of their sensitivity. They may not succeed in the material world as expected, which make them feel excluded and defeated. So, yes, HSP may develop a trauma disorder more easily than others not because they lack resilience, but because they may find the aggressiveness and lack of love of their environments too painful to bear and to manage. They can become sick of their stomach if they witness poverty, violence, abuse, etc., which puts their nervous system at risk. But can also resolve the traumatization faster and better than many because they can use their high sensitivity to find safety, beauty, and hope.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can a narcissist, at some point in life, realize they are a narcissist and make a conscious choice to remain one?
Answer: Accepting to be a narcissist is an oxymoron. How could someone who thinks so highly of themselves believe that their charm and superiority are 'defects'? Of course, narcissism, like any other disorder, exists on a spectrum, ranging from very severe (complete lack of awareness) to very mild (with the capacity for self-reflection). I don't even call individuals with some narcissistic traits NPD (Narcissistic Personality Disorder) if they can empathize and recognize the damage they inflict; hence, they can acknowledge their "narcissism." It's common to see how the term "narcissism" is used indiscriminately if one or just a few traits are displayed. This can lead to confusion about one's identity. In general, narcissism is characterized by a lack of accountability and empathy, and people with full-blown NPD are unlikely to recognize anything wrong about themselves. They find aspects of their behavior rewarding, such as seeking admiration, attention, or control over others. They may enjoy the feeling of superiority or entitlement that comes with their narcissistic behavior, leading them to perpetuate and reinforce these behaviors. On the other hand, some believe that individuals with NPD are protecting themselves from feelings of vulnerability and inadequacy. In those cases, they may not necessarily "like" being a narcissist, but their behavior becomes a strategy to maintain their self-image and avoid confronting their underlying emotional pain. However, they may learn that their self-centered behavior benefits them more than harms them, and thus continue behaving the same way. It's important to recognize that using labels to name various presentations of narcissistic traits may not capture the complexity of individual experiences. Not all "narcissists" are the same, and they may have different motivations and struggles. To answer your question, here and in many other questions, the answer is “it depends”. Disorders exist as indications of certain patterns, but they are not "all or nothing." Each individual has a unique internal universe, as well as their own personal external world and circumstances. Ultimately, individuals seek survival and adaptation. If being a narcissist leads to becoming president, one may protect their narcissism. On the other hand, if being narcissistic jeopardizes everything they have, they may choose to work on being less narcissistic (or to become accountable). However, there is a degree of narcissism that becomes self-destructive, where individuals stop caring about self-preservation if their primary goal is to destroy someone else. At that point, they may not make decisions but merely react like wounded animals.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why should we be so hard on a narcissist when we know that they are the way they are because of childhood trauma?
Answer: I hear you are asking why can’t we have compassion for people that because of their circumstances, they grew up to become abusers and manipulators? First, because before we can experience compassion, we need to resolve our natural instinct for survival. Second, because psNPD are among the people that don’t really put an effort on changing or stopping hurting others. There is a hierarchy in the way we react: First, we are primitive creatures that need to survive; then we are social creatures that need others, like a tribe or a family, to survive; then we are powerful creatures (humans) that are able to create love or to destroy others without even touching them, and after that, we are spiritual beings. Therefore, if someone treats you badly and hurts you, you'll instinctively reject or try to stop that person from continuing to hurt you. If you can't stop the person, you may suppress your feelings and fall into a sort of resignation because, as social beings, we sometimes prefer to endure a little suffering rather than being alone. We might come up with sophisticated ways to stop feeling, to dissociate, or to justify our own or the other person's actions to keep on surviving. We engage in many "creative" strategies before we can tap into our spiritual resources to feel less affected by someone's harming behavior. Secondly, even if we know that the person suffered maltreatment, abuse, or some other adversity in childhood, it doesn't necessarily make us feel less afraid or more understanding. Cognitively, we understand that everyone face adversity in one way or another, and many of us make an effort not to burden others with our emotional baggage. It's part of our human nature to experience suffering, but it's also human to do everything possible to minimize it. We work on our relationships, emotional reactions, and adapt by creating instead of destroying. If we observe someone showing no interest in caring for or considering others and using abuse for personal gain, we learn that we can't rely on them and, therefore, we need to protect ourselves from them. It's easy to exercise compassion when you are not personally experiencing the pain inflicted by a narcissist, but when you are the target of their worst behavior, it becomes almost unhealthy to be compassionate. Self-sacrifice is not something we praise in our society, nor does it make us more functional. Martyrdom is outdated.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why does my therapist want to do EMDR when we haven’t even discussed my trauma yet? Don’T we need to talk about my trauma before we start EMDR in order for EMDR to work?
Answer: More than one reason come to mind: cultish mentality, easy of use, structure, narrow focus, etc. Let me go through them one by one. I. For many decades, therapists adopted one school of thought and became part of a group (like a cult). Their specialization kind of gave them an identity: "I'm a Jungian psychoanalyst," "I'm a Freudian psychoanalyst," "I'm a Rogerian," etc. However, modalities have become much more common and numerous than schools of thought, and modalities don't give therapists an identity; they provide therapists with a set of tools! Still, EMDR was formed (in 1989) with an old-fashioned mentality that it was either "my school of thought" or nothing else. This might be a reason why many therapists want to adopt EMDR as their specialization and use it most of the time, as Francine Shapiro formed her own school of thought, and she has many followers who seem to work for Shapiro more than they work for the client. II. Another reason could be that EMDR is not as difficult for therapists to use because most of the work is done by the client. Many EMDR therapists, especially inexperienced ones, just keep saying "go with that," expecting the magic to happen at some point. EMDR trainers promise too much to trainees, and many believe that changes will happen eventually. Unfortunately, if the clinician doesn't know what they are doing, the magic may never appear. III. EMDR is one of the few modalities that offer a "formula" that is supposed to be applied exactly the same way regardless of the client. This may be very appealing to many therapists who do not want to think or participate much and instead prefer to apply something structured, simple, and easy to memorize. IV. Many people think that trauma is synonymous with traumatic memories and believe in going immediately to the loaded memories to reduce symptoms. But trauma treatment is not only about processing memories. All trauma-focused treatments are designed to use stages: Safety and Stabilization, Processing, and Integration. EMDRIA claims that EMDR includes all the stages in its 8-phase model, but most EMDR trainers emphasize phase 4, which is the "go with that" part (desensitization). Most people learn to do phases 1-3 in half an hour and spend the rest of treatment doing phase 4. This means there is a misunderstanding about what trauma really means for the whole system of the person. Processing memories alone doesn't heal trauma, but it is taking years for clinicians to understand this basic premise. If you read my book Traumatization and Its Aftermath (Routledge, 2023), you’ll understand what it’s required to treat and resolve traumatization. For example, in your question, you say, "Don't we need to talk about my trauma before we start EMDR in order for EMDR to work?" That shows that you also think that you need to talk about the horrors you went through to process them. However, that's not accurate. In order to heal and stop your system from continuing in survival mode, you have to do many things that don't involve talking about what happened in the past before you can reach the point where remembering won’t be destabilizing or re-traumatizing. If you talk about it before you are ready, you can get worse. The same goes for EMDR. If you do it before you are ready, it can worsen your symptoms. But if you have already done stabilization work for a while and have developed enough tolerance for experiencing intense emotions, then you can proceed with EMDR without having discussed the trauma extensively beforehand. During the processing, if necessary, you may choose to talk about it. Best of luck!

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What does being grounded feel like (I’ve been dissociating for a long time)?
Answer: I’m sorry to say it like this but your “dissociating for a long time” may be more narrative than reality. Let’s uncover some of the myths of dissociation! Do you know when to go to the bathroom? Yes, right? That means that you know when your body needs to pee or evacuate. Do you know when you feel hungry? Yes, right? you know when your body needs food, or when you are tired. That’s some level of groundedness. There is a lot of myth around the term “dissociation.” Dissociation can lead to feelings of detachment, unreality, or disconnection from oneself and the present moment but it’s not a “all or nothing” type of experience. Being grounded is basically to be in the here and now. We have many different functions that help us to understand ourselves in relationship with the here and now: neuroception, interoception, exteroception, proprioception, all our senses, and our awareness. We can’t “dissociate” from all of them because that would mean that we are comatose (insentient). To respond to your question I’m going to separate “dissociation” in only 2 groups: Disengagement from the environment: this experience move into a range from an instant to a longer period. It gives a sense of detachment or disconnection from one's surroundings or immediate reality. It is a phenomenon that can occur in response to various stressful or traumatic experiences and is often a coping mechanism to protect the individual from overwhelming emotions, thoughts, or experiences. When someone experiences dissociation as disengagement from the environment, they may feel as though they are mentally or emotionally "checking out" from the present moment. They might describe feeling numb, spaced out, or as if they are watching themselves from a distance, but as all defenses, are momentary and parcial. Nobody completely and permanently detaches from reality. If they do, they would be incapable to function in the world; they would be rolled over by a car, fall from the stairs, burn themselves, eat until they vomit or not eat at all, etc. We normally experience this type of disengagement for moments but some of the functions I mention bring our awareness back to our surroundings or to our body’s needs. That’s pure survival. Disconnection from emotions: this type of dissociation can be more permanent because it can imply unplugging some neuronal circuits to avoid being aware of the pain of some circumstances. While disconnecting emotionally, an individual may experience a detachment or numbing of their emotional responses. This dissociative process involves an inability to fully experience or express emotions in response to a situation or event. When someone experiences dissociation as disengagement from emotions, one may describe feeling emotionally numb, disconnected, or as if emotions are distant or inaccessible. It's as if there is a barrier or "wall" between oneself and one's feelings, leading to a reduced or muted emotional response. To be grounded is more connected with the first type of dissociation I mentioned: disengagement from the environment. Being grounded feels like having a strong and stable connection to your physical body and to the present moment. When you are grounded, you feel centered, anchored, and aware of what’s going on around (if it’s cold or warm, loud or silent, etc), and your sensations (hungry, sleepy, full, etc.). Some people talk about being grounded as something spiritual, but normally speaking, it’s a very physiological experience. It has to do with your level of awareness and everyone can get there. If disengaging has become a habit for your brain, being grounded might be unfamiliar or challenging at first. You can use engaging techniques to replace the habit of disconnecting with the habit of connecting. You have to bring your attention to your surrounding again and again until the habit of disengaging fades away. So, being grounded feel like being present, knowing what your body is experiencing such a cold or sweaty, and what’s going on around such as if it’s day or night.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Is it a mental problem that I’m highly submissive to pretty much everyone? I do tend to hope others will give love in return but it often backfires and I get abused. But I find it hard or impossible to stop being what I am.
Answer: I really like your candor! I work hard with my clients that go through something similar to what you are describing in finding what percentage of the behavior comes from a survival strategy and what percentage comes from their authentic altruistic nature. It’s common in my industry to immediately look for pathology or to assume there is something defective in the person that avoids conflict and likes pleasing others. Since I have a strong background in contemplative psychotherapy, I have also witnessed that there are individuals with enough satisfaction who need less and get real joy by giving. Altruism is actually a natural tendency in humans. Altruism refers to selfless concern for the well-being of others, often involving acts of kindness, compassion, or helping behavior without expecting anything in return. Submissiveness could be rooted in this altruistic impulse in people that have reached internal peace. But being submissive can also denote a strong desire to be accepted and liked by those around and can be rooted in social/cultural norms that make it habitual to behave submissive to be recognized as valuable, or can be rooted in fear of rejection, low self-esteem, or in the need to avoid causing someone to be angry, punitive, aggressive, etc., if the person voice up their needs. So, the key is finding the reasons beneath the behavior and then make decisions on how to exercise them. Giving too much promotes abuse, and therefore, those that are extremely generous should learn to assess who they are giving to. Those that give expecting recirpocity should understand that playing weak is a ticket for abuse. Learning how to draw internal boundaries would become part of having better results in your interactions. You are saying that you are expecting love in return. If you learn to love yourself, your risk of being abused will decrease.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is the most common type of relationship for a borderline personality?
Answer: I have not yet discovered how aware individuals with Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) are of the characteristics they find "attractive" before entering a relationship. One thing is clear: these characteristics have little to do with what brings pleasure to many. Instead, they are more connected to how “useful” they are in satisfying the myriad of needs experienced on a daily basis. The drawing I’m using tries to depict the fact that they need many “partners” to fulfill their requirements because there is no one person that can give them what they crave and need. One important characteristic is related to their lack of a strong sense of self. Depending on where they fall on the scale, ranging from "no self" to "almost self," they will seek out relationships that can provide them with a sense of identity. For instance, they may be attracted to partners who possess well-defined identities and clear life goals. Additionally, they may gravitate towards individuals who are well-traveled if they themselves haven't had such experiences, or to those with a heightened sense of aesthetics, as they may struggle with understanding what is considered beautiful. In an attempt to establish a more cohesive sense of self and alleviate feelings of inadequacy, they may adopt their partner's interests, goals, or even mimic their personality traits. Another characteristic they look for is connected to their often intense and fluctuating emotions. They are often drawn to partners who are empathetic, understanding, and skilled at providing emotional support. Seeking relationships with kind, tolerant individuals who validate their emotions, offer reassurance, and provide a sense of security is common. An obvious one that may not be as obvious to them is looking for a partner who offers a strong emotional connection and a heightened sense of intimacy. Since they suffer from fear of abandonment and deep-seated insecurities, pwBPD often crave someone that can “take care of them” and offer something similar to what they missed in their parent (mother specially). But this is tricky because they think they crave emotional bonds and closeness in their relationships but as soon as they get too close, they get scared. Another common characteristic they find not only attractive but necessary is a high sexual drive. Many people with BPD view sex as grounding and regulating, and they often seek partners who can meet their demands for a fulfilling sexual connection. These are some of the important characteristics, but there may be others depending on their specific interests and needs. Ultimately, those who can satisfy their immediate needs are the ones with a higher chance of being chosen. So, in short, the answer is a utilitarian relationship, or in other words, a relationship that serves a practical purpose. So, the short answer is: A UTILITARIAN RELATIONSHIP or in other words, a useful one.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How can you tell if you have a personality disorder if you don't remember your childhood or have any memories of childhood trauma?
Answer: A personality disorder is evident!! The way to notice is about how you behave and how you react in certain situations or if you act in what could be considered socially appropriate manner that creates dysfunction to you and others.. For example, to assess for personality disorders you should notice how you interpret events and perceiving others, how stable or unstable are your emotions and your emotional reactions, and how well or bad you are able to regulate your emotions or don’t, and therefore whether you become aggressive, violent, or shutdown and isolated, and if you practice self-destructive behaviors accompanied with difficulty following rules and regulations. Also, you should notice whether or not you struggle with maintaining healthy relationships, have difficulties with intimacy, trust, empathy, or have a pattern of unstable or turbulent relationships. You need to include how often you have extreme behaviors, how impulsive you behave and how impulsive and destructive those behaviors are, such as excessive spending, substance abuse, reckless driving, self-harm, or engaging in risky sexual activities. Additionally, you need to assess if you have an unstable or distorted self-image, whether you have no clue who you are, and if you struggle with low self-esteem, self-doubt, or an exaggerated sense of self-importance. Some personality disorders are characterized also by experiencing a persistent sense of emptiness or a feeling of being disconnected from oneself or others, and fearing loneliness as death itself. Personality disorders even if based (sometimes) in adversity experienced in childhood, take years to develop because the personality takes years to develop as well. When the individual has to adapt to their circumstances by modeling their personality according to those around, it doesn’t seem to be related to traumatic events but a disorder/unpredictable/disorienting environment instead. You don’t need to remember your childhood to know if you have a so called ‘personality disorder’ or as many call them “personality adaptations”. What you need to do is notice how your behavior affects others and whether it makes your life difficult because you have problems relating, regulating, and engaging in a healthy way internally and/or externally.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can people with post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) have children? If they can, can they be good parents to their kids?
Answer: You may be asking this question because you know someone with a severe presentation of PTSD, but I would say that they are the exception rather than the rule. Additionally, are you asking if having children for PTSD people is a biological impediment or if it is merely a permission granted to them? There is no biological impediment, that's for sure! Traumatization doesn’t cause infertility. My immediate response to your question is: "Of course, they can have children!" Not only that, but they can be great parents! However, I may be referring to individuals who are already working on their healing process and have not experienced severe and prolonged exposure to traumatic circumstances. In general, I would say that PTSD alone, resulting from a 'single' event, is not a disabling disorder. However, when we consider "war" as a single event and PTSD as a diagnosis for veterans, it becomes very difficult to assess and predict outcomes. There is an evident problem with the criteria for diagnosing PTSD. As it appears in the DSM, the symptoms can range widely in severity, and there is even an argument that it includes complex trauma. This ambiguity and lack of specificity make it challenging to determine how incapacitating PTSD can be. I have argued here on Quora, as well as in other places, that war survivors need a distinct diagnosis because it is unfair to put them in the same category as someone who had a car accident or was bitten by a dog. It is also unfair to therapists who often have insufficient understanding of the phenomenon and are asked to use an "evidence-based" approach (if any) to treat PTSD without considering the wide spectrum of manifestations that individuals exposed to the horrors of war can experience, or the repercussions on the entire system of someone who has been exposed to prolonged or severe traumatization. If we exclude veterans and assume that PTSD is a diagnosis for single traumatic events, we could say that PTSD makes life more challenging but does not disconnect the person from their positive qualities and doesn’t make anyone infertile. One aspect missing from the descriptions of PTSD is that it often dissipates naturally within a short period, even without therapy. It has recently been portrayed as a terrible mental illness that never goes away, but that is not accurate. Our bodies have a natural capacity to heal and tend to move towards healing unless there is something that impedes it. My book delves into explaining what can halt the natural healing process and how to remove those obstacles. So, while parenting with PTSD can present unique challenges, it does not automatically disqualify someone from being a loving, caring, and effective parent. With the right support, coping strategies, and treatment, individuals with PTSD can provide a safe and nurturing environment for their children. I believe they can be great parents because they understand what it means to feel unsafe and will strive to create a sense of safety for their children. In the case of complex trauma, it would be more challenging because the biological dysregulation of the parent can negatively impact the children’s development. Additionally, if the parent's behavior reflects the consequences of traumatization, the children would not only be affected but also learn that behavior. Therefore, the answer is yes and no, because it depends on the severity of the PTSD, the environment, the individual's awareness, the support network, and many other factors.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: After a few tough sessions of discussing my trauma in therapy, I slipped and started abusing pain pills again. Do I tell my therapist? Its been years since ive used and I dont want him to be disappointed in me.
Answer: I’m very sorry about your relapse! I know that setbacks can be discouraging, but relapses don't define your journey. I hope you go back to healthy habits soon. In terms of your question on whether you should tell your therapist, here are my 2 cents: Please remember that your therapist is there to support you! That’s why you hired him. In a way, your therapist is your employee, and his job is to help you with whatever you need to achieve a healthier life and overcoming the difficulties. You are not there to take care of his feelings. He should be able to take it! Being open and honest about your struggles is a crucial part of the therapeutic process. Being afraid of your therapist’s reaction is counterproductive and absurd. Your therapist should be 100% supportive and is trained to understand your struggles. If you can’t trust him because you have already experienced judgement and disappointing him, then you should not be with that therapist. Disappointment is the negative emotion we feel when an outcome doesn't match up to our expectations. A therapist should “meet you where you are at” is the motto of almost everyone in the mental health business. But if your fears are not because you know your therapist reaction will be bad, then you should use your therapy time to continue working on your growth. Your therapist will probably be concerned about you and will want to reconsider treatment to help you further. Yes, therapists sometimes have emotional reactions, but we know how to deal with them to avoid hurting the client or influencing treatment. Your therapist will understand that you slipped up. Almost every therapist know that recovery is not always linear, and that there will be setbacks along the way. Your therapist may even wonder whether discussing your trauma was activating and overwhelming to the extreme of pushing you to escape mentally with medication. Therefore, I’m pretty sure he won’t push you any further to process the traumatic memories because you are not ready for that. I’m not necessarily saying that discussing trauma is what caused you to take pills again, but it’s necessary to contemplate the possibility the 2 events are related.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: From a psychotherapist’s perspective, what happens to the emotional intimacy that was once present when the therapeutic relationship with a client ends? Where does it go? How do they think about it?
Answer: Amy had been with a therapist for several years when she got married and moved upstate. She announced her therapist that she had to end their work because her new town was 90 minutes away. Guess what the therapist did. She drove every week to the client’s town to have their session. And she didn’t even charged extra!!! That vignette shows an example of a therapist that became “too intimate” and was not able to let go of the emotional intimacy. As you can see, the idea of “emotional intimacy” brings noise into my system. It could be very confusing for clients and therapists to assume that therapy to be successful needs emotional intimacy if there is no agreement on what that means. Emotional intimacy, by definition, assumes deep and profound connection. It involves a sense of closeness, trust, vulnerability, and the ability to share one's authentic thoughts, feelings, and experiences with another person. Emotional intimacy goes beyond surface-level interactions and involves a mutual understanding and acceptance of each other's emotions. This last part is what bothers me. This type of picture depicts emotional intimacy. You don’t see this image in therapy. Why? Because there is very little “mutual” in therapy. Clients hardly understand or accept the therapist’s emotions because therapists don’t (and shouldn’t) share their emotions openly. They only share them when they consider could be beneficial for the client to know them, but it’s very measured as opposed to open. If the therapist is too invested emotionally, they will stop being objective, and they will suffer after the client ends. And they will have expectations about mutuality that may be detrimental for the client, because then the client may feel like “taking care” of the therapist. Terrible idea! Actually, one of the most common legal problems therapists get into relate to sexual intimacy. The relationship between client and therapist becomes “so close” than the boundaries get blurry and they feel attracted to the other, ending in a deeper intimacy. Not a good idea! So, what I’m saying is that even when the client feels emotionally close to the therapist, the therapist should know the internal boundaries they need to draw within themselves to keep certain distance and not get too intimate. If they do, then they will not be ok after the client ends. A good therapist know that after the work ends (no matter the reason), they will have great memories and good feelings connected to the past clients without getting emotionally hurt by the rupture. A well trained therapist knows that “letting go” is necessary to avoid burnout or damaging the client. Creating dependency is a mistake and a hindrance. The therapist profession is a hard one! Our “reward” is to observe how the client becomes stronger, more mature, and more independent while working together, but knowing that we won’t necessarily witness the fruits of it afterwards.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can over-apologizing be a sign of trauma?
Answer: I had a dentist who consistently said 'I'm sorry' as she worked on my mouth. We became friends, and during one lunch, I asked her why she was so apologetic. She explained that her cultural values emphasized excessive politeness and frequent apologies as a way to show respect. As you can appreciate, over-apologizing for her was not a sign of being traumatized but a way to follow her cultural values. We should avoid assuming that someone is traumatized based on a single characteristic. Nowadays, it seems like everything and everyone is labeled as "trauma," which can diminish the seriousness of genuine traumatic experiences. Developing resilience requires us to refrain from becoming easily hurt by everything and to avoid assuming that our behavior indicates deep-seated damage. In any case, it is indeed possible that over-apologizing could be a manifestation of insecurity. Traumatization often leads individuals to feel insecure about various aspects of their lives, which can manifest in behaviors such as excessive apologizing. Mainly, a prolonged or recurrent experience of traumatic stress can profoundly impact one's sense of self-worth, leading to heightened feelings of insecurity and a tendency to believe that one does everything wrong. In that case, to apologize excessively would be a consequence of feeling defective. But over-apologizing can also be a sign of perfectionism, communication style, fear of judgement, a habit, or as in my dentist, a sign of respect and consideration.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How can someone seek therapy anonymously? I'm concerned about the possibility of having a mental disorder on my medical/insurance records and not willing to seek help if there's the risk of future reprisal.
Answer: I know you are not alone fearing this. Many people think that if they get a diagnosis, everyone is going to find out. I can assure you that almost anyone would know, specially those that could use it to hurt you. Still, there are ways to minimize your risks. Let me give you options: What can be good for you to know is that therapists are bound by legal and ethical obligations to maintain client confidentiality. They are typically required to keep your personal information and therapy content confidential (unless there is an immediate risk of harm to yourself or others, or as otherwise mandated by law). In general, nobody, including your therapist and the insurance companies, are not permitted to share your mental health or medical information with almost anyone (including your employer or your mother) without your explicit consent. Almost every country has legal protections in place to safeguard the privacy and confidentiality of health information; in the USA, there is the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) that protects you from staying as anonymous as possible to avoid what you are fearing. HIPAA restricts the disclosure of individually identifiable health information by healthcare providers and insurance companies, and it includes provisions to protect sensitive mental health information. These regulations generally prevent insurance companies from sharing information about a client's diagnosis, treatment, or therapy sessions without the client's authorization. To make sure your personal stuff stays private, it's a good idea to check out your insurance company's privacy policies, talk to them about any worries you have regarding anyone getting hold of your info, and make it clear to your therapist what you want to keep confidential. Doing this will help you know exactly who can see your information and make sure your privacy is protected as much as possible.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Does trauma, abuse, or neglect experienced between the ages of 2 and 5 negatively affect a child's ability to develop empathy?
Answer: Empathy development begins in early childhood, and experiences during this critical period can significantly impact its development. It involves the interaction of various factors such as genetics, early experiences, socialization, and cognitive and emotional development. For example, during the preschool years (2–5), children begin to develop a rudimentary understanding of the mental and emotional states of others. This is known as "Theory of Mind." They start recognizing that others have different thoughts, feelings, and perspectives than their own. This understanding forms the basis for empathy as they begin to realize that others can experience joy, sadness, or pain. You may have read that many individuals who suffer from a personality disorder lack "mentalization." The thing is, if a person doesn't have the chance to develop a sense of self, they can’t understand others. When a child suffers from neglect, abuse, or traumatic stress, their system is too busy trying to regulate and survive. The neglected child is trying to learn to do everything on their own or get shut down. The abused child is learning how to defend themselves, while the extremely stressed child is trying to adjust to the circumstances. In any case, their brain doesn't have the mental space to be too interested in how others feel except for the caregiver or the person they depend on. We can also find an explanation in the Polyvagal Theory (PVT). It provides insights into the physiological mechanisms underlying social engagement and the ability to read and respond to others. The theory, developed by Dr. Stephen Porges, explores the role of the autonomic nervous system in shaping our social interactions and emotional experiences. The PVT theory introduces the concept of the Social Engagement System (SES). The SES promotes social interaction, communication, and empathy by enabling us to read and respond to the social cues and emotional states of others. It allows for facial expression recognition, vocal prosody perception, and nonverbal communication interpretation, which are crucial for empathetic understanding. As you can see in the picture, social engagement starts very early. The PVT theory suggests that individuals who have a well-regulated and flexible autonomic nervous system are more likely to engage in social interactions and demonstrate empathy. On the other hand, individuals with autonomic dysregulation, such as those with a history of traumatization, abuse, or neglect, may have difficulties with social engagement and empathic responses. Is it possible that a child who has suffered from adversity develops empathy? Yes, there are people who manage their stress well, find someone else they can model after, or catch up later in life. As always, it all depends on the severity of the adversity, the frequency, and the inner capacities of the child to adapt.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: If someone has been diagnosed with both depression and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), is it normal for them to feel like they only have depression?
Answer: I would go deeper first into investigating what you are calling depression. Many people think they are depressed when they experience sadness, hopelessness, and worthlessness. Most of the times, those feelings are in the range of “normal” and expected after certain circumstances. Our system needs some time to recover when we have experiences something that caused us to lose motivation. If someone is “diagnosed” with depression, that means that the person meets criteria for Major Depressive Disorder. To give the diagnosis, the individual must be experiencing five or more symptoms during the same 2-week period and at least one of the symptoms should be either (1) depressed mood or (2) loss of interest or pleasure. To receive a diagnosis of depression, these symptoms must cause the individual clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. Notice criterion 3: weight loss or gain without changing the diet. When people are clinically depressed, their system is consuming larger amounts of energy because it’s operating differently from what’s common for that person, and therefore, there are fluctuations in their metabolism and other physiological functions. The same applies to criterion 4. Fatigue is not only perceptual but also physiological because the body's energy is utilized differently, impacting brain functioning and slowing down certain circuits. This results in difficulties with concentration and decision-making. This type of depression is similar (or almost exact) to some presentations of PTSD or C-PTSD (the hypo-active or down-regulated). Some other presentations are more sympathetic driven (hyper-active), which means they are feisty, combative, energetic, and active people. Both can be due to nervous system dysregulation. If the person you are mentioning has experienced traumatic events or circumstances, I’d put much more emphasis on the PTSD than the depression. If you only treat the depression as mood, you may not help that person to find the balance that their entire system lost. Yes, it’s normal that they feel only depressed and not necessarily traumatized, but the depression may be the type of strategy that the person’s system chose for survival.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can I get somebody to simplify or dumb down the difference between PTSD and CPTSD?
Answer: PTSD develops after experiencing a single event that is perceived as jeopardizing the person's life or integrity, and after overwhelming their system to the point of feeling helpless and defeated. C-PTSD develops after prolonged or frequent exposure to traumatic circumstances that keep the system in a state of fearing the loss of life, integrity, and/or the integrity of the family and their stability. In the picture, I have a single cut as a representation of a single event that causes a wound, whereas the second picture shows a wound that may have developed after constant abrasion of the skin. I am using pictures of wounds that do not leave a significant scar or jeopardize the person just to illustrate the difference between the two of them. However, it is important to note that PTSD or C-PTSD develop after severe emotional injuries.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: How might a mother with histrionic personality disorder impact her children?
Answer: We often talk about the harm inflicted by narcissistic mothers, but we tend to forget the terrible impact on children of mothers with HPD. Their children are deeply affected at the core of their being in a long-lasting and debilitating way. I even think that many people that talk about narcissistic abuse are really talking about histrionic mothers. First and foremost, children of HPD mothers are never allowed to know their value because daring to find out would put them in danger. Histrionic mothers do not allow their children to shine more than them. A narcissistic mother will appropriate the child's success and use it to shine herself, while a histrionic mother will try to prevent the child's success from happening to avoid overshadowing her own. Due to the attention-seeking nature of HPD, a mother with this disorder prioritizes her own needs and desires over her children's well-being and sense of identity. She often competes with her children, lacks interest in understanding them, and struggles to provide consistent and reliable care. This leads to inconsistency in discipline, boundaries, routines, and the development of a sense of self-worth. A histrionic mother heavily relies on her children for emotional support and validation, blurring the lines between the parent-child relationship. This enmeshment inhibits the children's independence and autonomy, hinders the development of agency, and makes it challenging for them to establish their own identities. A mother with HPD may employ manipulation to gain attention and validation in the form of guilt, tantrums, or exaggerated displays of emotion to control her children into meeting her needs. This creates a skewed dynamic where the children feel responsible for their mother's emotional well-being and misery, resulting in neglect of their own needs and the development of codependency. In addition to that, the rapid shifting emotions of a person with HPD create an unpredictable and unstable environment for the children. They struggle to understand and cope with their mother's emotional highs and lows, leading to confusion, anxiety, and doubt about their own efficacy and role. In many cases, the children of a mother with HPD learn through observation and often emulate their parents' behaviors. A mother with HPD who engages in attention-seeking and dramatic behaviors teaches her children to seek attention in similar ways. This becomes the "language" the children adopt, which impacts their relationships and overall functioning until they recognize and work to eliminate these patterns. Note that learned behavior does not necessarily mean that the children will develop HPD themselves, but many do. Others may develop BPD when the histrionic mother's symptoms are severe and she is unable to bond with the child. This is particularly true for daughters. There are theories that connect HPD with strong fathers whom infant girls try to "attract," leading to the development of seductive skills. Sex is a big issue in their lives and create confusion in their children. Histrionic mothers often prefer male children and compete with female children. As a result, BPD may be the outcome for female children of a histrionic mom. As you can see, the impact on their children can have long-lasting consequences. Of course, there are resilient and fortunate children who are able to develop relatively well, with only some lingering traits that may be resolved through seeking professional help or seeking other adults who can model more healthy behavior. In those cases, the children often adopt opposite behaviors to those of their histrionic mother, becoming shy, humble, nice, maybe pleasers, and avoiding getting too much attention.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why do I have attachment/abandonment issues? I don't recall having any problems in my childhood.
Answer: Let me start with your second question about recalling memories from childhood. We don’t remember most of our early years. No one does. When we are born, the hippocampus, a region of the brain critical for memory formation, is particularly immature during infancy and therefore, forming and storing memories is basically impaired the first 3 years of our lives. Also, memories are often tied to a sense of self and personal experiences and since infants are still developing a sense of self, their memories may not be anchored to a coherent sense of identity, making them more difficult to recall later in life. Now, let me move into attachment issues and feeling of abandonment. They develop at the very beginning of our lives, within the first year. This period is called “preverbal;” explicit or conscious memory of events during the preverbal phase is basically absent. That’s why we don’t remember anything about that first year. The main reason we develop feelings of abandonment is because of the entire dependency on our caregivers for survival and emotional well-being. Any disruption in consistent caregiving, such as neglect, absence, or inconsistent responsiveness, can create feelings of abandonment and insecurity from the moment we are born. Even when children may experience feelings of abandonment if they perceive a significant loss or separation from their primary caregivers, such as parental divorce, the death of a loved one, or placement in foster care, the impact on the nervous system is not as severe as when it happens the first year of life. So, that you don’t recall something that affected the way you bonded with your mother is not unusual. It’s actually expected. Also, you should try to investigate whether your “attachment/abandonment issues” are serious or just the regular struggle we all experience in romantic relationships. Even the use of the word “abandonment” could carry a significance that can affect the perception of your experiences. Nobody likes to be “left” and we all fear loneliness. We are mammals and therefore, we need to belong to a tribe to feel ‘whole’. We could say that most people have attachment/abandonment issues. The question is Are they an impairment? Do you become dysfunctional if you feel that someone could “abandon” you when they leave the house or take long to respond your texts? Has it been impossible for you to maintain a ‘stable’ relationship? Only then, you should think of yourself as having “issues.” Otherwise, keep living and doing the best you can. Relationships are challenging for everyone.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is the difference between seeing a therapist and seeing an LCSW for therapy? What are the benefits of seeing someone who holds that license over just having their master’s in social work (MSW)?
Answer: Therapists come from many different professions: social workers, psychologists, psychiatrists, marriage and family therapists, and mental health counselors. They all (except psychiatrists) need to get a license to become authorized to do therapy. Social workers need 2 licenses: first they need to be licensed as social workers and then they need to become licenced as clinical social workers. It takes to a MSW more than 6 years of continuous supervised clinical work to become an LCSW. Some other professions may take less time to get a clinical license, but they all need one after being supervised doing one-on-one work with clients. MSW can’t give therapy, not even supervised. To give therapy, social workers need at least to be LMSW and work in a supervised environment. A LMSW can’t give therapy in a particular setting. That’s forbidden by the state they practice and by the The National Association of Social Workers (NASW) code of ethics. So, to avoid headaches, look for someone that has a clinical license or is supervised.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What are the signs that your therapist is re-traumatizing you?
Answer: Part of trauma treatment is to process traumatic memories. Many clinicians still think that it’s the main purpose but it’s become clear that nervous system dysregulation is at the bottom of the problem of traumatized individuals. The fact that traumatic memories are disturbing is just a manifestation of that dysregulation but many clinicians don’t understand the neurobiology of it. A premise of most trauma modalities is that the emotions associated to the traumatic memory need to be ‘activated’ in order to have access to the memory and ‘process’ it. Clinicians with no understanding of the neurobiology of trauma train in those modalities, or read about them, or take short webinars about it, and then apply the concepts to their clients. So, when they activate the emotions and the traumatic memories, they “wake up the best.” The person’s survival circuits become more active, assuming that the person is at the same level of risk they previously were. and the person’s nervous system becomes more dysregulated. The traumatization process gets ignited again and the person’s symptoms worsen. Here are some signs that your therapist may be re-traumatizing you: I explain this issue in depth in my book Traumatization and Its Aftermath (Routledge, 2023) and the ways to avoid this to happen to you.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Why do people choose to wear their trauma like a badge?
Answer: Different people may have different reasons. Prince Harry, for example, may have a different reason to expose his trauma than Lady Gaga. Traumatic experiences have the capacity to modify many aspects of the person including their identity by shaping their beliefs, values, and worldview. After experiencing a traumatic event, and especially when their are alterations in the system of the person, they may develop negative beliefs about themselves, such as feeling unworthy, damaged, or broken. Traumatization can erode self-esteem and lead to feelings of shame, guilt, or self-blame. This distorted self-perception can impact various aspects of their identity, including their self-confidence, self-image, and self-worth. Identity is an important reason why people may “wear their trauma as a badge.” They over identify themselves with what happened to them and project that identity to others. They may feel the need for validation, empathy, understanding, and connection because they may feel disoriented about who they are now and who they will be in the future. Remember that traumatization keeps people stuck in the past and the present/future stop making sense and relevance. All the focus goes to the traumatic event as a reference point of how the world or people can be dangerous. There is also the case where people use their traumatic experiences or circumstances to get sympathy or some sort of gain. They may even develop entitlement justified by their pain. Some traumatized people might feel helpless but many other people that experience traumatic events may not even get traumatized and still use the ‘trauma” as a way to manipulate the circumstances in their favor. They may present themselves as wounded to garner attention, support, and benefits. It could be a way for them to feel a sense of control or protection, avoid taking responsibility for their actions, or get special treatment. We really can’t know people’s motives. Many people would assume that Prince Harry talks about his trauma to get sympathy and understanding while others are certain he is using it to get notoriety. Lady Gaga came out about hers to bring awareness of the frequency or rape but who knows what’s to be in her head and experiences! Don’t you think?

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: What is the difference between surrender and acceptance?
Answer: Let me start with an example: a person in an abusive relationship may surrender to the abuser by dissociating from the pain caused by the abuse, while a person in an abusive relationship that finds acceptance would probably leave the relationship. In general, the difference is subtle but an important one. Surrender puts more emphasis in the act of letting go and yielding to the circumstances while acceptance is more connected to acknowledging and embracing the reality of a situation after processing the emotional reactions that normally keeps people stuck in resistance and judgement. Surrender may happen as a way to renounce not only to the fight, but to the possibility of getting what you want. Acceptance instead, gives more comfort to the person that is letting go because it normally implies that the person finds solace somehow and therefore, may not feel defeated. Acceptance does not necessarily imply approval or agreement, but rather a willingness to face and work with what is present. Since you question is so general, I’d add that surrender is a concept of great significance in several spiritual philosophies and practices. Some religions for example ask for surrender as a way to show full trust in a higher power, whether it is referred to as God, the Universe, Divine, or a transcendent reality. Other spiritual philosophies see surrender as a way to control the ego, desires, attachments, and the illusion of power. In Buddhism, surrender is viewed as a transformative process in spiritual paths and is part of the regular practices. Acceptance, even when is mentioned in spirituality, plays a more important role in the health world including psychological health. Acceptance is healing while surrender may not.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Do children see traumatic events as traumatic?
Answer: Before I respond, let me share that I just attended an international conference on consciousness that is super relevant to this question. On the evening of the 2nd day, a rapper scientist (Baba Brinkman) delivered an outstanding performance centered around his son, Dylan, and the questions surrounding Dylan's level of consciousness. Here it is for you to enjoy too: The topic of consciousness in infants was brought up as the ongoing research and debate among scientists and philosophers to determine the nature and level of consciousness in babies. It was mentioned there is evidence to suggest that infants possess some level of consciousness, different from that of adults. However, tit seems clear that infants don’t have awareness of concepts they have not yet acquired, such as "traumatic." In the early stages of infancy, before acquiring specific information, their consciousness and awareness are more focused on basic sensory experiences and immediate perceptual information. What children "see" is not as important in terms of traumatization as what they "feel." When their brain anticipates danger perceptually, their response is fear, and fear or extreme stress can activate their survival circuits. The fear must be intense enough for the brain to perceive the baby's life as being in jeopardy to be activated as traumatic. In cases of intense fear, their system will activate protections and defenses that could traumatize their system, especially if the perception of danger is recurrent, prolonged, or permanent. That is why the topic of resilience is often mentioned when discussing traumatization and children. A resilient child, or an infant with the natural ability to tolerate, adapt, and bounce back from challenging or adverse experiences, or one who does not experience intense fear, does not suffer the consequences as severely or at all. This resilience may even be connected to the level of emotional regulation of the mother during pregnancy and of the caregiver at birth. When the infant lives in a calm and harmonious environment, they will not experience the same level of fear or perceive events as dangerous as an infant living in a chaotic environment, and therefore, they won’t not suffer the effects of trauma. In summary, infants do not "understand" or "see" events as traumatic. They may experience events as traumatic when their nervous system cannot tolerate the level of stress they are under.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Can tapping with EFT be used as a standalone treatment or is it typically combined with other therapeutic approaches?
Answer: When I give my clients instructions on how to use EFT effectively, I always clarify that EFT is similar to an aspirin. It won’t heal the illness but it will help ameliorate the symptoms. If we that analogy, when you experience certain symptoms, you may need an aspirin and maybe a hot tea, or to use some cream in the area where there is pain, or maybe the aspirin is enough if what you have is just a headache. In the same way, EFT could be enough to help you shifting away from a bad feeling after an argument, but may be insufficient to deal with procrastination. You may use it, but you may also need to use others interventions to feel better or to better manage your symptoms. EFT is normally used as one of many “tools” that therapists have in their toolbox. A therapist with EFT as a main tool and not many others may be missing the reality that our minds are really complicated.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Does a narcissist get his karma? Do his terrible actions ever catch up with him?
Answer: Definitely! I may even dare to say that developing NPD is already enough bad karma to carry. We see people with Narcissistic Personality Disorder (NPD) and imagine that they have everything they want (or almost), but they don't. They suffer internally in ways you may not imagine. They carry their own hell inside them all the time in the form of guilt, shame, self-hatred, self-doubt, ambition, disatisfaction, etc., etc., etc. That's probably why they hurt so much; we could say that their energy is radioactive. They are like a bomb that could explode and disintegrate at any moment, but in the meantime, they are decaying and emanating pain to others. Being a full-blown narcissist is definitely not fun. I have seen them breaking, and I have heard their secrets. They live very tormented. Since you are using the word karma, let's incorporate another concept from Eastern traditions: the realm of the hungry ghosts (from Buddhist and Taoist traditions). It is explained as a realm where beings are believed to experience intense cravings, insatiable desires, perpetual need, and a constant state of dissatisfaction. They are seen as driven by greed, attachment, and addictive behaviors, trapped in a perpetual cycle of unfulfillment. If you view narcissists from this perspective and apply it to the experience of living with NPD, you may perceive that the constant search for admiration, success, possessions, and power speaks to that hunger. Their lack of empathy is more a penance than a choice; they know that not having the capacity to understanding how others feel is a handicap and they hate being defective. Still, according to the laws of karma, negative karma fades away as we accumulate merit, make good deed, and set our intentions correct. Karma is not solely determined by the action itself but also by the intention behind it. Karma is often seen as an opportunity for personal growth and spiritual evolution. It presents individuals with lessons and challenges that allow them to learn, grow, and develop as individuals. Suffering from NPD may be a karmic manifestation but it doesn’t mean it’ll last forever. Everybody has the opportunity to accumulate good karma and find equilibrium. A challenge that many people with NPD confront is related to the definitions of success in our westernized world for which success-seeking is seen as a positive trait, and success itself is considered a goal in life. That may stop them from seeing that real success lies in having internal peace and satisfaction, as opposed to having money in the bank and sexy partners. So, maybe you expect narcissists to lose their possessions or success as a sign that they "got their karma," but their achievements may actually be their baggage and bad karma because they keep them stuck in greed and dissatisfaction. I understand that what I'm saying may sound counterintuitive because Western philosophies have different parameters and goals, but we can't deny that suffering from a mental disorder is in no way a form of success. We may perceive the pwNPD as successful and see their success as appealing, but what we miss is the understanding of the cost of endlessly chasing that success and still falling short. To be real, let’s face that some narcissists never cease their harmful behavior and never experience apparent significant consequences. They may be so skilled at manipulating others, avoiding accountability, or deflecting blame that they may die without facing the consequences of the pain/hurt/damage they have inflicted. It may seem that their actions did not catch up with them in an obvious or immediate way, but remember that only they know how it feels to live in their minds, and I can assure you that the mind of a narcissist is not a peaceful place. They suffer every second and may never enjoy their pursuits or achievements.

Name: Antonieta Contreras
Question: Who hates being ignored more, a narcissist, borderline, or histrionic?
Answer: What a fun question! Let’s use real people scenarios and their use of social media to give you an idea of the differences on hoe each hates to be ignored: John suffers from NPD and obviously thrives when receiving attention and admiration. He shares his accomplishments on social media almost daily and expects immediate validation from his followers. One day, John posts an update about a recent promotion at work, but it went unnoticed, receiving no likes or comments. He felt ignored and unimportant which made him agitated him and destroyed his day. He did all sorts of passive-aggressive comments and shared more that day about his credentials to regain attention. That evening, he lashed out at his friends for not acknowledging his post. Sarah has BPD and therefore struggles with fear of abandonment. She has been in a romantic relationship for the last year and becomes highly anxious whenever her partner doesn't respond to her messages promptly. One day, her partner didn’t reply to her texts for several hours. Sarah's anxiety increased, and she was feeling ignored and therefore, abandoned. She bombarded her partner with messages, expressing her frustration. She even threatened them saying “you may not find me here tonight” as a way to regain their attention and reassurance but also feeling desperation for not knowing why they were not responding. As opposed to John, Sarah doesn’t even have a FB page. Her fear of rejection is so intense that she doesn’t dare to expose herself to it. Also, she lives in hyper alert and fears people knowing about her and choosing her as a possible target. Emily suffers from HPD (histrionic) and therefore seeks attention and validation unceasingly. She loves being the center of attention at social gatherings and becomes uncomfortable when someone else grabs the spotlight. One evening, Emily attended a party where a friend received a lot of praise for their recent achievements and also got a lot of compliments about their outfit. Feeling ignored and overshadowed, Emily became distressed. She started speaking louder, interrupting conversations, and making exaggerated gestures to regain attention. Eventually, she went to the extreme of climbing onto a table and belting out the song playing in the background. Compared to John and Sarah, Emily’s participation in social media is extensive including many videos of her, provocative photos, dramatic stories, hers ‘incredible’ adventures, and her striking personal experiences. As you can see, the 3 of them hate being ignored in different ways: NPD can't handle the idea of not being recognized in their grandiosity, BPD can't handle being ignored by the person they are emotionally dependent on at that moment, and HPD can't handle being ignored, period, and therefore they will do whatever it takes to be noticed.
